m: extremely unpleasant; deserving hatred or disgust
x: Cleaning the blocked drain was an odious job, but somebody had to do it before the guests arrived.
My manager handed me the odious task of telling the team that this year's bonuses had been cancelled.
Several historians found the author's attempt to excuse the massacre odious and demanded a public apology.
Many voters considered the candidate's remarks about refugees odious and said so loudly on social media.
She couldn't bear his odious habit of mocking waiters in front of everyone at dinner.
tc: Far from being charming, the landlord's treatment of his poorer tenants was frankly ______, and most of them moved out within a year.
'Far from being charming' and the tenants leaving signal a word meaning hateful or disgusting.
se: Most readers found the columnist's mockery of the flood victims ______ and cancelled their subscriptions.
repugnant
Both 'odious' and 'repugnant' mean deeply offensive, and both explain why readers cancelled.

m: having unlimited power; able to do anything
x: When you're five years old, your parents seem omnipotent, able to fix any toy and answer any question.
In that company the founder was practically omnipotent, and no decision was made without his approval.
Medieval theologians debated whether an omnipotent God could create a stone too heavy for Him to lift.
No government is omnipotent, as its failed attempt to control rice prices this year clearly showed.
She stopped treating her older brother as omnipotent once she realised he was just as confused about life as she was.
tc: The dictator wanted his people to believe he was ______, but the sudden uprising revealed how limited his power really was.
The contrast with 'how limited his power really was' shows the blank means having unlimited power.
se: The novel's villain is an apparently ______ ruler who controls every aspect of his subjects' lives.
almighty
Both 'omnipotent' and 'almighty' describe a ruler with unlimited power over everything.

m: knowing everything
x: Our local shopkeeper seemed omniscient; he knew about every wedding, quarrel and exam result before anyone else did.
Don't expect the IT department to be omniscient; give them the exact error message if you want help.
The novel is told by an omniscient narrator who reveals the secret thoughts of every character.
Some critics warn that companies collecting our data are becoming almost omniscient about our daily habits.
As a teenager I resented my mother's seemingly omniscient way of knowing exactly when I had skipped classes.
tc: Even the most experienced doctor is not ______; she must sometimes admit that she simply does not know what is causing a patient's symptoms.
Admitting she 'does not know' shows the blank means knowing everything.
se: Young children often assume their teachers are ______ and are shocked to discover that adults make mistakes too.
all-knowing
Both 'omniscient' and 'all-knowing' mean knowing everything, which contrasts with making mistakes.

m: happening at a convenient or especially suitable time
x: The rain stopped at the most opportune moment, just as we were leaving for the wedding.
Wait for an opportune time to ask for a raise, preferably after the project has been delivered successfully.
My supervisor said the conference was an opportune occasion to present our early research findings.
Coming just days before the election, the government's announcement was suspiciously opportune.
He found an opportune moment, when the others had left the room, to apologise to her quietly.
tc: Since the CEO was in an excellent mood after the record profits were announced, it seemed the most ______ moment to propose the new project.
The CEO's good mood after record profits signals a well-timed, convenient moment.
se: The investor's offer was ______, arriving just as the start-up was about to run out of cash.
timely
Both 'opportune' and 'timely' mean arriving at exactly the right moment.

m: the art or skill of formal, persuasive public speaking
x: Her oratory at the school prize-giving left many parents wiping away tears.
Lawyers in our firm are expected to master oratory as well as careful legal research.
This course examines the oratory of ancient Rome, from courtroom speeches to political addresses.
Fiery oratory alone cannot fix the economy, but it can certainly win an election.
My grandfather was famous in his village for his oratory, especially at weddings and funerals.
tc: Though his written arguments were dull, his ______ was so stirring that crowds hung on his every word.
The contrast with his dull writing and the stirred crowds point to skill in public speaking.
se: The candidate's ______ won over the audience, even though her actual policies were vague.
eloquence
Both 'oratory' and 'eloquence' refer to persuasive speaking that can win people over despite weak content.

m: to swing back and forth; to waver between two opinions, feelings or states
x: I oscillate between wanting to study abroad and wanting to stay near my family in Dhaka.
Our manager's mood oscillates between cheerful and furious, so we never know what to expect.
In the physics lab, we measured how quickly the pendulum oscillated after being released.
Share prices oscillated wildly all week as investors reacted to rumours of a merger.
Her feelings for him oscillated between affection and irritation throughout their long friendship.
tc: Unable to make up his mind, the committee chairman continued to ______ between the two proposals for weeks.
'Unable to make up his mind' signals moving back and forth between options.
se: Public opinion on the new tax tends to ______ depending on the latest headlines.
fluctuate
Both 'oscillate' and 'fluctuate' mean to move up and down or back and forth.

m: stated or appearing to be true, though not necessarily so
x: His ostensible reason for visiting was to return my book, but he really wanted to see my sister.
Budget planning was the ostensible purpose of the meeting, though everyone knew layoffs would be announced.
Officially, the study's ostensible aim was to test a new drug, but critics said it mainly served the sponsor's marketing.
Public safety is the ostensible goal of the law, yet opponents argue it targets peaceful protesters.
Her ostensible calm at the funeral hid a grief she shared only with her closest friends.
tc: The ______ purpose of the trip was to inspect the factory, but the executives spent most of their time on the golf course.
The 'but' shows the stated purpose differed from the real one, so the blank means apparent or professed.
se: The ______ reason for the minister's resignation was ill health, though few journalists believed it.
professed
Both 'ostensible' and 'professed' describe a stated reason that may not be the true one.

m: done or shown openly; not secret or hidden
x: There was no overt hostility at the family dinner, but the tension was obvious to everyone.
Overt discrimination in hiring is illegal, so some firms practise subtler forms of bias.
Researchers compared overt and hidden forms of cheating among university students.
Although the ministry made no overt threat, the newspaper understood the warning behind the letter.
He's not the type for overt displays of affection, though he always remembers my birthday.
tc: Unlike the covert operations of the past, the new campaign was entirely ______, with officials announcing every step on television.
The contrast with 'covert' and the public announcements show the blank means open.
se: The workers showed ______ hostility toward the new manager, refusing to attend any of his meetings.
open
Both 'overt' and 'open' describe hostility shown plainly rather than hidden.

m: to calm someone who is angry or upset; to restore peace
x: I gave the crying baby a bottle of warm milk, which pacified her within minutes.
Our manager tried to pacify the angry customer by offering a full refund and a free meal.
No amount of extra credit could pacify the students who felt the exam had been unfair.
Officials hoped the pay rise would pacify striking garment workers before the holiday season.
He bought her flowers to pacify her after forgetting their anniversary, but she wasn't impressed.
tc: Rather than inflaming the crowd further, the police chief spoke softly and tried to ______ the angry protesters.
'Rather than inflaming' signals the opposite action, so the blank means to calm.
se: The airline offered free hotel rooms to ______ passengers whose flights had been cancelled.
placate
Both 'pacify' and 'placate' mean to calm angry people, here with a concession.

m: done with great care and attention to detail
x: Restoring the old wooden chair took weeks of painstaking work, but it now looks brand new.
Our auditor's painstaking review of the accounts uncovered a small but serious error.
Her thesis is based on painstaking research in archives across three countries.
Detectives pieced together the timeline through painstaking analysis of hours of CCTV footage.
He wrote his wedding speech with painstaking care, rehearsing every line in front of the mirror.
tc: Far from being careless, the translator was ______, checking every word against three different dictionaries.
'Far from being careless' and checking every word signal great care.
se: Scientists spent years on the ______ task of mapping every neuron in the worm's brain.
meticulous
Both 'painstaking' and 'meticulous' describe work requiring extreme care and detail.

m: pleasant to taste; more broadly, acceptable or agreeable to someone
x: A squeeze of lime made the hospital soup slightly more palatable.
We tried to make the budget cuts more palatable to staff by promising there would be no job losses.
Our professor made statistics palatable to first-year students by using cricket scores as examples.
Neither option was palatable to voters, so the party delayed its decision until after the election.
She found his apology more palatable once he admitted he had been completely wrong.
tc: The original plan was so unpopular that the council revised it to make it more ______ to local residents.
The plan's unpopularity explains why it was revised to be more acceptable.
se: The compromise was ______ to both unions, so the strike ended the next day.
acceptable
Both 'palatable' and 'acceptable' mean agreeable enough for both sides to approve it.

m: so intense or obvious that it can almost be touched or felt
x: Excitement in the stadium was palpable as the final minutes of the match ticked away.
There was palpable relief in the office when the client finally signed the contract.
During her viva, her nervousness was palpable, but she answered every question well.
Fear in the village was palpable after the river burst its banks overnight.
From the moment the two sisters sat down together, the tension between them was palpable.
tc: Nobody said a word, but the hostility between the two rivals was so ______ that guests began leaving the party early.
Guests leaving even though nobody spoke shows the hostility was obvious and easily felt.
se: As the results were read out, the anticipation in the hall was ______.
tangible
Both 'palpable' and 'tangible' describe a feeling so strong it seems almost physical.

m: more important than anything else; supreme
x: When you're driving through heavy rain, safety is paramount, so slow down.
For our team, meeting the client's deadline is paramount, even if it means working this weekend.
In laboratory work, accuracy is of paramount importance, as one mistake can ruin months of data.
Officials insisted that public health remained paramount throughout the vaccination campaign.
For my parents, my education was always paramount, and they sacrificed a great deal for it.
tc: Although cost and speed matter, patient safety remains ______ in every decision the hospital makes.
'Although cost and speed matter' contrasts them with what matters most of all.
se: For the new principal, discipline was the ______ concern, outweighing everything else.
foremost
Both 'paramount' and 'foremost' mean most important, as 'outweighing everything else' confirms.

m: obvious and clear; easily recognised
x: His excuse that the dog ate his homework was a patent lie, and the teacher knew it.
Our report contained several patent errors that any careful reader should have spotted.
Within five minutes of the interview, the candidate's patent lack of preparation was clear to everyone.
Critics said the new bridge was a patent waste of money, since the old one carried very little traffic.
Her patent delight at seeing her old friend made everyone at the station smile.
tc: The witness's story was full of ______ contradictions, so obvious that even the jury laughed.
'So obvious' restates the meaning of the blank.
se: The minister's claim that prices had fallen was ______ nonsense, contradicted by every shopping receipt.
obvious
Both 'patent' and 'obvious' mean clearly false here, since every receipt contradicts the claim.

m: a quality in art, speech or a situation that arouses pity or sadness
x: That film's final scene, with the old man waiting alone at the bus stop, is full of pathos.
Our copywriter added a touch of pathos to the charity advert, showing a child studying by candlelight.
In our literature seminar, we discussed how the author uses pathos without becoming sentimental.
Reporters captured the pathos of families searching for missing relatives after the flood.
There was real pathos in his last letter, which apologised to the son he had not seen in years.
tc: The play mixes broad comedy with moments of deep ______, so audiences often leave both laughing and in tears.
'In tears', set against 'comedy', points to a quality that arouses sadness.
se: The novel's portrayal of the dying soldier is filled with ______ that moves many readers to tears.
poignancy
Both 'pathos' and 'poignancy' describe a quality that evokes sorrow and pity.

m: strange or unusual; also, belonging characteristically to one person, place or group
x: There's a peculiar smell coming from the fridge; I think the fish has gone off.
My new colleague has the peculiar habit of eating lunch standing up at his desk.
Researchers noticed something peculiar in the data: every result recorded on Mondays was unusually high.
Residents reported peculiar lights over the lake, which turned out to be a drone display.
It felt peculiar to walk through my childhood home after all the furniture had been taken away.
tc: Everyone else at the party wore casual clothes, so his tuxedo and top hat looked rather ______.
The contrast with everyone else's casual clothes shows his outfit looked odd.
se: Visitors found the silence of the old house ______, though none of them could explain exactly why it unsettled them.
strange
Both 'peculiar' and 'strange' mean oddly unusual in a way that unsettles people.

m: better than all others; having no equal
x: Everyone agrees that my aunt's mango pickle is peerless, and she refuses to share the recipe.
As a negotiator she is peerless, which is why the firm sends her to close its toughest deals.
Professor Rahman's peerless knowledge of medieval manuscripts attracted students from around the world.
Critics praised the orchestra's peerless performance of the symphony at last night's concert.
He was a peerless friend, always there when I needed him and never asking for anything back.
tc: Rivals tried for decades to match her skill at the piano, but her technique remained ______.
Rivals trying and failing to match her shows the blank means unequalled.
se: The museum's collection of Mughal miniatures is ______, with no other museum holding anything comparable.
unrivalled
Both 'peerless' and 'unrivalled' mean having no equal, as 'nothing comparable' confirms.

m: feeling or showing sorrow and regret for having done wrong
x: Our puppy looked penitent after chewing my shoes, but it did exactly the same thing the next day.
A penitent junior employee admitted to the manager that he had deleted the client files by mistake.
After plagiarising his essay, the student wrote a penitent letter to the examination board.
In court the former official appeared penitent, apologising to the families he had cheated.
She was genuinely penitent after shouting at her mother and spent the evening trying to make amends.
tc: Far from being defiant, the young offender was ______, weeping as he apologised to his victim.
'Far from being defiant' and his tearful apology signal sorrow for wrongdoing.
se: The boy seemed truly ______ after breaking the window and offered to pay for it from his savings.
contrite
Both 'penitent' and 'contrite' mean sincerely sorry for a wrong one has done.

m: deeply, often sadly, thoughtful
x: She sat by the window in a pensive mood, watching the monsoon rain flood the street below.
After the board meeting, our director looked pensive and spent the afternoon alone in his office.
Long walks across campus always put him in a pensive frame of mind before exams.
This photograph shows a pensive young soldier writing a letter home on the eve of battle.
My husband grows quiet and pensive whenever I mention his late father.
tc: Normally cheerful and talkative, Rafiq became quiet and ______ after hearing about his friend's illness, staring silently out of the window.
The contrast with 'cheerful and talkative' and his silent staring signal deep, sad thought.
se: The old man grew ______ as he looked through photographs of his youth.
reflective
Both 'pensive' and 'reflective' mean quietly absorbed in thought, here about the past.

m: of minor importance; not central; relating to the edge of something
x: I caught a movement in my peripheral vision and turned to see a cat on the wall.
Let's focus on the main budget question and leave peripheral issues for the next meeting.
Her thesis supervisor warned her that the chapter on trade policy was peripheral to her argument.
Small parties played only a peripheral role in the election, winning just a handful of seats.
He felt peripheral in his own family, as though decisions were always made without him.
tc: The lawyer urged the jury to ignore such ______ details and focus on the central question of whether the defendant was at the scene.
The contrast with 'the central question' shows the blank means of minor importance.
se: The scandal was ______ to the main story, so the editor cut it from the article.
tangential
Both 'peripheral' and 'tangential' mean only loosely connected to the main subject.

m: to spread throughout something completely
x: The smell of frying onions permeated the whole flat within minutes.
A culture of fear permeated the office after the new director fired three managers in a week.
In our experiment, water slowly permeated the soil samples at very different rates.
According to the report, corruption has permeated almost every level of local government.
A quiet sadness permeated her letters during the months after her divorce.
tc: Within an hour of the fire starting, smoke had begun to ______ every room in the building, even those with closed doors.
'Every room... even those with closed doors' shows the smoke spread throughout.
se: Religious imagery continues to ______ the poet's later work, appearing in almost every line.
pervade
Both 'permeate' and 'pervade' mean to spread through every part of something.

m: never ending or changing; occurring constantly or repeatedly
x: Our neighbour's perpetual complaints about parking have made him unpopular on the street.
Working in a perpetual state of urgency, the team has no time to think about long-term plans.
Physicists long ago showed that a perpetual motion machine is impossible.
Many city dwellers live with the perpetual noise of car horns and construction.
Their perpetual arguments about money eventually ended the marriage.
tc: Unlike the brief storms of spring, the noise from the construction site seemed ______, continuing day and night for months.
The contrast with 'brief' and 'day and night for months' signal something never-ending.
se: The villagers lived in ______ fear of the river, which flooded their homes almost every year.
constant
Both 'perpetual' and 'constant' describe a fear that never goes away.

m: to keep trying to do something despite difficulty or delay
x: Learning to swim was hard for me as an adult, but I persevered and can now swim a kilometre.
If you persevere with the new software for a few weeks, you'll find it saves a lot of time.
She failed the university admission test twice but persevered and finally got into engineering.
Researchers persevered for a decade before finding a vaccine that actually worked.
He persevered with the relationship even when his friends told him to walk away.
tc: Although the first few months brought nothing but losses, the founders decided to ______ rather than give up.
'Rather than give up' shows the blank means to keep going.
se: Despite repeated failures, the inventor continued to ______ until his machine finally worked.
persist
Both 'persevere' and 'persist' mean to keep trying in spite of failure.

m: relevant to the matter being considered
x: That's a pertinent question, and I'm glad you asked it before we booked the tickets.
Please include only pertinent information in the report; the board won't read twenty pages.
The examiner praised her for citing studies directly pertinent to her research question.
Journalists have asked pertinent questions about how the bridge contract was awarded.
My father's advice, though brief, was pertinent to every decision I made that year.
tc: The judge told the lawyer to stop wandering off the subject and confine himself to facts that were ______ to the case.
'Stop wandering off the subject' signals that the blank means relevant.
se: The interviewer asked several ______ questions about my previous projects.
relevant
Both 'pertinent' and 'relevant' mean directly connected to the matter at hand.

m: to read or examine something carefully and thoroughly
x: Before signing the lease, she perused every clause to make sure there were no hidden fees.
Our lawyer will peruse the contract carefully before we sign anything.
Graduate students must peruse dozens of journal articles before writing a literature review.
Reporters perused the leaked documents for hours, looking for evidence of fraud.
He perused her old letters slowly, lingering over every line she had written.
tc: Rather than merely skimming the report, the auditor took the time to ______ each page closely.
The contrast with 'merely skimming' shows the blank means to read carefully.
se: Investors should ______ the prospectus carefully before buying shares in the company.
examine
Both 'peruse' and 'examine' mean to read through something carefully.

m: deeply religious; sometimes, making a self-righteous show of virtue
x: My pious grandmother never missed her morning prayers, even when she was ill.
Being a pious man, our office manager never scheduled meetings during Friday prayers.
This historian studies how pious donors funded hospitals and schools in the medieval period.
Voters grew tired of the politician's pious speeches about honesty once the scandal broke.
She was raised in a pious family where every meal began with a prayer of thanks.
tc: Unlike his ______ brother, who prayed five times a day, Karim rarely thought about religion at all.
The brother who prays five times a day is contrasted with Karim's indifference to religion.
se: The village priest was a deeply ______ man who spent hours each day in prayer.
devout
Both 'pious' and 'devout' mean deeply committed to religion.

m: brief but full of meaning; concise and forceful
x: My mother always had a pithy saying ready for every situation, usually about saving money.
Keep your emails pithy; nobody in this office reads past the second paragraph.
Professor Ahmed's pithy comments on my draft were more useful than pages of feedback.
Easy to remember, the campaign's pithy slogan appeared on billboards across the country.
He summed up our failed relationship in one pithy sentence that still makes me laugh.
tc: Unlike the long, rambling speeches of his predecessors, the new chairman preferred ______ remarks that made their point in a sentence or two.
The contrast with 'long, rambling speeches' and 'a sentence or two' signal brief, meaningful remarks.
se: Readers loved the columnist's ______ style, which packed sharp ideas into short sentences.
succinct
Both 'pithy' and 'succinct' describe expression that is brief yet meaningful.

m: a very small or inadequate amount of money
x: He sold his old motorbike for a pittance because he needed the cash quickly.
Interns at the firm work long hours for a pittance, hoping to be offered a permanent job.
Research assistants are paid a pittance, though the experience helps their future applications.
Garment workers complain that they earn a pittance compared with the profits of the brands they supply.
She left a well-paid job to work for a pittance at a charity she truly believed in.
tc: Despite the company's record profits, the cleaners were still paid only the ______ they had earned ten years earlier.
The contrast with 'record profits' shows the cleaners' pay is a tiny amount.
se: For all their months of hard work, the farmers received a mere ______ for their crop.
trifle
Both 'pittance' and 'trifle' mean a tiny, inadequate amount of money.

m: a dangerous, difficult or unfortunate situation
x: We were in quite a plight when the car broke down on a dark road with no phone signal.
Our union representative raised the plight of contract workers at the annual staff meeting.
Her dissertation examines the plight of farmers displaced by riverbank erosion in Bangladesh.
International attention has finally turned to the plight of refugees stranded at the border.
My best friend listened sympathetically as I described my plight after losing my job.
tc: Hoping to raise money for shelters, the charity's advert drew attention to the ______ of children living on the streets.
Raising money for shelters for street children implies the blank means a difficult situation.
se: Journalists were moved by the ______ of the stranded fishermen, who had survived for days without food.
predicament
Both 'plight' and 'predicament' mean a dangerous or unfortunate situation.

m: to think about something carefully, especially before deciding
x: I pondered whether to take an umbrella, then decided the sky looked clear enough.
The board will ponder the proposal over the weekend and give its answer on Monday.
Philosophers have pondered the nature of consciousness for thousands of years.
Economists are still pondering why inflation fell so quickly last year.
She sat for hours pondering his marriage proposal before finally saying yes.
tc: Instead of answering immediately, the candidate paused to ______ the question carefully.
'Instead of answering immediately' signals taking time to think.
se: Before accepting the job abroad, he took a week to ______ the offer.
consider
Both 'ponder' and 'consider' mean to think carefully about something before deciding.

m: happening, awarded or published after a person's death
x: Van Gogh's posthumous fame would have astonished him, since he sold almost nothing while alive.
Our company dedicated its new laboratory as a posthumous honour to the engineer who founded it.
Her posthumous novel, found in a drawer after she died, became an international bestseller.
Decades after his wrongful execution, the soldier was granted a posthumous pardon.
Reading his letters, published posthumously, his daughter finally understood how much he had loved her.
tc: Although he died unknown and penniless, the painter eventually enjoyed enormous ______ fame.
Dying unknown yet later becoming famous shows the fame came after death.
se: The scientist's ______ reputation far exceeded anything he achieved while he was alive.
postmortem
Both 'posthumous' and 'postmortem' describe something arising after death, contrasted with 'while he was alive'.

m: having great power, influence or effect
x: This coffee is so potent that one cup keeps me awake until midnight.
Word of mouth remains a potent marketing tool, especially for small businesses.
Researchers found the new antibiotic far more potent than older drugs against resistant bacteria.
Social media has become a potent force in shaping public opinion during elections.
Her quiet disappointment was a more potent punishment than any angry words could have been.
tc: The new painkiller is so ______ that doctors prescribe it only in tiny doses.
Prescribing only tiny doses shows the drug is very strong.
se: Fear of unemployment remains a highly ______ motivator for many voters.
powerful
Both 'potent' and 'powerful' mean having a strong effect.

m: an introductory statement or preliminary part before the main point
x: Without any preamble, my sister announced that she was getting married next month.
After a short preamble about the company's history, the CEO got to the bad news.
Students must memorise the preamble to the constitution for their civics exam.
The preamble of the treaty sets out the shared goals of the signing nations.
He launched into a long preamble about his feelings before finally apologising.
tc: Skipping the usual ______, the lecturer began the class by plunging straight into the hardest equation.
'Plunging straight into' signals that the introduction was skipped.
se: The speaker's long ______ about his childhood bored the audience before he reached his main point.
introduction
Both 'preamble' and 'introduction' mean the opening part before the main point.

m: a general rule intended to guide behaviour or thought
x: My father lived by one simple precept: never borrow money from friends.
Honesty with clients is the first precept of our firm, and every new employee is trained in it.
This course examines the moral precepts of several ancient philosophical schools.
Many religions share the basic precept that we should treat others as we wish to be treated.
She tried to follow her grandmother's precept of never going to bed angry with her husband.
tc: The monk had always followed the ______ that one should speak only when silence cannot be improved upon.
The clause 'that one should speak only when...' states a rule guiding behaviour.
se: The central ______ of the school's philosophy is that every child can learn.
tenet
Both 'precept' and 'tenet' mean a guiding principle or belief.

m: a statement or idea assumed to be true and used as the basis for an argument
x: We planned the picnic on the premise that it wouldn't rain, which turned out to be a mistake.
Our whole business plan rests on the premise that customers will pay extra for faster delivery.
If the first premise of your argument is false, your conclusion cannot be trusted.
Critics say the policy is built on the flawed premise that poverty is caused by laziness.
Their marriage was based on the premise that neither would ever keep secrets from the other.
tc: Since the study's central ______ was false, all the conclusions drawn from it were worthless.
Conclusions being 'drawn from it' shows the blank is the assumption an argument rests on.
se: The economist's argument rests on the ______ that consumers always act rationally.
assumption
Both 'premise' and 'assumption' mean an idea taken as true on which an argument is built.

m: to suppose that something is true without having proof
x: I presume you'll want dinner after such a long flight.
Don't presume that the client has read your email; call her to confirm.
Under the law, a defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty.
Scientists had presumed the species was extinct until a farmer photographed one last year.
He presumed she would forgive him, but this time she packed her bags and left.
tc: Without any evidence that the missing hiker had died, the court was reluctant to ______ him dead.
'Without any evidence' signals supposing something without proof.
se: When nobody answered the phone, we could only ______ that the office had closed early.
assume
Both 'presume' and 'assume' mean to suppose something without proof.

m: trying to seem more important, intelligent or cultured than one really is
x: That restaurant was so pretentious that the menu described a fried egg as 'a sunlit ovum'.
His pretentious emails, full of jargon and Latin phrases, irritate everyone on the team.
The examiner called her essay pretentious, saying simple language would have been more convincing.
Critics dismissed the film as pretentious nonsense, though it won awards at several festivals.
I stopped seeing him because he was too pretentious to admit he enjoyed ordinary pop music.
tc: Unlike his ______ cousin, who name-drops famous authors at every dinner, Tanim is modest about his wide reading.
The contrast with 'modest' and the name-dropping show the cousin tries to seem more cultured than he is.
se: The novelist's ______ prose, crammed with obscure words, made the book almost unreadable.
affected
Both 'pretentious' and 'affected' describe writing that is showy and unnatural to impress readers.

m: widespread in a particular area or at a particular time
x: Dengue fever is especially prevalent in Dhaka during the monsoon season.
Burnout has become prevalent among junior doctors working long night shifts.
According to the survey, cheating was more prevalent in courses with online exams.
Misinformation is increasingly prevalent on social media, especially during elections.
Among my friends, the view that marriage can wait until thirty is very prevalent.
tc: Once rare, the disease has become so ______ that almost every family in the region knows someone affected.
The contrast with 'once rare' and 'almost every family' show the blank means widespread.
se: Such attitudes are still ______ in rural areas, where traditions change slowly.
widespread
Both 'prevalent' and 'widespread' mean common across a large area or group.

m: to keep delaying something that should be done, often out of laziness or reluctance
x: I always procrastinate when it comes to filing my taxes, then panic in the final week.
If you procrastinate on this report, the whole team will miss the client's deadline.
Many students procrastinate until the night before the exam and then study until dawn.
Researchers found that people procrastinate more when a task feels boring or unclear.
She procrastinated for months before finally calling her old friend to apologise.
tc: Instead of starting the assignment right away, he chose to ______, watching videos until the deadline was only hours away.
'Instead of starting... right away' and waiting until the deadline signal putting things off.
se: If you ______ any longer, you'll miss the application deadline.
delay
Both 'procrastinate' and 'delay' mean to put off action, risking the deadline.

m: showing disrespect for religion or sacred things; vulgar or obscene
x: My grandmother was shocked by the profane language in the film and walked out halfway.
Our manager warned staff that profane comments in the company chat would not be tolerated.
This art history course explores the line between sacred and profane subjects in Renaissance painting.
Protesters called the advertisement profane because it used a holy symbol to sell beer.
He apologised for his profane outburst after stubbing his toe in front of her parents.
tc: The priest was horrified by the tourists' ______ behaviour, which showed no respect for the sacred shrine.
'Showed no respect for the sacred shrine' defines the blank as disrespectful of holy things.
se: Many believers found the comedian's ______ jokes about the saints deeply offensive.
blasphemous
Both 'profane' and 'blasphemous' mean disrespectful toward sacred things.

m: a forecast of the likely course of a disease or situation
x: Our vet's prognosis was good, and the dog was running around again within a week.
Analysts gave a gloomy prognosis for the company's sales in the coming year.
This study compares the prognosis of patients who received early treatment with those who did not.
Economists offered a cautious prognosis for the garment industry after the new tariffs.
Hearing the doctor's prognosis, she held her father's hand and tried not to cry.
tc: Although the initial diagnosis was frightening, the doctors' ______ was hopeful: with treatment, she was likely to recover fully.
'Likely to recover fully' is a prediction of the illness's course.
se: The economists' ______ for the coming year is bleak, with growth expected to slow sharply.
outlook
Both 'prognosis' and 'outlook' mean a forecast of how things will develop.

m: important, well known or easily noticed
x: Put the fire extinguisher in a prominent place so everyone can find it quickly.
She quickly became a prominent figure in the firm, leading its biggest international deals.
Several prominent scientists signed a letter warning about the dangers of rising sea levels.
Most newspapers gave the story a prominent position on their front pages.
Her father, a prominent lawyer, hoped she would follow him into the profession.
tc: Once an obscure researcher, she became ______ after her discovery was reported in newspapers around the world.
The contrast with 'once an obscure researcher' shows the blank means well known.
se: The conference featured several ______ economists whose work is cited worldwide.
eminent
Both 'prominent' and 'eminent' mean famous and respected in a field.

m: to make an idea or belief widely known; to officially announce a law
x: My aunt loves to promulgate her theories about healthy eating at every family gathering.
Head office promulgated the new dress code in an email that nobody read carefully.
After several high-profile cases, the university promulgated stricter rules on plagiarism.
Unions protested when the government promulgated the new labour law without consulting them.
Through his letters, he tried to promulgate the ideas of tolerance he had learned from his mother.
tc: Instead of keeping the new regulations secret, the ministry decided to ______ them through newspapers and radio.
The contrast with 'keeping... secret' shows the blank means to make widely known.
se: The council plans to ______ the new rules on its website next week.
publicize
Both 'promulgate' and 'publicize' mean to make something publicly known.

m: likely to suffer from, do or experience something, usually something bad
x: I'm prone to headaches when I skip breakfast, so I always carry a snack.
Tired staff are more prone to making mistakes, especially late on Friday afternoons.
First-year students are prone to underestimating how much reading their courses require.
Coastal areas of Bangladesh are prone to cyclones, especially before and after the monsoon.
My brother is prone to jealousy, which has caused problems in his relationships.
tc: Because the old bridge had been poorly maintained for decades, engineers warned that it was ______ to collapse during heavy floods.
Decades of poor maintenance explain why the bridge is likely to collapse.
se: Elderly people are more ______ to falls, especially on wet floors.
susceptible
Both 'prone' and 'susceptible' mean likely to suffer something harmful.

m: to spread an idea or belief widely; also, to breed or grow new plants
x: My mother propagates her money plants by putting cuttings in glasses of water.
Some employees propagated rumours about layoffs, which caused panic across the company.
In the lab, we learned how sound waves propagate through different materials.
Fake news propagates rapidly on messaging apps, especially during a crisis.
He felt hurt that his own friends had helped propagate lies about him.
tc: Rather than correcting the false story, the website chose to ______ it further, sharing it with millions of readers.
'Sharing it with millions' shows the blank means to spread widely.
se: The group used leaflets and social media to ______ its extremist ideas.
disseminate
Both 'propagate' and 'disseminate' mean to spread ideas widely.

m: accurately describing or predicting what will happen in the future
x: My father's warning that the car would break down on the trip turned out to be prophetic.
Ignored at the time, the consultant's report proved prophetic when the company collapsed two years later.
Scholars now regard the novel as prophetic, since it imagined smartphones long before they existed.
Her prophetic articles about the housing bubble were dismissed until prices crashed.
Looking back, his joke that we would one day marry seems strangely prophetic.
tc: Her warning seemed alarmist when she made it, but it proved ______ when the dam failed exactly as she had predicted.
'Exactly as she had predicted' shows the warning correctly foretold the future.
se: The economist's ______ remarks about the crisis, made years earlier, earned him new respect.
prescient
Both 'prophetic' and 'prescient' mean correctly foreseeing future events.

m: the main character in a story; also, a leading figure or supporter of a cause
x: In my favourite childhood book, the protagonist is a young girl who runs away to join the circus.
She was a key protagonist in the merger talks, working late into the night for months.
For the assignment, each student had to analyse the protagonist's motives in the novel.
Several protagonists of the reform movement were arrested during last year's protests.
He always casts himself as the protagonist of every story, even when it's about someone else.
tc: Although the villain gets the best lines, the film's ______ is a quiet schoolteacher whose choices drive the whole story.
The contrast with 'the villain' and 'whose choices drive the whole story' point to the main character.
se: The novel's ______ is an orphaned boy who slowly discovers the truth about his parents.
hero
Both 'protagonist' and 'hero' mean the central character of a story.

m: to make something last longer than necessary; to prolong
x: Arguing with the waiter only protracted an already uncomfortable evening.
Lawyers on both sides seemed determined to protract the negotiations so they could charge more fees.
Constant changes to the research design protracted her PhD by nearly two years.
Neither side wanted to protract the war, yet peace talks kept collapsing.
She didn't want to protract the goodbye, so she hugged him quickly and walked to the gate.
tc: Eager to end the meeting quickly, the chairwoman refused to let anyone ______ the discussion with irrelevant questions.
'Eager to end the meeting quickly' contrasts with making the discussion last longer.
se: The defence team tried to ______ the trial by filing one appeal after another.
prolong
Both 'protract' and 'prolong' mean to make something last longer.

m: narrow-minded and unsophisticated; limited in outlook to one's own small area
x: My cousin mocks my hometown as provincial, but I love its slow pace and friendly neighbours.
The new manager's provincial attitude toward foreign suppliers cost the company several good contracts.
Studying abroad helped him outgrow his rather provincial views about other cultures.
Critics called the party's policies provincial, focused on local grievances rather than national needs.
She found his provincial ideas about women working after marriage hard to accept.
tc: After years of living in cities across the world, she found her old classmates' views surprisingly ______ and resistant to new ideas.
The contrast with her worldly life and 'resistant to new ideas' signal narrow-mindedness.
se: The editor criticised the newspaper's ______ outlook, which ignored everything happening beyond the town.
parochial
Both 'provincial' and 'parochial' mean narrowly focused on one's own small area.

m: intended or likely to cause anger, strong reaction or debate
x: My brother loves making provocative comments at dinner just to start an argument.
Our CEO's provocative memo, which called the staff lazy, leaked to the press within hours.
Our lecturer opened with a provocative question: is economic growth always a good thing?
The minister's provocative remarks about the neighbouring country sparked diplomatic protests.
Her provocative silence after the argument hurt him more than any words could have.
tc: Hoping to start a lively debate, the professor opened the seminar with the deliberately ______ claim that democracy was overrated.
'Hoping to start a lively debate' shows the claim was meant to provoke a strong reaction.
se: The magazine's ______ cover, showing a fictional president as a clown, angered many readers.
inflammatory
Both 'provocative' and 'inflammatory' describe something likely to cause anger.

m: exceptional skill or ability in a particular activity or field
x: Her prowess in the kitchen means every family gathering ends up at her house.
Recruiters were impressed less by his degree than by his technical prowess with large databases.
Few students could match her academic prowess, yet she never boasted about her grades.
The country's military prowess has grown steadily over the past two decades, worrying its neighbours.
He tried to impress her with his dancing prowess, but mostly stepped on her feet.
tc: Although he had never taken a formal lesson, his ______ on the piano astonished trained musicians.
The contrast with 'never taken a formal lesson' and the fact that he 'astonished trained musicians' signal remarkable skill.
se: The young batsman's ______ at the crease earned him a place in the national team.
skill
Both 'prowess' and 'skill' refer to the batsman's outstanding ability, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: nearness in space, time, or relationship
x: We chose the flat mainly for its proximity to the school and the market.
Working in close proximity to the same colleagues all day can test anyone's patience.
The university's proximity to several research hospitals makes it attractive to medical students.
Residents worried about the proximity of the new chemical plant to their children's playground.
Being in such close proximity to her ex at the wedding made her surprisingly nervous.
tc: Because of the hotel's ______ to the airport, guests could sleep until an hour before their flights.
Being able to sleep until an hour before a flight implies that the hotel is very near the airport.
se: The shop's main advantage is its ______ to the railway station.
nearness
Both 'proximity' and 'nearness' describe how close the shop is to the station.

m: intended as punishment; harshly severe
x: My landlord charges a punitive fee if the rent arrives even one day late.
Management's punitive approach to minor mistakes left the staff anxious and unwilling to take risks.
Critics argue that punitive grading policies discourage students from attempting difficult courses.
The government imposed punitive tariffs on imported steel after the trade talks collapsed.
Her silence after the argument felt punitive, as if she wanted him to suffer for a while.
tc: Rather than rehabilitating offenders, the new law was purely ______, aimed only at making them suffer for their crimes.
'Rather than rehabilitating' and 'making them suffer' point to a law whose purpose is punishment.
se: Teachers were warned that ______ measures alone would not improve student behaviour.
disciplinary
Both 'punitive measures' and 'disciplinary measures' mean actions taken to punish misbehaviour.

m: attractively unusual or old-fashioned
x: We stayed in a quaint little cottage with a thatched roof and a crooked chimney.
His habit of sending handwritten memos seemed quaint to younger colleagues used to instant messaging.
The professor still uses an overhead projector, which students find quaint rather than annoying.
Tourists flock to the quaint fishing village, though locals complain about rising rents.
She found his old-fashioned courtesy rather quaint, and secretly she loved it.
tc: Though modern visitors might call its cobbled lanes and gas lamps ______, the villagers see them simply as home.
Cobbled lanes and gas lamps are charmingly old-fashioned, which is how outsiders would describe them.
se: The old town is full of ______ shops selling hand-made toys and lace.
charming
Both 'quaint' and 'charming' describe the shops as pleasantly old-fashioned and appealing.

m: to forcibly put an end to something, or to officially reject or cancel a legal decision
x: Mum quickly quashed our plan to stay up all night watching films.
The CEO moved fast to quash rumours that the company was about to be sold.
An appeals court quashed the conviction after new DNA evidence came to light.
The department quashed the proposal for a new research centre, citing budget cuts.
She tried to quash her jealousy, but it surfaced every time he mentioned his old friend.
tc: Far from encouraging debate, the regime used every means available to ______ dissent.
'Far from encouraging' signals the opposite action, so the blank must mean to suppress.
se: Troops were sent to ______ the uprising before it spread to other provinces.
quell
Both 'quash' and 'quell' mean to crush the uprising by force.

m: having or showing extreme, fanatical, unreasoning support or feeling
x: My uncle is a rabid cricket fan who refuses to leave the TV during a Test match.
The meeting turned ugly when a rabid critic of the merger started shouting at the board.
Some scholars became rabid defenders of the theory, refusing to consider any contrary evidence.
Rabid nationalism spread quickly through the country's online forums during the border dispute.
Her rabid jealousy eventually drove away the friends who had once supported her.
tc: Unlike his calm, open-minded brother, Karim was a ______ supporter of the party who tolerated no criticism of it.
The contrast with 'calm, open-minded' and the phrase 'tolerated no criticism' point to fanatical support.
se: The film attracted a ______ following of fans who quoted every line.
fanatical
Both 'rabid' and 'fanatical' describe fans with extreme, obsessive enthusiasm.

m: spreading or growing unchecked, especially of something unwelcome
x: Weeds grew rampant in the garden while we were away for the summer.
Office gossip was rampant for weeks after the manager's sudden resignation.
Plagiarism had become so rampant that the university introduced new detection software.
Rampant inflation wiped out the savings of millions of ordinary families.
Rumours about their divorce were rampant, though neither of them ever said a word.
tc: Once officials stopped enforcing the rules, corruption became ______, spreading through every department.
The end of enforcement and 'spreading through every department' indicate something growing unchecked.
se: During the epidemic, misinformation was ______ on social media.
widespread
Both 'rampant' and 'widespread' say the misinformation was everywhere and out of control.

m: a close, friendly relationship in which people understand each other well
x: Our new neighbour has a lovely rapport with the children on our street.
Building rapport with clients takes time, patience and a lot of listening.
Students learn more easily from teachers with whom they share a genuine rapport.
The two leaders' warm rapport raised hopes for a breakthrough in the negotiations.
They had an instant rapport, finishing each other's sentences by the end of their first date.
tc: Because the doctor took time to listen to every worry, she quickly developed a strong ______ with her patients.
Listening patiently to every worry naturally builds mutual understanding and trust.
se: The coach had an easy ______ with his players, who trusted him completely.
understanding
Both 'rapport' and 'understanding' describe a relaxed, trusting relationship between coach and players.

m: completely fascinated or absorbed by what one is seeing or hearing
x: The children sat in rapt silence as their grandmother told stories of the old village.
The entire boardroom listened with rapt attention to the intern's surprisingly brilliant pitch.
Students gave the visiting astronaut their rapt attention for the whole lecture.
A rapt audience of thousands watched as the rocket lifted off into the night sky.
He gazed at his newborn daughter with a rapt expression, unable to look away.
tc: Usually restless and noisy, the class fell silent and remained ______ throughout the magician's performance.
The contrast with 'usually restless and noisy' shows the class was completely absorbed.
se: Throughout the documentary, the children sat ______, their eyes fixed on the screen.
spellbound
Both 'rapt' and 'spellbound' describe children totally absorbed in what they are watching.

m: acting or done hastily, without careful thought about the consequences
x: Buying a car on the first day of looking was a rash decision I soon regretted.
Don't make any rash promises to the client until we've checked the budget.
In a rash moment, he dropped out of engineering school just weeks before his final exams.
Analysts warned that rash interest-rate cuts by the central bank could fuel inflation.
She said some rash things in anger and spent the next week apologising to her sister.
tc: Investors who are ______ rarely last long; the market rewards those who weigh every risk carefully.
The contrast with those 'who weigh every risk carefully' shows the blank means reckless.
se: It would be ______ to resign before you have another job lined up.
reckless
Both 'rash' and 'reckless' describe acting without thinking about the consequences.

m: the set of reasons or the logical basis for a decision, action, or belief
x: I still don't understand the rationale behind closing the library on weekends.
Please include a brief rationale for each budget request you submit.
Your thesis proposal should explain the rationale for choosing this research method.
The government has yet to offer a convincing rationale for the sudden tax increase.
She tried to explain the rationale for ending the relationship, but he wasn't ready to listen.
tc: The committee rejected the proposal because its authors never explained the ______ behind it; no one could see why the change was needed.
'No one could see why the change was needed' restates the missing reasons behind the proposal.
se: Few employees understood the ______ for the new attendance policy.
justification
Both 'rationale' and 'justification' refer to the reasons given for the policy.

m: making or being a harsh, loud, and disorderly noise
x: Raucous laughter from the next table made it impossible to hear our waiter.
The office party grew so raucous that security came up to ask us to quieten down.
Students held a raucous celebration in the dormitory after the final exams ended.
The parliamentary debate turned raucous as members shouted over the speaker.
Even after years of marriage, they still enjoyed raucous arguments followed by quiet reconciliations.
tc: In contrast to the hushed reading room upstairs, the student café was ______, full of shouting and clattering dishes.
The contrast with 'hushed' and the 'shouting and clattering' show the café was loud and disorderly.
se: Outside the stadium, ______ fans gathered, chanting and banging drums.
rowdy
Both 'raucous' and 'rowdy' describe a loud, unruly group of fans.

m: to cause severe and widespread damage to
x: Termites ravaged the old wooden furniture in my grandparents' storeroom.
A cyberattack ravaged the company's systems, shutting down operations for a week.
The historian studied how plague ravaged medieval European cities.
Floods ravage parts of northern Bangladesh almost every monsoon, destroying crops and homes.
Years of grief had ravaged his face, though his smile was still the same.
tc: Experts predicted that the storm would merely brush the coast, but instead it went on to ______ entire towns, leaving thousands homeless.
'But instead' and 'leaving thousands homeless' signal severe, widespread destruction.
se: Scientists fear that the new pest could ______ the region's wheat harvest.
devastate
Both 'ravage' and 'devastate' mean to cause severe damage to the harvest.

m: to reject someone or something abruptly or ungraciously
x: When I offered to help with the dishes, she rebuffed me with a curt 'No, thanks.'
The board rebuffed the takeover bid, calling it far below the company's real value.
The journal rebuffed his paper twice before finally accepting a revised version.
Union leaders rebuffed the government's offer of a modest pay rise.
He was too shy to ask her out again after she had rebuffed him at the party.
tc: Hoping for a warm welcome, the diplomat was dismayed when officials chose to ______ his overtures without even a polite reply.
The contrast with 'hoping for a warm welcome' and 'without even a polite reply' indicate a curt rejection.
se: Every time she tried to make friends with her new colleagues, they would ______ her.
snub
Both 'rebuff' and 'snub' mean to reject her coldly and rudely.

m: a statement or argument that contradicts or disproves another
x: My brother's only rebuttal to my complaint was a shrug and 'You started it.'
Our lawyers prepared a detailed rebuttal of the competitor's claims about our product's safety.
Each debate team gets three minutes for its rebuttal after the opening speeches.
The ministry issued a sharp rebuttal to the newspaper's report on hospital deaths.
She had no rebuttal when her friend pointed out how unfair she had been.
tc: The scientist's ______ was devastating: she disproved each of her critic's claims with fresh data.
Disproving each of a critic's claims is exactly what a refutation does.
se: The senator's office released a forceful ______ of the allegations within hours.
refutation
Both 'rebuttal' and 'refutation' mean a statement arguing that the allegations are false.

m: willing to consider or accept new ideas, suggestions, or proposals
x: My parents were more receptive to the idea of my studying abroad than I'd expected.
The new manager is receptive to feedback, so don't hesitate to share your concerns.
Young children are highly receptive to learning languages through songs and games.
Voters seem increasingly receptive to candidates who promise to tackle climate change.
After the argument, he wasn't receptive to her apology until the next morning.
tc: Far from rejecting the proposal outright, the committee was surprisingly ______ and asked for more details.
'Far from rejecting' signals the opposite attitude: openness to the idea.
se: The headmaster was ______ to the students' request for a longer lunch break.
amenable
Both 'receptive to' and 'amenable to' mean willing to consider and agree to the request.

m: to respond to an action or feeling by giving or feeling the same in return
x: Our neighbours always bring us sweets at Eid, so we reciprocate during Pohela Boishakh.
If you help a colleague meet a deadline, they will usually reciprocate when you're overloaded.
The two universities reciprocate by hosting each other's exchange students every year.
Both countries promised to reciprocate any easing of travel restrictions.
He loved her deeply, but she never reciprocated his feelings.
tc: She had shown him kindness for years, yet he never once bothered to ______, not even with a thank-you card.
'Yet' and 'not even with a thank-you card' show he failed to return her kindness.
se: He hoped she would ______ his affection, but she treated him only as a friend.
return
Both 'reciprocate' and 'return' mean to feel the same affection back.

m: to put something right; to correct an error or problem
x: The restaurant offered a free dessert to rectify the mix-up with our order.
Our IT team is working around the clock to rectify the fault in the email server.
Students have one week to rectify any errors in their registration forms.
Campaigners urged the city council to rectify decades of underinvestment in poorer neighbourhoods.
She wanted to rectify the hurt she had caused, so she called her friend to apologise.
tc: The accountant discovered a serious error in the tax return and worked late into the night to ______ it before the deadline.
Discovering an error and racing a deadline imply working to correct it.
se: The company promised to ______ the billing mistake as soon as possible.
correct
Both 'rectify' and 'correct' mean to put the mistake right.

m: to recover health or strength after illness, injury, or exhaustion
x: After the long flight, I spent a whole day at home just recuperating.
She took two weeks off work to recuperate after her surgery.
Exhausted after exams, many students go home to recuperate before the new term.
The injured striker is expected to recuperate in time for next month's cup final.
Her friends visited every day while she recuperated, bringing soup and gossip.
tc: Doctors told him that he would need several weeks of rest to ______ fully from the operation.
'Several weeks of rest' after an operation points to recovering health.
se: After the marathon, the runners needed a few days to ______.
recover
Both 'recuperate' and 'recover' mean to regain strength after exhaustion.

m: strongly suggestive or reminiscent of something; also, smelling strongly of something
x: The kitchen was redolent of garlic and frying onions when I came home.
The CEO's speech was redolent of the empty promises staff had heard many times before.
The novel's descriptions are redolent of village life in nineteenth-century England.
Critics said the new law was redolent of the censorship of an earlier, darker era.
That old song is redolent of the summer we first met, so I can't hear it without smiling.
tc: The old house, with its faded photographs and creaking floorboards, was ______ of a vanished era.
Faded photographs and creaking floorboards call to mind the past, so the blank means strongly suggestive of.
se: His prose style is ______ of the great Victorian novelists.
reminiscent
Both 'redolent of' and 'reminiscent of' mean that his style brings those novelists to mind.

m: to remedy or set right an injustice, wrong, or imbalance
x: I complained to the bank, but it took months for them to redress the error on my statement.
HR has set up a new process to redress grievances raised by junior staff.
The scholarship scheme aims to redress the shortage of women in engineering faculties.
The new law seeks to redress decades of discrimination against indigenous communities.
He tried to redress the wrong he had done his brother by finally repaying the loan.
tc: Rather than ignoring the historical injustice, the government set up a commission to ______ it through compensation and a formal apology.
'Rather than ignoring' plus 'compensation and a formal apology' indicate setting the injustice right.
se: The policy was designed to ______ the imbalance between urban and rural schools.
rectify
Both 'redress' and 'rectify' mean to correct the unfair imbalance.

m: to say something again or several times, usually for emphasis or clarity
x: Let me reiterate: nobody leaves the house until their homework is done.
In her email, the manager reiterated that the deadline could not be moved.
The professor reiterated the key points of the lecture before the exam.
The minister reiterated the government's commitment to free primary education.
He kept reiterating how sorry he was, but she needed actions, not words.
tc: Since many guests had not heard the first announcement, the host had to ______ the safety instructions.
Guests who missed the first announcement need the instructions said again.
se: The spokesman was careful to ______ that the company had broken no laws.
reaffirm
Both 'reiterate' and 'reaffirm' mean to state the point again firmly.

m: to make someone or something look or feel younger, fresher, or more lively
x: A week by the sea completely rejuvenated my exhausted parents.
The new director has rejuvenated a department that many considered dead.
A short walk between study sessions can rejuvenate a tired mind.
City planners hope the new metro line will rejuvenate the old commercial district.
Falling in love again seemed to rejuvenate her; she laughed more than she had in years.
tc: The once-dying town hoped that the new arts festival would ______ its economy and bring young people back.
'Once-dying' and 'bring young people back' point to restoring life and energy.
se: Investors believe the new chief executive can ______ the struggling brand.
revitalise
Both 'rejuvenate' and 'revitalise' mean to give the brand new energy and life.

m: to give up or let go of something, especially power, control, or a claim
x: My little brother refused to relinquish the TV remote, even at dinner.
The founder finally relinquished control of the company to a younger team.
After two years, she relinquished her scholarship to start her own business.
The dictator was forced to relinquish power after months of mass protests.
He found it hard to relinquish the hope that she might one day return.
tc: Despite his poor health, the old chairman refused to ______ his position, insisting he could still lead the board.
'Refused' and 'insisting he could still lead' show he would not give up his position.
se: The rebels agreed to ______ their weapons in exchange for amnesty.
surrender
Both 'relinquish' and 'surrender' mean to hand over the weapons.

m: to think or talk fondly about past experiences
x: Whenever my grandparents visit, they reminisce about growing up in a village without electricity.
At the retirement party, old colleagues reminisced about the company's chaotic early days.
Graduates returned to campus to reminisce about late nights in the library.
Veterans gathered at the memorial to reminisce and honour fallen comrades.
Lying awake, she would reminisce about the summer they had spent together in Italy.
tc: Looking at the old photograph album made the sisters ______ about their childhood holidays.
Old photographs prompt fond memories of the past.
se: In old age, he liked to sit by the window and ______, lost in memories of his years at sea.
remember
Both 'reminisce' and 'remember' describe him thinking fondly about his past.

m: careless in performing one's duty; negligent
x: It would be remiss of me not to thank everyone who helped organise tonight's dinner.
The auditors found the finance team remiss in keeping proper records.
I was remiss in not citing that source, and I've corrected the essay.
Inspectors said the hospital had been remiss in failing to report the outbreak promptly.
He felt he had been remiss as a friend, never once calling during her illness.
c: it would be remiss of me
tc: The guard was dismissed for being ______: he had slept through his shift and left the gate unlocked.
Sleeping on duty and leaving the gate unlocked, explained after the colon, define negligence.
se: Parents would be ______ if they ignored such obvious warning signs.
negligent
Both 'remiss' and 'negligent' mean failing in their duty of care.

m: filled or well supplied with something; also, pleasantly full after eating
x: After Grandma's feast, we all lay on the sofa, replete and drowsy.
The report was replete with errors, so the manager sent it back.
Her thesis is replete with references to obscure medieval texts.
History is replete with examples of empires that collapsed from within.
Their letters were replete with tenderness, even during the hardest years apart.
tc: Far from being sparse, the museum's archive is ______ with letters, maps and diaries from the colonial period.
'Far from being sparse' signals the opposite: well filled.
se: The speech was ______ with clichés.
filled
Both 'replete with' and 'filled with' mean the speech contained a great many clichés.

m: to hold back or restrain a feeling or reaction, or to subdue people by force
x: I had to repress a laugh when my teacher's chair squeaked loudly in the silent hall.
Employees often repress their frustration rather than risk confronting their boss.
Psychologists have long debated whether people can truly repress painful childhood memories.
The regime repressed all opposition, jailing journalists and banning protests.
She repressed her tears until the guests had gone, then cried for an hour.
tc: Though she was furious, she managed to ______ her anger and answer the customer politely.
The contrast between 'furious' and 'politely' shows she held her anger back.
se: He tried to ______ a yawn during the long presentation.
stifle
Both 'repress' and 'stifle' mean to hold back the yawn.

m: a temporary relief from something unpleasant, or the cancellation or postponement of a punishment
x: A sudden power cut gave us a welcome reprieve from the neighbour's loud music.
The factory won a six-month reprieve after a buyer expressed interest in it.
Students got a reprieve when the exam was postponed by a week.
The condemned man received a last-minute reprieve from the state governor.
Her phone call was a reprieve from the loneliness of that long winter.
tc: The rain stopped for an hour, giving the exhausted rescue workers a brief ______ before the storm returned.
A short pause 'before the storm returned' is a temporary relief.
se: Thanks to the donation, the hospital ward earned a six-month ______ from closure.
respite
Both 'reprieve' and 'respite' mean a temporary delay of the threatened closure.

m: to criticize someone sharply or formally for doing something wrong
x: My mother reprimanded me for leaving the gate open again.
The supervisor formally reprimanded two employees for sharing confidential client data.
The professor reprimanded the class for talking during the guest lecture.
The football association reprimanded the coach for his comments about the referee.
She reprimanded herself for snapping at her best friend over something so trivial.
tc: Instead of praising the intern for her initiative, the manager chose to ______ her for not following procedure.
'Instead of praising' signals the opposite: a sharp criticism.
se: The judge was forced to ______ the lawyer for his disrespectful remarks.
rebuke
Both 'reprimand' and 'rebuke' mean to criticize the lawyer sharply.

m: extremely distasteful or offensive
x: I find the smell of durian repugnant, but my wife adores it.
Employees found the company's new surveillance policy morally repugnant.
Many scholars find the author's views on race repugnant, yet still admire his prose.
The court ruled that the law was repugnant to the constitution and struck it down.
Lying to her friends was repugnant to her, even when the truth would hurt.
tc: Though some found the joke harmless, most of the audience considered it ______ and walked out.
The contrast with 'harmless' and the audience walking out show they found it deeply offensive.
se: The idea of profiting from others' suffering was ______ to him.
abhorrent
Both 'repugnant' and 'abhorrent' mean deeply offensive to him.

m: firmly determined and unwavering in purpose
x: Despite the heavy rain, my resolute father still went for his morning walk.
Her resolute leadership kept the team together through two difficult years.
He remained resolute in his decision to study physics, despite pressure to choose medicine.
The villagers mounted a resolute campaign against illegal sand mining on their riverbank.
She was resolute: she would not call him first, no matter how much she missed him.
tc: While others in the party wavered under pressure, the senator stayed ______, refusing to abandon the bill.
The contrast with 'wavered' and 'refusing to abandon' point to firm determination.
se: The athlete was ______ in her pursuit of an Olympic medal.
determined
Both 'resolute' and 'determined' describe her firm, unwavering purpose.

m: deep, clear, and echoing in sound; also, evoking strong images, memories, or emotions
x: My uncle's resonant voice could be heard clearly from the other end of the house.
The speaker's resonant baritone held the conference hall's attention for an hour.
The poem's resonant images of rivers and rain stayed with students long after class.
Few symbols are as resonant for the nation as the old bridge that survived the war.
The song was deeply resonant for her, recalling her late mother's lullabies.
tc: Unlike the thin, reedy voices of the other singers, his was deep and ______, filling every corner of the cathedral.
The contrast with 'thin, reedy' and 'filling every corner' indicate a deep, echoing sound.
se: The actor's ______ voice carried easily to the back of the theatre.
sonorous
Both 'resonant' and 'sonorous' describe a deep, full voice that carries well.

m: a short period of rest or relief from something difficult or unpleasant
x: The afternoon shower brought a brief respite from the sticky Dhaka heat.
Lunch breaks offer a short respite from the endless phone calls.
Winter vacation gave the students a much-needed respite from exams.
Aid agencies called for a ceasefire to give civilians some respite from the fighting.
Her sister's visit gave her a few days' respite from caring for her sick husband.
tc: After months of working without a single day off, the nurses were desperate for some ______.
Months without a day off create a need for rest and relief.
se: The cool breeze offered welcome ______ from the summer heat.
relief
Both 'respite' and 'relief' mean a break from the discomfort of the heat.

m: the return of something lost or stolen to its owner, or payment for loss or injury caused
x: When the neighbour's boy broke our window, his father insisted on making restitution.
The firm agreed to pay restitution to customers who had been overcharged.
The history seminar debated whether museums should agree to the restitution of artefacts taken during colonial rule.
The court ordered the fraudster to make full restitution to his victims.
He believed that an apology was not enough and that restitution was owed to his family.
tc: Since the bank had wrongly seized the family's savings, the judge demanded full ______ of every taka taken.
Money 'wrongly seized' must be returned, which is what the blank describes.
se: Victims of the scam are seeking ______ for their losses.
compensation
Both 'restitution' and 'compensation' mean payment to make up for the losses.

m: to attack or harm someone in return for a similar attack or harm
x: When his sister hid his phone, he retaliated by eating her chocolates.
Employees who report misconduct should not fear that managers will retaliate against them.
The study examines why some animals retaliate when attacked while others simply flee.
The government vowed to retaliate if new tariffs were imposed on its exports.
She was tempted to retaliate after his cruel remark, but she simply walked away.
tc: Though deeply insulted, the diplomat decided not to ______, hoping that restraint would cool tensions.
'Though deeply insulted' and 'restraint' show he chose not to hit back.
se: If attacked, the army was ordered to ______ immediately.
counterattack
Both 'retaliate' and 'counterattack' mean to strike back at the attacker.

m: to withdraw a statement, accusation, or offer as untrue or no longer valid
x: My little brother retracted his accusation once Mum found the missing biscuits in his room.
The company retracted its job offer after the background check revealed problems.
The journal retracted the paper after other scientists failed to reproduce its results.
The newspaper retracted the story and published a full apology.
He wished he could retract the hurtful words he had said to her in anger.
tc: Once it became clear that her claims were false, the witness was forced to ______ her testimony.
Claims shown to be false must be withdrawn.
se: The politician refused to ______ his controversial remarks despite public outrage.
withdraw
Both 'retract' and 'withdraw' mean to take back the remarks.

m: looking back on past events; also, applying to a time before it was enacted
x: Looking through old diaries put me in a retrospective mood all evening.
The team held a retrospective meeting to discuss what went wrong with the launch.
Her retrospective study analysed hospital records from the past twenty years.
Critics objected to the retrospective tax, which applied to profits earned three years earlier.
On their anniversary, they took a retrospective look at fifty years of marriage, laughing at old photographs.
tc: Rather than predicting future trends, the report took a ______ approach, examining what had gone wrong over the previous decade.
The contrast with 'predicting future trends' and 'examining the previous decade' indicate looking back.
se: Many objected to the ______ law, which punished actions that had been legal when they were taken.
retroactive
Both 'retrospective' and 'retroactive' describe a law applied to actions taken before it existed.

m: to take great pleasure or delight in something
x: My little cousins revelled in the first proper rain of the monsoon, splashing in every puddle.
Some managers seem to revel in making their staff wait outside their offices.
She revelled in the freedom of university life after years at a strict boarding school.
The opposition party revelled in the government's embarrassment over the leaked memo.
He revelled in her attention, though he pretended not to notice it.
tc: Unlike her shy brother, who hated being in the spotlight, Nadia seemed to ______ in the applause.
The contrast with a brother who 'hated being in the spotlight' shows she greatly enjoyed it.
se: The winning team took time to ______ in their hard-earned victory.
bask
Both 'revel in' and 'bask in' mean to enjoy the victory to the full.

m: to feel deep respect or admiration for someone or something
x: In our family, everyone revered my grandmother, whose word was final on every matter.
The founder is still revered by employees who joined in the company's early days.
Students revere the old professor, whose lectures have inspired three generations of engineers.
Many cultures revere their ancestors through annual rituals and offerings.
He revered her so much that he could never bring himself to disagree with her.
tc: Rather than mocking the elderly poet as some critics did, the young writers came to ______ him as their master.
'Rather than mocking' and 'as their master' indicate deep respect.
se: Villagers still ______ the ancient banyan tree, believing it protects the community.
venerate
Both 'revere' and 'venerate' mean to regard the tree with deep respect.

m: to criticize someone in an abusive or angrily insulting way
x: The referee was reviled by both sets of fans after the controversial penalty.
The new boss was reviled at first, but staff eventually came to appreciate his reforms.
Once reviled by critics, the painter is now studied in every art history course.
The minister was widely reviled for his handling of the flood relief effort.
She reviled her ex-husband to anyone who would listen, which only made her friends uncomfortable.
tc: Instead of praising the whistleblower for her courage, the tabloids chose to ______ her as a liar and a traitor.
'Instead of praising' and the insults 'liar and traitor' point to abusive criticism.
se: It is easy to ______ politicians, but much harder to do their jobs.
vilify
Both 'revile' and 'vilify' mean to attack politicians with harsh, abusive criticism.

m: to officially cancel a law, decision, licence, or promise
x: If you keep driving that recklessly, the authorities will revoke your licence.
The company revoked his access to the building on the day he resigned.
The university revoked her degree after discovering that she had plagiarised her thesis.
The government revoked the mining permit after protests by local farmers.
He was hurt when his father revoked his promise to pay for the trip.
tc: After the inspectors found repeated safety violations, the city had no choice but to ______ the factory's operating licence.
Repeated safety violations lead the city to cancel the licence officially.
se: The embassy may ______ your visa if you overstay.
cancel
Both 'revoke' and 'cancel' mean to officially end the visa's validity.

m: an expression of intense enthusiasm or delight in speech or writing
x: My aunt went into rhapsodies over the mangoes from her village garden.
The product launch was met with rhapsodies from tech bloggers, though sales were modest.
