The essay is less a critical analysis than a rhapsody about the poet's genius.
Food critics wrote rhapsodies about the new restaurant's lamb biryani.
His letters to her were rhapsodies of love, filled with extravagant praise.
tc: Far from offering a balanced review, the critic's article was pure ______, praising the film as flawless in every respect.
'Far from offering a balanced review' and 'flawless in every respect' signal an outpouring of enthusiasm.
se: Her farewell speech was an emotional ______ of gratitude to everyone who had helped her.
effusion
Both 'rhapsody' and 'effusion' describe an enthusiastic outpouring of feeling.

m: (of something bad) widespread or common; also, full of something undesirable
x: Our neighbourhood chat group is rife with rumours about the new building next door.
The office was rife with speculation about who would replace the director.
The draft was rife with errors, so the editor returned it to the author.
Corruption was rife in the ports, according to the official inquiry.
Their marriage was rife with tension long before they admitted anything was wrong.
tc: Because sanitation was poor and clean water scarce, disease was ______ in the refugee camps.
Poor sanitation and scarce clean water cause disease to become widespread.
se: During the election, misinformation was ______ online.
rampant
Both 'rife' and 'rampant' say misinformation was widespread and unchecked.

m: a serious break in a friendly relationship; also, a crack or split
x: A disagreement over parking spaces created a rift between neighbours on our street.
A rift has opened between the sales and engineering teams over the new product.
The theory caused a lasting rift within the physics department.
The vote exposed a deep rift within the ruling party over immigration.
It took years for the sisters to heal the rift caused by their father's will.
tc: The two old friends had not spoken for a decade, but a chance meeting at a funeral finally healed the ______ between them.
Not speaking for a decade and the word 'healed' indicate a break in their friendship.
se: The disagreement over strategy created a deep ______ within the board.
split
Both 'rift' and 'split' mean a serious division between board members.

m: extremely thorough, careful, and accurate; strictly applied
x: She follows a rigorous exercise routine, even when she's on holiday with friends.
Every new hire goes through a rigorous training programme before meeting clients.
The paper was rejected because its methods were not rigorous enough.
New medicines must pass rigorous clinical trials before they can be sold.
He applied rigorous standards to everyone except himself, which annoyed his partner.
tc: Unlike the careless survey that preceded it, the new study was ______, checking every figure twice and controlling for every variable.
The contrast with 'careless' and the detail of checking every figure twice point to thoroughness.
se: Applicants must pass ______ examinations before they are admitted.
stringent
Both 'rigorous' and 'stringent' describe demanding, strictly applied examinations.

m: strong and healthy; sturdy and able to withstand pressure or difficulty
x: My grandfather is still robust enough to walk five kilometres every morning.
We need a more robust system for backing up client data.
Her findings were robust, holding up across several independent datasets.
Despite the global slowdown, the country's economy remained surprisingly robust.
Their friendship proved robust, surviving distance, marriage and years of silence.
tc: Although the bridge looked delicate, engineers insisted it was ______ enough to withstand the strongest earthquakes.
The contrast with 'looked delicate' and the ability to withstand earthquakes indicate strength.
se: The new phone comes with ______ casing that survives repeated drops.
sturdy
Both 'robust' and 'sturdy' describe casing strong enough to resist damage.

m: involving only the most basic principles or facts; undeveloped
x: I have only a rudimentary knowledge of cooking, so we mostly eat rice and eggs.
The startup's first office had only rudimentary furniture and a single shared laptop.
The course assumes a rudimentary understanding of calculus and statistics.
Many rural clinics in the region still lack even rudimentary medical equipment.
Their conversation was rudimentary at first, since neither spoke the other's language well.
tc: Though the early settlers had only ______ tools, they managed to build sturdy homes and farms.
'Though' and 'managed to' show the tools were very basic.
se: The shelter offered only ______ facilities: a roof, a few cots and a water tank.
basic
Both 'rudimentary' and 'basic' describe facilities limited to the bare essentials.

m: to deliberately destroy, damage, or obstruct something
x: My younger brother tried to sabotage my diet by hiding sweets all over the kitchen.
A disgruntled employee sabotaged the project by deleting key files.
Some students sabotage their own grades by leaving every assignment to the last minute.
Rebels sabotaged the railway line, cutting off supplies to the capital.
She feared that her own insecurity would sabotage yet another relationship.
tc: Jealous of his colleague's success, he secretly tried to ______ her presentation by deleting the slides from the shared drive.
Jealousy and secretly deleting slides indicate deliberate damage.
se: Hardliners on both sides threatened to ______ the peace talks.
undermine
Both 'sabotage' and 'undermine' mean to deliberately weaken the talks so they fail.

m: disrespectful treatment of something sacred or highly valued
x: In my family, putting ketchup on biryani is considered sacrilege.
For our old-school editor, missing a print deadline was sacrilege.
Some purists regard any rewriting of Shakespeare's verse as sacrilege.
Vandals who damaged the temple's sacred statues were charged with sacrilege.
To her, forgetting their anniversary was nothing short of sacrilege.
tc: To devout pilgrims, wearing shoes inside the shrine is ______, an insult to everything they hold holy.
'An insult to everything they hold holy' defines the violation of something sacred.
se: Locals viewed the destruction of the ancient mosque as ______.
desecration
Both 'sacrilege' and 'desecration' mean violating a sacred place.

m: producing a good or helpful effect, often through an unpleasant experience
x: Missing the last bus home was a salutary reminder to check the timetable before going out.
For the young manager, losing the contract proved a salutary lesson in preparing properly for client meetings.
Failing my first statistics exam had a salutary effect on my study habits for the rest of the year.
The flood was a salutary warning that the city's drainage system could not cope with heavier monsoon rains.
Her brother's blunt criticism was painful to hear, but it was ultimately salutary for their relationship.
tc: Although the defeat was humiliating at the time, it proved ______, forcing the team to rethink its lazy training habits.
The defeat led the team to improve, so the blank must mean beneficial despite being unpleasant.
se: The scandal's effect on the industry proved ______, prompting firms to tighten their accounting rules.
beneficial
Both 'salutary' and 'beneficial' describe an effect that ended up doing good, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: barely enough; very little in amount
x: She paid scant attention to the instructions and ended up assembling the bookshelf upside down.
With scant time left before the deadline, the team skipped lunch to finish the report.
The theory has attracted plenty of attention, but there is scant evidence to support it.
Officials showed scant regard for residents' safety when they approved the unsafe building.
He had shown scant interest in his cousin's wedding plans, which hurt her more than she admitted.
tc: Despite the committee's confident claims, there was ______ data to support the new policy, only a single small survey.
'Only a single small survey' restates that there was very little data.
se: Investigators found ______ evidence linking the company to the fraud, so the case was dropped.
meager
Both 'scant' and 'meager' mean too little, which explains why the case was dropped.

m: harshly and severely critical
x: My sister wrote a scathing review of the hotel after finding cockroaches in the bathroom.
The audit produced a scathing report on how the department had wasted its budget.
His supervisor's scathing comments on the draft thesis left him rewriting whole chapters.
In a scathing editorial, the newspaper accused the city council of ignoring flood warnings.
She fired off a scathing reply to her ex-boyfriend's message and then immediately regretted it.
tc: Far from praising the film, the critic's review was ______, calling the plot lazy and the acting wooden.
'Far from praising' and the harsh descriptions show the review was severely critical.
se: The minister faced ______ criticism from opposition members after the bridge collapsed.
withering
Both 'scathing' and 'withering' describe extremely harsh criticism.

m: to speak about something in a mocking, scornful way
x: My grandfather scoffs at anyone who claims you can learn a language in a month.
When I suggested working from home on Fridays, my boss scoffed and changed the subject.
Many geologists initially scoffed at the idea that continents could drift.
Critics scoffed at the government's promise to end power cuts within a year.
She used to scoff at romantic films, until she met someone who made her cry at one.
tc: Experts who once used to ______ at the idea of electric cars now concede that they will dominate the market.
'Once' contrasts with 'now concede', so the blank must mean to mock or dismiss.
se: Seasoned investors tend to ______ at get-rich-quick schemes that promise huge returns overnight.
sneer
Both 'scoff at' and 'sneer at' mean to treat something with open contempt.

m: calm, quiet and unhurried; dignified
x: We spent a sedate afternoon by the lake, reading and drinking tea.
After years at a hectic startup, she welcomed the sedate pace of a government office.
The professor delivered his lecture in a sedate tone that sent half the class to sleep.
The village has a sedate charm that attracts retirees looking to escape city life.
Their courtship was sedate and old-fashioned, with long walks and letters rather than late-night parties.
tc: Unlike the frenzied nightlife of the capital, the seaside town offered a pace of life that was ______ and predictable.
'Unlike the frenzied' signals a contrast, so the blank must mean calm and unhurried.
se: The old car's pace along the country road was ______, and every other vehicle overtook it.
unhurried
Both 'sedate' and 'unhurried' describe a slow, calm pace.

m: encouraging people to rebel against the government or lawful authority
x: In colonial times, owning a seditious pamphlet could land a person in prison.
The editor was charged with publishing seditious material after printing calls to overthrow the regime.
Historians study how seditious writings spread among students in the years before independence.
Rights groups argue that the law against seditious speech is used to silence ordinary critics.
My uncle still jokes that his college poems were so seditious that his father hid them in the attic.
tc: The military government banned the newspaper, claiming its articles were ______ and designed to incite revolt against the state.
'Designed to incite revolt against the state' restates the meaning of the blank.
se: The pamphlet was declared ______ because it urged soldiers to turn their weapons against their commanders.
subversive
Both 'seditious' and 'subversive' describe material meant to undermine authority.

m: having many curves and turns; moving in a graceful, winding way
x: The sinuous road up to the tea gardens made my little brother carsick.
The designer's sinuous lines gave the new office furniture a soft, organic feel.
Biology students watched the sinuous movement of an eel through the tank.
From the air, the river's sinuous course across the delta is clearly visible.
She moved across the dance floor with a sinuous grace that left him staring.
tc: Rather than running straight, the mountain trail was ______, twisting around boulders and doubling back along streams.
'Rather than running straight' and 'twisting' show the trail was full of curves.
se: The ______ path through the forest doubled back on itself so often that we lost our sense of direction.
winding
Both 'sinuous' and 'winding' describe a path with many turns.

m: unwillingness to work or make any effort; laziness
x: After a week of sloth on holiday, getting up for work on Monday felt impossible.
The manager blamed the project's failure on bureaucratic sloth rather than any lack of money.
His academic sloth caught up with him when he realized he had three essays due on the same day.
Critics accused the agency of sloth in responding to the cyclone warnings.
She loved him, but his sloth around the house was slowly wearing down her patience.
tc: His colleagues were diligent and energetic, but Rafiq was known for his ______, often leaving work half-finished for days.
The contrast with 'diligent and energetic' and the half-finished work point to laziness.
se: The report blamed the delays not on a lack of funding but on the ______ of officials who rarely answered their mail.
indolence
Both 'sloth' and 'indolence' mean laziness, so the officials are blamed for the same fault.

m: a temporary stay in a place
x: After a brief sojourn in Lisbon, they flew home with a suitcase full of tiles and pastries.
Her six-month sojourn at the London office taught her more than any training course.
During his sojourn in Paris as a visiting scholar, he finished the book's final chapters.
The astronauts' long sojourn on the space station gave researchers valuable data on muscle loss.
He still talks fondly about his summer sojourn in the hills, where he first fell in love.
tc: The writer never settled in Tangier permanently; his months there were merely a pleasant ______ before he moved on to Cairo.
'Never settled permanently' and 'moved on' show the blank means a temporary stay.
se: After a short ______ in the mountains, she returned to the city feeling refreshed.
stay
Both 'sojourn' and 'stay' refer to a short period spent somewhere.

m: comfort in a time of sadness or distress
x: After a long day, she finds solace in a cup of tea and a good book.
When the merger fell through, he took solace in the fact that his team had kept their jobs.
Many students found solace in the library's quiet reading room during exam season.
After the tragedy, the community sought solace in shared prayers and candlelit vigils.
Music was his only solace during the lonely months after the divorce.
tc: Grieving the loss of his dog, the boy took ______ in the photographs that reminded him of their happy afternoons together.
His grief and the reminders of happy times show the blank means comfort.
se: During the difficult months of her illness, she drew ______ from the letters her friends sent every week.
comfort
Both 'solace' and 'comfort' mean emotional relief in hard times.

m: to ask for or try to obtain something from someone
x: Our building committee is soliciting suggestions for how to spend the maintenance fund.
The company regularly solicits feedback from customers before launching new products.
The professor solicited comments from colleagues before submitting the paper for publication.
Candidates are forbidden from soliciting donations from foreign governments.
He hated soliciting favors, even from close friends, so he struggled alone.
tc: Before finalizing the design, the architect decided to ______ the opinions of the residents who would actually live in the building.
Wanting residents' input before finalizing shows the blank means to ask for.
se: The charity plans to ______ donations from local businesses to fund the new shelter.
seek
Both 'solicit' and 'seek' mean to ask for the donations.

m: having enough money to pay all of one's debts
x: Since starting a strict budget, I've managed to stay solvent until the end of each month.
The bank must remain solvent if it is to keep the trust of its depositors.
Graduate students often take tutoring jobs just to stay solvent between scholarship payments.
The government stepped in with emergency loans to keep the national airline solvent.
He felt proud the day he became solvent enough to send money home to his parents.
tc: After years of mounting debts, the company finally became ______ again, able to pay its suppliers on time.
'Able to pay its suppliers on time' defines the blank as having enough money to cover debts.
se: The bank refused the loan because the firm could not prove that it was ______.
creditworthy
Both 'solvent' and 'creditworthy' describe a firm able to meet its financial obligations.

m: dark or dull in color; gloomy and serious in mood
x: The sky turned somber as the monsoon clouds rolled in over the city.
The mood in the office was somber after the layoffs were announced.
The lecture ended on a somber note, with the professor discussing the risks of climate change.
Thousands gathered for a somber ceremony to remember the victims of the factory collapse.
His usually cheerful face grew somber when she mentioned his late father.
tc: Although the party was meant to be festive, the atmosphere was ______ because everyone had just heard about the accident.
'Although ... festive' signals a contrast, and the bad news shows the mood was gloomy.
se: The mood at the ceremony was ______ as the speaker reflected on the lives lost in the war.
solemn
Both 'somber' and 'solemn' describe a serious, grave mood.

m: to reject someone or something with contempt
x: She spurned my offer of help and carried all the shopping bags herself.
The startup spurned a buyout offer from a larger rival, hoping to grow on its own.
Many young researchers spurn industry jobs in favor of academic freedom, despite the lower pay.
The opposition spurned the government's invitation to talks, calling it a publicity stunt.
Spurned by the girl he loved, he poured his heartbreak into song lyrics.
tc: Too proud to accept charity, the old man would ______ any gift that looked like pity, even from his own children.
'Too proud to accept charity' signals contemptuous rejection.
se: The union decided to ______ the management's final offer, calling it an insult to its members.
reject
Both 'spurn' and 'reject' mean to turn down the offer.

m: not flowing or moving; showing no activity, growth or development
x: Mosquitoes breed quickly in stagnant water left in flowerpots and old tires.
With salaries stagnant for three years, many employees started looking for new jobs.
His research had become stagnant until a new collaborator brought fresh ideas.
Economists warn that a stagnant economy could push millions back into poverty.
After years of the same routine, she felt their marriage had grown stagnant.
tc: While neighboring economies grew rapidly, the country's own economy remained ______, with almost no new jobs created in a decade.
The contrast with 'grew rapidly' and the lack of new jobs show the blank means not growing.
se: Sales have been ______ for months, and the board is demanding a new marketing strategy.
static
Both 'stagnant' and 'static' mean sales have not grown or changed.

m: loyal, reliable and hardworking
x: Our neighbor has been a stalwart friend, checking on my mother every day while I'm abroad.
She has been a stalwart member of the finance team for over twenty years.
The professor was a stalwart defender of academic freedom throughout his career.
Stalwart supporters of the party turned out in the pouring rain to vote.
Through every argument and hardship, he remained her stalwart companion.
tc: Even when the club was losing every match, its most ______ fans never missed a game or wavered in their loyalty.
'Never missed a game or wavered in their loyalty' restates the meaning of loyal and dependable.
se: Throughout the scandal, the senator's ______ allies refused to abandon him.
staunch
Both 'stalwart' and 'staunch' describe firmly loyal supporters.

m: angry or bitter conflict or disagreement
x: Arguments over the inheritance caused years of strife in my friend's family.
Constant strife between the two department heads made the office a miserable place to work.
The historian's book examines the religious strife that tore the region apart in the sixteenth century.
Years of civil strife have left the country's schools and hospitals in ruins.
They had weathered plenty of strife in their marriage, but this argument felt different.
tc: After decades of ______, the two communities finally signed a peace agreement and began to rebuild trust.
A peace agreement and rebuilding trust imply that the blank means bitter conflict.
se: The party was weakened by internal ______ as rival factions fought over the leadership.
discord
Both 'strife' and 'discord' mean conflict within the party.

m: strict, precise and demanding
x: Our apartment building has stringent rules about pets, so we had to leave our cat with my parents.
The firm introduced stringent security checks after a laptop containing client data was stolen.
The scholarship has stringent eligibility requirements, including a minimum GPA of 3.8.
Environmental groups are pushing for more stringent limits on factory emissions.
Her parents were stringent about curfews, which made her teenage years feel endless.
tc: Unlike the relaxed rules of the old system, the new regulations are ______, and even minor violations lead to heavy fines.
'Unlike the relaxed rules' and heavy fines for minor violations show the blank means strict.
se: Pharmaceutical companies must meet ______ safety standards before a new drug can be sold.
rigorous
Both 'stringent' and 'rigorous' describe strict, demanding standards.

m: ready to obey others without question; meek
x: The puppy rolled onto its back in a submissive gesture whenever the older dog growled.
He was tired of being submissive in meetings and finally voiced his objections.
Researchers studied how submissive behavior in primates relates to social rank.
Activists criticized the textbook for portraying women as submissive and passive.
She refused to play the submissive wife her in-laws expected her to be.
tc: Once bold and outspoken, the young clerk became ______ after his harsh new boss punished every sign of disagreement.
'Once bold and outspoken' signals a contrast, and the punishment explains why he now obeys meekly.
se: The coach wanted players who would think for themselves, not ______ ones who simply did as they were told.
obedient
Both 'submissive' and 'obedient' describe players who follow orders without question.

m: seeking to undermine or overthrow an established system or authority
x: The comedian's jokes seem harmless, but they carry a subversive message about class.
Management viewed the employees' unofficial chat group as subversive and tried to shut it down.
The course explores subversive art movements that challenged censorship in the twentieth century.
The regime arrested dozens of students for alleged subversive activities.
Her quiet, subversive humor was what first made him fall for her.
tc: The censors banned the novel, believing its gentle satire was secretly ______ and aimed at weakening respect for the government.
'Aimed at weakening respect for the government' restates the meaning of the blank.
se: The secret police kept files on anyone suspected of ______ activities against the state.
seditious
Both 'subversive' and 'seditious' describe activities meant to undermine the state.

m: help and support given in times of hardship or distress
x: The neighbors offered succor to the family after their house burned down.
During the financial crisis, the small business found little succor from its bank.
Medieval monasteries often gave succor to travelers and the sick.
Aid agencies rushed to bring succor to villages cut off by the floods.
In her darkest weeks, his steady presence was her only succor.
tc: Cut off by the storm and running out of food, the stranded villagers desperately awaited ______ from the rescue teams.
Being stranded without food shows they needed help, which is what the blank means.
se: The charity's mission is to bring ______ to refugees who have lost everything.
relief
Both 'succor' and 'relief' mean help for people in hardship.

m: to give way to pressure, temptation, illness or a stronger force
x: I promised myself no sweets this week but succumbed to a slice of chocolate cake on Tuesday.
Under pressure from investors, the board finally succumbed and replaced the chief executive.
Exhausted after three all-nighters, she succumbed to sleep in the middle of the lecture.
Many patients in the outbreak succumbed to the disease before vaccines arrived.
He resisted her charm for weeks before finally succumbing and asking her to dinner.
tc: Though the fortress withstood months of siege, its starving defenders were eventually forced to ______ to the invading army.
'Though ... withstood' contrasts with 'eventually forced', so the blank means to give in.
se: Despite her strong will, she began to ______ to the temptation of checking her phone every few minutes.
yield
Both 'succumb to' and 'yield to' mean to give in to the temptation.

m: concerned only with what is obvious or on the surface; lacking depth
x: The paint job hid only superficial damage; the wall underneath was crumbling.
His superficial knowledge of the software became obvious when the client asked detailed questions.
The essay offered a superficial analysis that ignored most of the key evidence.
Critics dismissed the reforms as superficial changes that left the real problems untouched.
She found him charming at first, but their conversations always stayed superficial.
tc: The inspector's review was ______, taking only ten minutes and missing cracks that a careful examination would have revealed.
The contrast with 'a careful examination' and the missed cracks show the review lacked depth.
se: The film's treatment of a complex historical period is ______, skipping over its deeper causes.
shallow
Both 'superficial' and 'shallow' mean the treatment lacks depth.

m: to take the place of someone or something, often by force or scheming
x: Streaming services have largely supplanted the DVD rentals we grew up with.
The ambitious deputy spent months quietly trying to supplant her manager.
In many universities, online journals have supplanted printed copies in the library.
Solar power could eventually supplant coal as the region's main source of electricity.
He felt jealous when his sister's new boyfriend seemed to supplant him as her closest confidant.
tc: Many experts predict that electric vehicles will ______ petrol cars entirely within a few decades, just as cars once replaced horses.
'Just as cars once replaced horses' shows the blank means to take the place of.
se: Few believed that the young challenger could ______ the long-serving champion at the top of the rankings.
displace
Both 'supplant' and 'displace' mean to push the champion out and take his place.

m: able to bend and move easily; flexible
x: Regular yoga has kept my mother supple well into her sixties.
The new leather seats were soft and supple, unlike the cracked ones in our old car.
Athletes stretch before training to keep their muscles supple and avoid injury.
Researchers have developed a supple plastic that can bend repeatedly without breaking.
Dancers need supple bodies, but their teacher believed they also needed supple minds.
tc: Unlike the stiff, cracked boots he had worn for years, the new pair were ______ enough to bend easily with every step.
'Unlike the stiff' and 'bend easily' show the blank means flexible.
se: Gymnasts usually begin training young, when their bodies are still ______.
flexible
Both 'supple' and 'flexible' describe bodies that bend easily.

m: to guess or suppose something without firm evidence
x: From the muddy shoes by the door, I surmised that my brother had been out in the rain.
Seeing her manager's frown, she surmised that the meeting had not gone well.
Scholars can only surmise what the damaged inscription originally said.
Investigators surmised that the fire had started in the kitchen, though they could not confirm it.
He surmised from her short replies that she was still angry with him.
tc: With no written records to go on, historians can only ______ why the city was suddenly abandoned.
'No written records' means historians must guess, which is what the blank means.
se: Without the full data, we can only ______ that the drop in sales was caused by the price increase.
suppose
Both 'surmise' and 'suppose' mean to assume something without proof.

m: likely to be affected, influenced or harmed by something
x: Small children are more susceptible to colds when the weather suddenly changes.
Older computers are susceptible to viruses if the software isn't regularly updated.
The study found that sleep-deprived students were more susceptible to stress.
Low-lying coastal districts are highly susceptible to flooding during the monsoon.
She was always susceptible to flattery, which made her an easy target for smooth talkers.
tc: Because the new rice variety has little natural resistance to pests, it is far more ______ to insect damage than traditional strains.
'Little natural resistance' explains why the crop is easily harmed.
se: People with weakened immune systems are especially ______ to infections.
vulnerable
Both 'susceptible' and 'vulnerable' mean easily affected by infections.

m: a sudden change of subject away from the main topic
x: My aunt asked about my job, but the conversation soon went off on a tangent about her neighbor's goats.
The meeting dragged on because the director kept going off on tangents.
Our history professor is brilliant but tends to wander off on tangents during lectures.
The debate fell apart when one candidate launched into a long tangent about his childhood.
Talking with her was exhausting yet delightful, because every story spun off into a new tangent.
tc: The speaker kept drifting away from his main topic, and the audience grew restless with every ______ about his travels.
'Drifting away from his main topic' defines the blank as a digression.
se: The lecture lost focus when the professor launched into a long ______ about his days as a student.
digression
Both 'tangent' and 'digression' mean a move away from the main subject.

m: real and able to be seen, felt or measured; concrete
x: After months of saving, we could finally see tangible progress toward buying a car.
The manager wanted tangible results, not just more promises of improvement.
The researchers found no tangible evidence that the supplement improved memory.
Residents say they have yet to see tangible benefits from the new highway.
There was a tangible tension in the room when her ex walked in.
tc: The investors were tired of vague promises; they wanted ______ results they could actually measure in profits.
The contrast with 'vague promises' and 'actually measure' show the blank means concrete.
se: The police found no ______ evidence linking him to the crime.
concrete
Both 'tangible' and 'concrete' describe real, definite evidence.

m: equal in seriousness or effect to something else (used with 'to')
x: Not replying to her wedding invitation would be tantamount to an insult.
Missing the deadline again would be tantamount to resigning, as far as the client is concerned.
The professor warned that copying a friend's code was tantamount to plagiarism.
Critics argued that the new law was tantamount to censorship of the press.
For her, forgetting their anniversary was tantamount to saying he no longer cared.
tc: The lawyer warned that refusing to answer the question would be ______ to admitting guilt in the eyes of the jury.
The refusal would have the same effect as admitting guilt, so the blank means equivalent.
se: Cutting the budget by half would be ______ to closing the department altogether.
equivalent
Both 'tantamount to' and 'equivalent to' mean having the same effect as closing it.

m: to damage or spoil the good quality or reputation of something
x: One rude waiter can tarnish an entire restaurant's reputation online.
The accounting scandal tarnished the firm's image for years.
Evidence of fabricated data tarnished the scientist's otherwise distinguished career.
Allegations of match-fixing have tarnished the image of cricket in several countries.
He feared that admitting his mistake would tarnish her opinion of him.
tc: Having spent decades building a spotless record, the judge was horrified that a single careless remark could ______ his reputation.
The contrast with 'spotless record' shows the blank means to damage.
se: The company worried that the product recall would ______ its brand among loyal customers.
taint
Both 'tarnish' and 'taint' mean to damage the brand's good name.

m: not certain or fixed; done hesitantly
x: We have tentative plans to go camping next weekend, depending on the weather.
The two companies reached a tentative agreement, which still needs board approval.
The researchers offered a tentative explanation but called for more experiments.
Both sides took tentative steps toward peace talks after months of fighting.
She gave him a tentative smile, unsure whether he would remember her.
tc: The date for the conference is still ______, so please don't book flights until the organizers confirm it.
'Until the organizers confirm it' shows the date is not yet fixed.
se: The schedule is only ______ and may change once we hear back from the venue.
provisional
Both 'tentative' and 'provisional' mean not yet final.

m: to prevent someone from doing what they are trying to do
x: A sudden downpour thwarted our plans for a picnic in the park.
Quick action by the IT team thwarted a hacking attempt on the company's servers.
A lack of funding thwarted the lab's efforts to expand its research.
Police say they thwarted a plot to rob the central bank.
Her parents tried to thwart the romance, but that only made the couple more determined.
tc: The guards managed to ______ the prisoners' escape just as they reached the outer wall.
'Just as they reached the outer wall' implies the escape was stopped at the last moment.
se: Security experts are working to ______ cyberattacks before they can cause damage.
foil
Both 'thwart' and 'foil' mean to stop the attacks from succeeding.

m: calm, peaceful and free from disturbance
x: We rented a tranquil cottage by the lake, far from traffic and noise.
The office has a tranquil garden where staff can take a quiet break.
The library's tranquil reading room is perfect for long hours of study.
Scientists say tranquil green spaces can lower stress levels in city dwellers.
After the chaos of the wedding, they spent a tranquil week alone together by the sea.
tc: After the roaring traffic of the city, the mountain village felt wonderfully ______, with only birdsong breaking the silence.
The contrast with 'roaring traffic' and 'only birdsong' show the blank means peaceful.
se: The lake was perfectly ______ at dawn, its surface as smooth as glass.
calm
Both 'tranquil' and 'calm' describe the undisturbed lake.

m: to go beyond the usual limits of something
x: Good food has a way of transcending language barriers at a family dinner.
The new manager's vision transcended old departmental rivalries and brought everyone together.
Great literature transcends its own time and speaks to readers centuries later.
In South Asia, cricket transcends sport and becomes a matter of national pride.
Their friendship transcended distance, surviving years of living on different continents.
tc: Rather than being confined to one culture, her music seems to ______ national borders, finding fans on every continent.
'Rather than being confined' signals that the blank means to go beyond limits.
se: A truly great teacher can ______ the limits of the textbook and inspire a lifelong love of learning.
surpass
Both 'transcend' and 'surpass' mean to go beyond the textbook's limits.

m: willing to betray trust; disloyal
x: My treacherous roommate told our landlord about the cat I'd been hiding.
The company discovered that a treacherous employee had been leaking its plans to a competitor.
The novel's plot turns on a treacherous adviser who secretly poisons the king.
Historians still debate whether the general was treacherous or simply incompetent.
She never forgave the treacherous friend who spread her secrets around campus.
tc: The king trusted his advisers completely, never suspecting that the most ______ among them was secretly plotting with his enemies.
Secretly plotting with enemies despite being trusted shows the blank means disloyal.
se: The rebels were betrayed by ______ officers who revealed their hiding place to the enemy.
traitorous
Both 'treacherous' and 'traitorous' describe officers who betrayed their side.

m: fear or anxiety about something that may happen
x: I opened the electricity bill with some trepidation after a month of running the air conditioner.
She walked into her first board meeting with a mixture of excitement and trepidation.
Many students approach their thesis defense with trepidation, no matter how well prepared they are.
Investors are watching the upcoming election with growing trepidation.
He dialed her number with trepidation, unsure whether she would even pick up.
tc: Although she had rehearsed for weeks, she stepped onto the stage with ______, her hands shaking as she reached for the microphone.
Her shaking hands show the blank means nervous fear.
se: Many parents feel considerable ______ as their children leave home for university abroad.
apprehension
Both 'trepidation' and 'apprehension' mean anxious worry about what may happen.

m: a cause of great trouble or suffering
x: Learning to drive in Dhaka traffic came with its share of trials and tribulations.
The book describes the tribulations of running a small bakery during a recession.
My thesis came with countless tribulations, from crashed hard drives to missing data.
The documentary follows the tribulations of migrant workers living far from their families.
Through every tribulation of their early marriage, they stuck together.
tc: The refugees had endured hunger, illness and every other kind of ______ before finally reaching safety.
The list 'hunger, illness and every other kind of' shows the blank means suffering.
se: Her memoir describes the ______ she faced as a single mother working two jobs.
hardship
Both 'tribulation' and 'hardship' mean the suffering she went through.

m: a loud, confused noise or a state of great disorder
x: I could barely hear my mother on the phone over the tumult of the street market.
After the founder's sudden resignation, the company was in tumult for weeks.
The professor waited for the tumult in the lecture hall to die down before announcing the results.
The country was plunged into political tumult after the disputed election.
Her calm voice was a refuge from the emotional tumult of his divorce.
tc: When the referee's controversial decision was announced, the stadium erupted in ______, with fans shouting and throwing bottles onto the field.
'Shouting and throwing bottles' describes noisy disorder.
se: The ______ in the streets after the announcement made it impossible to hear anything.
uproar
Both 'tumult' and 'uproar' mean loud, confused noise.

m: cruel, unjust and absolute use of power or government
x: My grandfather still remembers the fear people felt under the tyranny of a military regime.
Employees complained about the tyranny of a manager who controlled every minute of their day.
The course examines how ordinary citizens resisted tyranny in twentieth-century Europe.
The revolution promised to free the people from decades of tyranny.
She finally escaped the emotional tyranny of a partner who dictated whom she could see.
tc: After years of ______ under a ruler who jailed all critics, the citizens finally rose up and demanded free elections.
A ruler who jailed all critics describes cruel, oppressive rule.
se: The pamphlet urged citizens to resist the king's ______ and fight for their freedom.
oppression
Both 'tyranny' and 'oppression' describe the king's cruel, unjust rule.

m: not embarrassed or ashamed; open and unapologetic
x: He is an unabashed fan of cheesy pop songs and sings along loudly in the car.
She showed unabashed ambition in her interview, saying she wanted the director's job within five years.
The professor admitted with unabashed enthusiasm that he had read the novel twenty times.
The minister's unabashed support for the coal industry drew protests from environmental groups.
Their unabashed affection for each other made some of their friends roll their eyes.
tc: Far from hiding his love of children's cartoons, he was ______ about it and happily discussed them at dinner parties.
'Far from hiding' and 'happily discussed' show he was not embarrassed.
se: She spoke with ______ pride about her humble beginnings in a small village.
unashamed
Both 'unabashed' and 'unashamed' mean she felt no embarrassment.

m: fully in agreement; agreed to by everyone involved
x: After a brief debate, the decision to order pizza for dinner was unanimous.
The board gave unanimous approval to the new hiring policy.
The thesis committee reached a unanimous verdict that her work deserved distinction.
Parliament passed the flood relief bill by a unanimous vote.
Her friends were unanimous in their opinion that she should leave him.
tc: Not a single member objected, so the committee's decision was ______.
'Not a single member objected' defines the blank as agreed by everyone.
se: The proposal received the ______ support of the staff, with no one voting against it.
undivided
Both 'unanimous' and 'undivided' mean every staff member supported it.

m: modest and not wanting to attract attention
x: The best biryani in town comes from an unassuming little shop near the railway station.
Despite running the company, he was an unassuming man who ate lunch with the junior staff.
The unassuming graduate student turned out to be the author of the department's most cited paper.
From the outside, the unassuming building gives no hint of the research being done inside.
She was drawn to his unassuming manner, so different from the loud men she usually met.
tc: Although he had won several international prizes, the scientist remained ______, never mentioning his awards unless someone asked.
Never mentioning his prizes shows he was modest despite his success.
se: Despite her enormous wealth, she was ______ and preferred to shop at the local market.
modest
Both 'unassuming' and 'modest' describe someone who does not show off.

m: uncontrolled; unrestrained
x: The children greeted the snow with unbridled joy, running outside without their coats.
The firm's collapse was blamed on unbridled greed among its senior executives.
The young researcher's unbridled enthusiasm sometimes ran ahead of the evidence.
Critics warn that unbridled capitalism widens the gap between rich and poor.
She burst into the room with unbridled excitement to tell him the news.
tc: Without any regulators to restrain them, the banks gave free rein to their ______ greed, lending recklessly to anyone.
'Without any regulators to restrain them' shows the greed was uncontrolled.
se: The fans' ______ joy after the final whistle spilled out into the streets.
unrestrained
Both 'unbridled' and 'unrestrained' mean the joy was not held back.

m: not discouraged or frightened by difficulty or danger
x: My grandmother was undaunted by the long queue and waited three hours to renew her passport.
Two failed product launches left the team undaunted, and work on a third began immediately.
She remained undaunted when reviewers rejected her paper, and resubmitted it to another journal.
Rescue workers, undaunted by the storm, continued searching for survivors through the night.
Undaunted by her parents' disapproval, he kept writing to her every week.
tc: Though the climbers had lost two tents in the avalanche, they remained ______ and pressed on toward the summit.
'Though' signals contrast, and 'pressed on' shows they were not discouraged.
se: ______ by repeated rejections, the young writer kept sending her manuscript to publishers.
undeterred
Both 'undaunted' and 'undeterred' mean she was not discouraged by the rejections.

m: to gradually or secretly weaken or damage something
x: Constant late-night snacking undermines all the effort I put in at the gym.
Gossip about the new manager undermined her authority before she had even started.
The discovery of a coding error undermined the study's main conclusions.
Repeated corruption scandals have undermined public trust in the police across the country.
Over the years, his jealousy and constant suspicion slowly undermined their relationship.
tc: The minister's repeated U-turns began to ______ public confidence, until few voters believed anything he promised.
Voters no longer believing him shows their confidence was gradually weakened.
se: Leaked documents threaten to ______ the government's claim that the project was safe.
weaken
Both 'undermine' and 'weaken' mean to make the claim less believable.

m: to move or lie in smooth, wavelike curves; to rise and fall gently
x: The fields of ripe wheat undulated gently in the evening breeze.
The new logo features a line that undulates across the page like a sound wave.
Students watched on screen as the jellyfish undulated slowly through the water.
The road undulates across the hills for miles before reaching the coast.
Her voice undulated softly as she sang the old lullaby to her baby.
tc: As the wind swept across the lake, the reeds began to ______ in long, rolling waves.
'In long, rolling waves' describes a smooth wavelike motion.
se: The silk banners began to ______ in the breeze, rising and falling like waves.
ripple
Both 'undulate' and 'ripple' describe a gentle wavelike movement.

m: leaving no doubt; completely clear and definite
x: When I asked my father if I could borrow the car, his answer was an unequivocal no.
After weeks of revisions, the client finally gave unequivocal approval to the final design.
The study provides unequivocal evidence that smoking damages the lungs.
The government issued an unequivocal denial of the reports about secret military talks.
She made her feelings unequivocal: she would not move abroad without him.
tc: Unlike his earlier vague statements, the coach's latest comment was ______: he would resign at the end of the season.
'Unlike his earlier vague statements' signals that the blank means completely clear.
se: The board gave its ______ support to the merger, leaving no room for doubt.
unambiguous
Both 'unequivocal' and 'unambiguous' mean the support was completely clear.

m: free from restrictions or control
x: With my parents away for the weekend, I enjoyed unfettered access to the television.
The new director was given unfettered control over hiring decisions.
Academic freedom means researchers should enjoy unfettered inquiry, whatever their conclusions.
Critics worry that unfettered surveillance could threaten citizens' privacy.
After the divorce, she relished the unfettered freedom to plan her own life.
tc: Once the censorship laws were repealed, journalists finally enjoyed ______ freedom to report on the government.
The repeal of censorship laws means the journalists' freedom was no longer restricted.
se: The investigators were promised ______ access to all company records.
unrestricted
Both 'unfettered' and 'unrestricted' mean access without any limits.

m: done by one person, group or country alone, without the agreement of others
x: My roommate made a unilateral decision to get a dog, without even asking me.
Management's unilateral change to working hours angered the union.
The professor's unilateral extension of the deadline surprised the other examiners.
The country declared a unilateral ceasefire, hoping the rebels would follow its lead.
Her unilateral decision to move to Canada felt like a betrayal to him.
tc: Instead of consulting its allies, the government took ______ action, imposing sanctions entirely on its own.
'Instead of consulting its allies' and 'entirely on its own' define the blank.
se: The landlord's ______ decision to raise the rent without any discussion upset every tenant.
one-sided
Both 'unilateral' and 'one-sided' mean the decision was made by the landlord alone.

m: having no moral principles; willing to act dishonestly or unfairly to get what one wants
x: An unscrupulous mechanic charged my father for repairs that were never actually done on his car.
Several unscrupulous managers took credit for their juniors' work and quietly blocked their promotions.
Students should be wary of unscrupulous agents who promise guaranteed admission to foreign universities for a hefty fee.
Regulators have accused unscrupulous lenders of trapping poor families in endless cycles of debt.
She realised too late that her charming business partner was utterly unscrupulous about money.
tc: Unlike his honest predecessor, the new contractor was entirely ______, cutting corners and bribing inspectors whenever he could.
The contrast with 'his honest predecessor' and the examples of bribery show the blank means lacking moral principles.
se: The elderly are often targeted by ______ salesmen who pressure them into buying worthless insurance policies.
unprincipled
Both 'unscrupulous' and 'unprincipled' describe people with no moral restraint, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: not justified or deserved; lacking a good reason
x: Your anger at the waiter was unwarranted, since the delay was entirely the kitchen's fault.
Management apologised for the unwarranted criticism directed at the night shift in last week's meeting.
Reviewers felt the paper's sweeping conclusions were unwarranted given its very small sample size.
Civil liberties groups condemned the unwarranted searches carried out without any evidence of wrongdoing.
He felt hurt by his sister's unwarranted suspicion that he had taken the money.
tc: Since the engineers' tests showed the bridge was perfectly safe, the public panic about its collapse was ______.
The tests proving the bridge safe show the panic had no justification.
se: The committee rejected the complaint, calling the accusations against the referee entirely ______.
unjustified
Both 'unwarranted' and 'unjustified' mean lacking a good reason, so the meaning stays the same.

m: refusing to change one's position or give way; firm and inflexible
x: My grandmother was unyielding on one rule: nobody ate dinner until everyone was at the table.
Despite weeks of negotiations, the union remained unyielding in its demand for higher wages.
Her thesis supervisor was unyielding about deadlines, so she submitted every chapter on time.
The government's unyielding stance on the new tax law sparked protests across the country.
His unyielding pride kept him from apologising, even when he knew he was wrong.
tc: Although her colleagues pleaded with her to compromise, the chairwoman was ______ and refused to alter a single clause.
Refusing to change anything despite colleagues' pleading signals a firm, inflexible attitude.
se: The coach was ______ in his insistence that every player attend morning practice.
adamant
Both 'unyielding' and 'adamant' describe someone who will not back down, giving the same meaning.

m: polished, courteous and sophisticated in manner, especially in social situations
x: Our urbane host moved easily between guests, making everyone feel welcome at the dinner party.
Clients loved dealing with the firm's urbane senior partner, who never lost his composure.
The professor's urbane lectures, full of wit and literary references, were always packed.
Known for his urbane manner, the ambassador defused the diplomatic row with a few well-chosen words.
She was drawn to his urbane charm, though her friends found him a little too smooth.
tc: Whereas his brother was loud and awkward at parties, Daniel was ______, charming every guest with his polished conversation.
'Whereas' contrasts loud and awkward behaviour with polished conversation, so the blank means sophisticated and courteous.
se: The novel's narrator is ______ and witty, a man perfectly at ease in the finest drawing rooms of London.
sophisticated
Both 'urbane' and 'sophisticated' describe a refined, worldly person, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: showing courage or determination, especially in a difficult or dangerous situation
x: Despite a valiant effort, the firefighters could not save the old warehouse from the flames.
Our small team put up a valiant fight against the corporate giant for the government contract.
In a valiant last stand, the Bangladeshi tail-enders batted for over an hour to save the Test match.
Historians praise the valiant soldiers who held the bridge against overwhelming odds.
She made a valiant attempt to hide her disappointment when she opened the rejection letter.
tc: Although the rescuers ultimately failed, their ______ efforts in the freezing storm earned them medals for bravery.
'Medals for bravery' shows the efforts were courageous.
se: The ______ villagers defended their homes against the floodwaters for three days without rest.
courageous
Both 'valiant' and 'courageous' mean brave and determined, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to confirm or prove that something is true, correct or legitimate
x: Her doctor ran a second test to validate the surprising results of the first one.
The engineering team needs two more weeks to validate the new software before release.
Later experiments validated the young researcher's controversial hypothesis about the virus.
Election officials worked through the night to validate thousands of disputed ballots.
Sometimes you don't want advice; you just want a friend to validate your feelings.
tc: The theory remained mere speculation until a series of careful experiments began to ______ it.
'Remained mere speculation until' signals that the experiments finally confirmed the theory.
se: Independent laboratories were asked to ______ the company's claims about the drug's effectiveness.
verify
Both 'validate' and 'verify' mean to check and confirm that something is true.

m: the leading position or people in a movement, field or new development
x: My aunt was in the vanguard of women in our village who went to university.
Our company wants to stay in the vanguard of renewable energy technology for the next decade.
These young poets formed the vanguard of a new literary movement in the 1950s.
Students formed the vanguard of the 1952 Language Movement in Dhaka.
She has always felt happiest in the vanguard, trying new ideas before anyone else dares to.
tc: Far from lagging behind its rivals, the small startup was in the ______ of artificial intelligence research.
'Far from lagging behind' signals the opposite idea: the leading position.
se: The city has been in the ______ of efforts to reduce plastic waste.
forefront
'In the vanguard of' and 'in the forefront of' both mean leading, so the meaning is the same.

m: to defeat thoroughly; to overcome completely
x: After months of practice, he finally vanquished his older brother at chess.
Our sales team vanquished its closest competitor to win the lucrative government contract.
Medical researchers hope that new vaccines will one day vanquish malaria for good.
The rebels were vanquished in a single battle, and their leaders fled abroad.
She worked with a therapist for a year to vanquish her fear of public speaking.
tc: Rather than merely holding off the invading army, the general was determined to ______ it completely.
'Rather than merely holding off' signals a stronger action: total defeat.
se: In the final round, the young champion managed to ______ an opponent twice her age.
defeat
Both 'vanquish' and 'defeat' mean to beat an opponent, giving the same meaning.

m: marked with patches or streaks of different colours; varied in appearance
x: My mother grows variegated ivy on the balcony because its green-and-white leaves brighten the flat.
The new office carpet has a variegated pattern that hides coffee stains remarkably well.
Botanists study why some plants produce variegated leaves with pale, chlorophyll-free patches.
The city's variegated population includes migrants from dozens of countries and cultures.
She remembered the variegated sky of her childhood evenings, streaked with orange, pink and violet.
tc: Unlike the plain green species, this hybrid has ______ leaves splashed with cream and yellow.
The contrast with 'plain green' and the mention of cream and yellow splashes point to many colours.
se: The gardener chose a ______ shrub whose leaves were patterned with green, white and gold.
multicoloured
Both 'variegated' and 'multicoloured' describe leaves of several colours, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: punishment inflicted on someone in return for an injury or wrong; revenge
x: After his bicycle was stolen, my cousin swore vengeance on whoever had taken it.
The fired employee sought vengeance by leaking confidential documents to the press.
Greek tragedies often explore how the desire for vengeance destroys entire families.
Police fear the shooting was an act of vengeance for last month's gang killing.
She had to let go of her thirst for vengeance before she could finally move on.
tc: Instead of forgiving those who had wronged him, the count spent twenty years plotting his ______.
'Instead of forgiving' signals the opposite of forgiveness: revenge.
se: The villagers feared the warlord would take ______ on them for sheltering his enemies.
revenge
'Take vengeance on' and 'take revenge on' mean exactly the same thing.

m: green with grass or other rich, healthy vegetation
x: After the monsoon rains, the fields around our village become verdant and lush again.
We took our lunch break in the verdant courtyard behind the office building.
Ecologists warn that parts of the verdant rainforest could become dry savanna within decades.
The brochure promised verdant hills, but we arrived to find brown, parched grass everywhere.
She often thought fondly of the verdant garden where she had played as a child.
tc: Years of drought had turned the once ______ meadows into dusty, barren fields.
'Once' and the contrast with 'dusty, barren fields' show the meadows used to be green and lush.
se: The train wound through ______ valleys covered in tea bushes and tall grass.
lush
Both 'verdant' and 'lush' describe richly green vegetation, so the meaning stays the same.

m: the everyday language spoken by ordinary people in a region, rather than formal or literary language
x: My grandfather told his best stories in the local vernacular, full of words I never learned at school.
The new manager insisted that customer letters be written in the vernacular rather than legal jargon.
Linguists recorded hundreds of hours of rural speech to document the regional vernacular.
Reformers translated the Bible into the vernacular so that ordinary people could read it themselves.
He felt closest to his old friends when they slipped into the familiar vernacular of their hometown.
tc: Rather than writing in the formal Latin of scholars, the poet composed his verses in the ______ of the common people.
The contrast with 'formal Latin of scholars' and the phrase 'of the common people' point to everyday speech.
se: In the local ______, the word 'lift' simply means a free ride in someone's car.
dialect
Both 'vernacular' and 'dialect' refer to the everyday speech of a region, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: able to adapt to many different activities, or to be used for many different purposes
x: A good cast-iron pan is so versatile that you can fry, bake and roast with it.
Employers value versatile engineers who can switch easily between design, testing and client meetings.
As a versatile scholar, she has published widely on economics, history and philosophy.
Scientists describe graphene as one of the most versatile materials ever discovered.
He admired how versatile his wife was, equally at ease fixing a tap or writing a poem.
tc: Unlike his narrowly specialised rivals, the actor was remarkably ______, playing comedy, tragedy and action roles with equal ease.
The contrast with 'narrowly specialised rivals' and the range of roles show the blank means adaptable.
se: The company needs a ______ assistant who can handle accounts, scheduling and customer queries.
adaptable
Both 'versatile' and 'adaptable' describe someone able to do many different tasks.

m: a small remaining trace of something that has disappeared or no longer exists
x: A few crumbling walls are the only vestiges of the old palace in the centre of town.
The new chief executive swept away every vestige of the founder's informal management style.
Biologists once regarded the human appendix as a vestige of a larger digestive organ.
Some politicians argue that the old law is a vestige of colonial rule and should be repealed.
When she saw him again, she felt not a vestige of her old affection for him.
tc: Although the empire had collapsed centuries earlier, one ______ of its grandeur survived: a single ruined temple on the hill.
The empire's collapse and the single surviving temple point to a remaining trace.
se: By the end of the interview, the last ______ of her confidence had disappeared.
trace
'The last vestige' and 'the last trace' both mean the final small remainder of something.

m: a change of circumstances or fortune, usually an unwelcome one; (plural) ups and downs
x: Their friendship has survived the vicissitudes of three moves, two marriages and a pandemic.
Small business owners must learn to cope with the vicissitudes of the market.
The biography traces the vicissitudes of the composer's career, from fame to poverty and back.
Farmers in the delta have always lived with the vicissitudes of monsoon floods and drought.
Through all the vicissitudes of life, her mother's love remained constant.
tc: Every ______ of fortune, whether sudden wealth or sudden ruin, seemed only to make the old merchant calmer.
'Sudden wealth or sudden ruin' defines the blank as a change in fortune.
se: She endured every ______ in her long career with remarkable good humour.
upheaval
Both 'vicissitude' and 'upheaval' refer to a disruptive change in circumstances.

m: to compete eagerly with others in order to win or achieve something
x: My two nephews vie for their grandmother's attention whenever we visit her.
Dozens of candidates are vying for just three positions in the graduate trainee programme.
Top students from across the country vie for a handful of seats at the engineering university.
Three cities are vying to host the next Olympic Games.
Her heart and her head vied with each other as she decided whether to accept his proposal.
tc: With only one scholarship available, the forty applicants had no choice but to ______ fiercely for it.
One scholarship among forty applicants means they must compete for it.
se: Several technology giants continue to ______ for dominance in the cloud computing market.
compete
Both 'vie' and 'compete' mean to struggle against rivals for something.

m: keeping careful watch for possible danger or difficulties
x: Parents need to stay vigilant when their toddlers are playing near the pond.
Our IT department warns staff to be vigilant about suspicious emails asking for passwords.
During the exam, three vigilant supervisors patrolled the hall to prevent any cheating.
Health officials urged citizens to remain vigilant as dengue cases rose across the city.
After the break-in, she became more vigilant and checked the locks twice every night.
tc: Because thieves had been active in the neighbourhood, residents were urged to stay ______ rather than complacent.
The threat of thieves and the contrast with 'complacent' show the blank means watchful.
se: Lifeguards must stay ______ at all times, scanning the water for swimmers in trouble.
alert
Both 'vigilant' and 'alert' mean watching carefully for danger.

m: a person with outstanding technical skill, especially in music or another art
x: My neighbour's son is a violin virtuoso who practises six hours a day.
In our office, Rafiq is the spreadsheet virtuoso everyone calls when a formula breaks.
The conservatory accepts only students it believes could become true virtuosos.
Critics hailed the young pianist as a virtuoso after her stunning debut with the orchestra.
Watching her father, a sitar virtuoso, play at weddings always filled her with pride.
tc: Far from being an amateur, the guitarist was a true ______, dazzling audiences with breathtaking technique.
'Far from being an amateur' and 'breathtaking technique' point to a supremely skilled performer.
se: The festival will close with a recital by a cello ______ famous for his flawless technique.
maestro
Both 'virtuoso' and 'maestro' mean a highly skilled musician, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: expressing opinions or feelings loudly and forcefully
x: My uncle is a vociferous critic of the city's traffic and complains about it at every family dinner.
Despite vociferous objections from staff, management went ahead and cut the annual bonus.
The seminar turned into a vociferous debate about the ethics of genetic engineering.
Vociferous protesters gathered outside parliament on Sunday, demanding urgent action on air pollution.
She was vociferous in defending her younger brother whenever anyone teased him.
tc: Far from accepting the decision quietly, the fans were ______ in their protests, chanting and shouting outside the stadium for hours.
'Far from accepting the decision quietly' and the chanting and shouting point to loud, forceful protest.
se: The proposal to close the library met with ______ opposition from local residents.
vehement
Both 'vociferous' and 'vehement' describe strong, forcefully expressed opposition.

m: the power of making one's own choices or decisions; free will
x: My son started reading novels entirely of his own volition, without any pushing from us.
She left the company of her own volition; she was not fired, whatever the rumours say.
Philosophers have long debated whether human volition is truly free or determined by prior causes.
The court had to decide whether the confession was an act of genuine volition or the result of pressure.
He wanted her to stay with him of her own volition, not out of guilt or duty.
tc: Nobody pressured her into volunteering; she joined the relief effort of her own ______.
'Nobody pressured her' shows she acted by her own free choice.
se: He insisted that he had resigned of his own ______ and not under pressure from the board.
accord
'Of his own volition' and 'of his own accord' both mean voluntarily.

m: to choose not to insist on or use a right, claim, fee or rule
x: The restaurant manager waived the service charge because our food arrived so late.
HR agreed to waive the usual two-year experience requirement for the talented applicant.
Several American universities waive application fees for students from low-income countries.
The defendant waived his right to a jury trial and chose to be tried by a judge alone.
She waived her share of the inheritance so that her younger sister could keep the family house.
tc: Because the student could not afford the charge, the university agreed to ______ it rather than enforce payment.
'Rather than enforce payment' signals that the university chose not to insist on the charge.
se: She chose to ______ her right to compensation so that the small shop would not go bankrupt.
relinquish
Both 'waive' and 'relinquish' mean to give up a right voluntarily.

m: difficult to control or predict; straying from what is expected or proper
x: Our wayward goat keeps escaping and eating the neighbour's vegetables.
The manager spent hours tracking down a wayward shipment that had been sent to the wrong city.
The school runs a mentoring programme to guide wayward teenagers back to their studies.
Engineers safely destroyed the wayward rocket after it veered off course.
Her parents prayed that their wayward son would one day come home and settle down.
tc: Unlike her obedient older sisters, the youngest daughter was ______, running away from home twice before she turned fifteen.
The contrast with 'obedient' and running away from home point to someone hard to control.
se: The charity helps ______ teenagers who have dropped out of school and drifted into crime.
unruly
Both 'wayward' and 'unruly' describe young people who are hard to control.

m: to persuade someone to do or give something by flattery or gentle coaxing
x: My little sister always manages to wheedle extra pocket money out of our father.
He tried to wheedle a day off from his boss by praising her leadership all week.
The student wheedled an extension from his professor with a sad story about his broken laptop.
Lobbyists spent months trying to wheedle concessions out of reluctant lawmakers.
She refused to be wheedled into lending him money again, no matter how sweetly he asked.
tc: Rather than demanding the car keys outright, the teenager tried to ______ them from his mother with compliments and promises.
'Rather than demanding' and 'compliments and promises' point to persuasion by flattery.
se: The children tried to ______ their grandmother into letting them stay up past midnight.
cajole
Both 'wheedle' and 'cajole' mean to persuade by flattery or sweet talk.

m: clever at gaining an advantage, often by tricks or deceit; cunning
x: A wily street vendor quickly doubled his prices when he spotted the tourists.
The wily negotiator let the other side talk until they revealed their real budget.
In the folk tale, a wily fox tricks the crow into dropping its piece of cheese.
The wily senator had survived five elections by changing sides at just the right moment.
Her grandmother was a wily old woman who always knew when the children were lying.
tc: Although he seemed simple and harmless, the old trader was actually quite ______, outwitting every buyer who tried to cheat him.
'Although he seemed simple' sets up a contrast, and outwitting buyers shows cunning.
se: The ______ fox slipped past the farmer's traps night after night.
cunning
Both 'wily' and 'cunning' mean clever at tricking others.

m: having or showing a gentle, sad longing for something lost or out of reach
x: Looking at old photos of our school trips always makes me a little wistful.
On his last day at the firm, he took a wistful look around the office where he had spent twenty years.
The professor's essay is a wistful account of the village school where he first learned to read.
The documentary paints a wistful portrait of the old Dhaka neighbourhoods now being demolished.
She gave a wistful smile when her friend mentioned the boy she had loved at university.
tc: Hearing the old song on the radio, he felt ______, longing for the carefree summers of his youth.
'Longing for the carefree summers of his youth' defines the gentle, regretful feeling in the blank.
se: She cast a ______ glance at the house where she had grown up.
nostalgic
Both 'wistful' and 'nostalgic' express a sad longing for the past.

m: to become dry and shrivelled; to lose strength or gradually decline
x: I forgot to water the plants for a week, and the basil withered on the windowsill.
Without fresh investment, the company's research division slowly withered away.
Studies show that language skills wither quickly if students stop practising them after exams.
Many rural towns have withered as young people move to the cities for work.
Her hopes of a reconciliation withered when he failed to answer any of her letters.
tc: Without the summer rains, the crops began to ______ and turn brown in the scorching sun.
The lack of rain, the scorching sun and turning brown all point to drying up.
se: Flowers left in a hot car will quickly ______ and lose their colour.
wilt
Both 'wither' and 'wilt' mean to droop and dry out from lack of water.

m: to take something from someone by force or with great effort
x: My son wrested the remote control from his sister and changed the channel.
After a long boardroom battle, the investors wrested control of the company from its founder.
Scientists are still trying to wrest meaningful patterns from the huge amount of climate data.
The opposition hopes to wrest power from the ruling party in next year's election.
She finally wrested a confession from him about where he had been all night.
tc: Unable to win power through elections, the rebels tried to ______ it from the government by force.
'By force' after failing to win legitimately signals taking something violently.
se: The small party is determined to ______ control of the city council from its rivals.
seize
Both 'wrest' and 'seize' mean to take control forcefully.

m: using or showing dry, slightly mocking humour
x: When the bus broke down again, my father made a wry comment about Dhaka's 'world-class' transport.
Our manager gave a wry smile when the printer jammed for the third time that morning.
The professor's wry asides kept the dull statistics lecture surprisingly entertaining.
The columnist offers a wry look at the absurdities of modern politics.
She had a wry sense of humour that took strangers a while to appreciate.
tc: Instead of complaining openly, the old man responded with ______ humour, joking dryly about his own misfortune.
'Joking dryly' about misfortune defines the dry, mocking humour in the blank.
se: His ______ remarks about the company's endless meetings made everyone at the table laugh.
sardonic
Both 'wry' and 'sardonic' describe dry, mocking humour.

m: a soft, gentle breeze
x: A cool zephyr drifted through the open window and finally broke the afternoon heat.
We held the team lunch on the terrace, where a light zephyr kept everyone comfortable.
Romantic poets often used the zephyr as a symbol of spring and renewal.
Sailors in the regatta complained that a mere zephyr was not enough to fill their sails.
As they sat on the riverbank, a gentle zephyr carried the scent of jasmine towards them.
tc: Far from the fierce gale the sailors had feared, only the softest ______ stirred the sails.
The contrast with 'fierce gale' and 'softest' point to a gentle breeze.
se: On the veranda, a warm evening ______ rustled the pages of her book.
breeze
Both 'zephyr' and 'breeze' mean a light, gentle wind.

m: to make someone feel embarrassed, ashamed or self-conscious
x: I was thoroughly abashed when I realised I had been calling my new neighbour by the wrong name for months.
Nothing seemed to abash the new intern, who asked the chief executive questions at every meeting.
The student was abashed to discover that her professor had read her rude comments online.
The minister looked abashed when reporters asked about his missing tax returns.
His sincere apology abashed her, and she regretted shouting at him.
tc: The brash young lawyer believed nothing could ______ him, until the judge publicly mocked his careless error.
The contrast between his brash confidence and being publicly mocked shows the blank means to embarrass.
se: Even harsh criticism from the senior editors failed to ______ the bold young reporter.
disconcert
Both 'abash' and 'disconcert' mean to make someone lose composure or feel uneasy.

m: to encourage or help someone do something wrong, especially a crime
x: My brother abetted my late-night snacking by hiding chocolate at the back of the kitchen cupboard.
The accountant was fired for abetting his boss in hiding losses from the shareholders.
The study examines how social media algorithms may abet the spread of misinformation.
He was charged with aiding and abetting the robbers by driving their getaway car.
She felt guilty for having abetted her friend's lies to his parents.
tc: Although he did not steal anything himself, the guard was accused of conspiring to ______ the thieves by leaving the vault unlocked.
Leaving the vault unlocked for thieves shows he helped them commit a crime.
se: Officials who ______ smugglers by ignoring illegal shipments will face prosecution.
assist
Both 'abet' and 'assist' mean to help, here in wrongdoing.

m: causing disgust and hatred; morally repugnant
x: My mother finds the idea of wasting food abhorrent, so we always finish our plates.
Bullying of junior staff is abhorrent and will not be tolerated in this company.
The historian described the colonial labour camps as abhorrent violations of human dignity.
World leaders condemned the abhorrent attack on the hospital, which killed dozens of patients.
Lying to his own family was abhorrent to him, even to protect their feelings.
tc: Far from finding the practice merely distasteful, the reformers considered child labour utterly ______ and campaigned to abolish it.
'Far from merely distasteful' signals a much stronger word meaning disgusting and morally wrong.
se: Most citizens find the idea of torturing prisoners ______.
repugnant
Both 'abhorrent' and 'repugnant' mean morally disgusting.

m: extremely bad, miserable or degrading; also completely lacking pride or dignity
x: My cousin offered an abject apology after crashing my car into the gate.
The project ended in abject failure after the client suddenly withdrew its funding.
Sociologists have studied the abject living conditions in the city's informal settlements.
Millions of people still live in abject poverty despite the country's economic growth.
After the breakup he sank into abject misery that none of his friends could ease.
tc: Far from enjoying modest comfort, the refugees lived in ______ poverty, without clean water or shelter.
'Far from enjoying modest comfort' and the lack of water and shelter point to extreme, wretched poverty.
se: The family's ______ circumstances shocked the visiting doctors.
wretched
Both 'abject' and 'wretched' describe extremely miserable conditions.

m: to give up or reject something valued or desired; to deny oneself
x: He decided to abnegate all luxuries for a year and live on a strict budget.
The founder abnegated her salary for six months so the struggling startup could pay its staff.
Some philosophers argue that true wisdom requires us to abnegate worldly desires.
The government cannot simply abnegate its responsibility for the safety of factory workers.
She refused to abnegate her own dreams just to satisfy her family's expectations.
tc: Unlike his brothers, who indulged every whim, the young monk chose to ______ all comforts and possessions.
The contrast with brothers who 'indulged every whim' shows the monk gave up comforts.
se: The ascetic chose to ______ all personal wealth and live among the poor.
renounce
Both 'abnegate' and 'renounce' mean to give up something valued.

m: to hate something intensely; to regard with disgust
x: My father abominates loud music, so we keep the volume low when he's home.
Most of the staff abominate the new open-plan office and its constant noise.
The essayist abominated hypocrisy and attacked it in nearly everything he wrote.
Human rights campaigners abominate the use of child soldiers in civil wars.
She abominates being lied to, even about small things like where her husband spent the evening.
tc: Although he tolerated many faults in his friends, he came to ______ dishonesty and cut off anyone who lied to him.
The contrast with 'tolerated many faults' and cutting off liars show intense hatred of dishonesty.
se: Many voters ______ the corruption that has spread through local government.
detest
Both 'abominate' and 'detest' mean to hate intensely.

m: honest, legitimate and open; without any secrecy or deception
x: Don't worry, the car sale was completely aboveboard, and I have all the receipts.
The auditors confirmed that every transaction in the accounts was aboveboard.
