The manager burst into the meeting brandishing the sales figures as proof that the plan had failed.
Brandishing her acceptance letter, she ran to tell her parents she had been admitted to medical college.
Police said the robber had brandished a knife before escaping with the cash.
She brandished the old love letters in his face and demanded to know who had written them.
tc: Instead of keeping the knife hidden, the robber chose to ______ it in front of the terrified cashier to frighten her into opening the till.
The contrast with 'keeping the knife hidden' and the aim 'to frighten her' show he waved it threateningly.
se: The protesters began to ______ their placards angrily as the minister's car drove past.
wave
Both 'brandish' and 'wave' mean to move something about vigorously in the air, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a bold show of courage or confidence meant to impress, often hiding fear
x: Despite his bravado about the haunted house, my cousin refused to go upstairs alone.
The new trader's bravado vanished the moment he lost a large sum on his first deal.
Teenage bravado led several students to skip the safety briefing before the chemistry practical.
Behind the general's public bravado, the army was running short of food and ammunition.
She knew his bravado was only a mask for how frightened he felt about the surgery.
tc: His loud claims that he wasn't scared were pure ______; his shaking hands told everyone how frightened he really was.
The contrast between his loud claims and his shaking hands reveals a false show of courage.
se: Underneath all the ______, the young boxer was terrified of losing his first professional fight.
swagger
Both 'bravado' and 'swagger' mean a showy display of confidence, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: an act of breaking a law, agreement, rule or relationship of trust
x: Reading my diary without asking was a serious breach of trust, and I told my sister so.
The company fired him for a breach of confidentiality after he shared client data with a rival.
Copying a classmate's lab report is considered a breach of the university's academic code.
A massive data breach exposed the personal details of millions of bank customers.
Their friendship never recovered from the breach caused by that bitter argument.
tc: By leaking the confidential report to journalists, the official committed a clear ______ of his duty to the government.
Leaking a 'confidential report' signals the breaking of a duty, which is a breach.
se: The supplier's failure to deliver on time was a serious ______ of the agreement.
violation
Both 'breach' and 'violation' mean the breaking of an agreement, so the meaning stays the same.

m: to tolerate or allow something, usually used in the negative
x: My mother brooks no argument once she has decided what we are having for dinner.
Our new director brooks no delays and expects every report on her desk by Friday.
The professor brooked no excuses for late assignments, not even illness without a doctor's note.
The regime brooked no dissent, jailing anyone who criticised the government in public.
He was a proud man who would brook no criticism, even from the people who loved him.
tc: The general was so autocratic that he would ______ no disagreement from his officers, however politely it was expressed.
'So autocratic' signals that he would not tolerate any disagreement.
se: The strict headmistress would ______ no rudeness from her pupils.
tolerate
Both 'brook no' and 'tolerate no' mean refuse to put up with, so the sentence means the same.

m: to frighten someone into doing something with stern words, threats or looks
x: The car salesman tried to browbeat my father into buying the most expensive model.
Employees complained that the manager browbeat them into working unpaid overtime.
A good thesis supervisor guides students rather than browbeating them into agreeing.
Lawyers for the defence were accused of browbeating the young witness during cross-examination.
She refused to let her controlling boyfriend browbeat her into giving up her friends.
tc: Rather than persuading the committee with evidence, the chairman tried to ______ its members with threats and angry glares.
The contrast with 'persuading ... with evidence' and the mention of 'threats and angry glares' point to intimidation.
se: Some parents try to ______ their children into studying medicine, regardless of the children's own interests.
bully
Both 'browbeat someone into' and 'bully someone into' mean to pressure by intimidation, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a person or thing that protects or defends against danger; originally a defensive wall
x: For our family, my grandmother's savings were a bulwark against hard times.
A strong compliance team acts as a bulwark against costly legal mistakes.
Historians describe medieval monasteries as bulwarks of learning during centuries of turmoil.
The Sundarbans mangrove forest serves as a natural bulwark against cyclones for Bangladesh's coastal villages.
Her friends were a bulwark of support during the worst months of her divorce.
tc: Independent courts are often seen as the last ______ against tyranny, protecting citizens when every other safeguard has failed.
'Protecting citizens when every other safeguard has failed' restates the idea of a defensive barrier.
se: A free press remains the most important ______ against corruption in any democracy.
safeguard
Both 'bulwark' and 'safeguard' mean a protection against danger, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to lift someone's spirits or keep something, such as prices, at a high level
x: A long phone call with my best friend buoyed me up after a miserable week.
Strong holiday sales buoyed the company's share price despite fears of a recession.
Buoyed by his excellent mid-term results, he decided to apply for a scholarship abroad.
Rising oil prices continued to buoy the economies of the Gulf states.
She felt buoyed by her family's support when she decided to start her own business.
tc: Although the team was exhausted, the roar of the home crowd seemed to ______ the players, who found fresh energy in the final minutes.
The contrast with 'exhausted' and the phrase 'found fresh energy' show the crowd lifted their spirits.
se: The good news from the doctors did much to ______ the anxious family during a difficult week.
hearten
Both 'buoy' and 'hearten' mean to raise someone's spirits, so the sentence means the same.

m: a small, secret group of people plotting together, especially for political power
x: My sisters formed a little cabal to plan Mum's surprise birthday party without her finding out.
Staff suspected that a cabal of senior managers was secretly planning the layoffs.
The historian traces how a small cabal of courtiers controlled the young king's decisions.
The journalist exposed a cabal of businessmen who had been rigging government contracts.
She felt shut out by the cabal of old friends who always whispered together at family gatherings.
tc: The coup was not a popular uprising but the work of a tiny ______ of officers who had met in secret for months.
The contrast with 'a popular uprising' and the phrase 'met in secret' point to a small plotting group.
se: Rumours spread that a secret ______ of bankers was controlling the government's economic policy.
clique
Both 'cabal' and 'clique' mean a small, exclusive group acting together, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: the rhythmic rise and fall of a voice, piece of music or other sound
x: I love the gentle cadence of my grandmother's voice when she tells old stories.
After a month in London, his colleagues noticed a British cadence creeping into his speech.
Poetry students learn to hear the cadence of each line before analysing its meaning.
The speaker's slow, measured cadence gave her speech a sense of calm authority.
Falling asleep, she listened to the steady cadence of the monsoon rain on the tin roof.
tc: The actor read so mechanically that the poem lost its natural ______, sounding flat instead of rising and falling like music.
'Rising and falling like music', set against 'flat', defines a rhythmic cadence.
se: The marching soldiers kept a steady ______ as they crossed the parade ground.
rhythm
Both 'cadence' and 'rhythm' mean a regular beat or pattern, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to adjust something carefully and precisely so that it is accurate or suited to its purpose
x: You should calibrate the kitchen scale before weighing the flour for the cake.
Our team calibrated its prices carefully to stay competitive without losing money.
The lab assistant calibrates every instrument before students begin their experiments.
Central banks must calibrate interest-rate changes to slow inflation without causing a recession.
Over the years, she learned to calibrate her honesty so that she could be truthful without hurting her friends.
tc: Because even a tiny error could ruin the experiment, the technician had to ______ the thermometer against a known standard before each test.
'Even a tiny error' and 'against a known standard' signal precise adjustment.
se: Diplomats must ______ their words carefully when discussing such a sensitive conflict.
adjust
Both 'calibrate' and 'adjust' mean to fine-tune for a purpose, so the sentence means the same.

m: a feeling of trust and friendship among people who spend time or work together
x: There's a real camaraderie among the regulars at our neighbourhood tea stall.
Long nights before deadlines built a strong camaraderie among the members of the design team.
Many graduates say the camaraderie of their hostel days was the best part of university.
The soldiers' camaraderie helped them endure months of hardship at the front.
When she moved abroad, she missed the camaraderie of her old job more than the salary.
tc: Having survived the shipwreck together, the strangers developed a deep ______ that kept them in touch for the rest of their lives.
Shared hardship and lifelong contact point to a strong bond of friendship among companions.
se: Team sports are a great way for children to build a sense of ______ and learn to cooperate.
fellowship
Both 'camaraderie' and 'fellowship' mean friendly companionship within a group, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a false or unfounded rumour or story
x: The idea that eating mangoes with milk is poisonous is an old canard my aunt still believes.
The rumour that the company was about to close turned out to be a canard spread by a rival firm.
The professor spent a whole lecture debunking the canard that we use only ten percent of our brains.
Health officials worked hard to counter the canard that the vaccine caused infertility.
He was hurt to learn that his friends had believed the canard about him cheating in the exam.
tc: Although the claim had been disproved many times, the ______ that the moon landings were faked continued to circulate online.
A claim that 'had been disproved many times' yet keeps spreading is an unfounded rumour.
se: Her opponents spread the ______ that she had once been arrested, though no record of any arrest existed.
falsehood
Both 'canard' and 'falsehood' mean an untrue story, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: insincere, hypocritical talk, especially about morality or religion; also the special jargon of a group
x: I'm tired of all the cant about family values from people who never visit their own parents.
Staff dismissed the CEO's speech about putting people first as corporate cant.
The philosopher's essays attack the moral cant of a society that preached virtue while tolerating poverty.
Voters have grown weary of political cant and want leaders who say what they mean.
She could not stand the pious cant of relatives who criticised her divorce while ignoring their own failings.
tc: The politician's speeches about honesty were mere ______, since everyone knew he had lied repeatedly to win office.
Talk of honesty from a known liar points to hypocritical, insincere talk.
se: The editorial dismissed the bishop's sermon on humility as self-righteous ______ from a man who lived in luxury.
hypocrisy
Both 'cant' and 'hypocrisy' describe insincere moralising, so the sentence means the same.

m: to ask many people for their votes, opinions or support
x: Before choosing a new school, my parents canvassed every family on our street for recommendations.
The HR team canvassed staff opinion before changing the office working hours.
The researchers canvassed more than two thousand students about their study habits.
Volunteers spent weeks canvassing door to door for the candidate in the run-up to the election.
Before proposing, he quietly canvassed her closest friends to see how she might react.
tc: To find out what voters really thought, the campaign sent volunteers to ______ every household in the district.
'To find out what voters really thought' and visiting 'every household' signal asking people for their opinions.
se: Before launching the new menu, the restaurant decided to ______ its regular customers about their favourite dishes.
survey
Both 'canvass' and 'survey' mean to ask people for their opinions, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: tending to find fault or raise petty objections
x: My captious uncle complained about the salt, the rice and even the colour of the tablecloth at dinner.
The project was delayed by a captious client who objected to every minor detail.
A captious reviewer criticised the book for a few trivial typos while ignoring its argument.
The debate was spoiled by captious objections that had nothing to do with the real issues.
Living with such a captious partner left her feeling that nothing she did was ever good enough.
tc: Unlike his generous colleagues, the ______ examiner deducted marks for every trivial slip, from a missing comma to slightly untidy handwriting.
The contrast with 'generous colleagues' and penalising 'every trivial slip' signal petty fault-finding.
se: Nobody wanted to work with the ______ editor, who found something to complain about in every draft.
hypercritical
Both 'captious' and 'hypercritical' mean excessively fault-finding, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: an exaggerated and often ridiculous picture or description of a person or thing
x: A street artist at the fair drew a funny caricature of me with an enormous nose.
The difficult customer in the training video was such a caricature that nobody took it seriously.
The author's portrait of the professor is less a real character than a caricature of academic vanity.
The film was criticised for presenting a crude caricature of small-town life.
After years of bitterness, he had turned his ex-wife into a caricature of selfishness in his own mind.
tc: The play reduces its complex hero to a mere ______, exaggerating his flaws until he becomes a figure of ridicule.
'Exaggerating his flaws until he becomes a figure of ridicule' defines a caricature.
se: Critics called the film's portrayal of teachers a cruel ______ of the profession, mocking every flaw and ignoring every virtue.
parody
Both 'caricature' and 'parody' mean a mocking, exaggerated imitation, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: relating to the physical, especially sexual, desires of the body rather than the spirit
x: The monk spent decades trying to rise above carnal desires through prayer and fasting.
Medieval sermons warned against carnal pleasures such as gluttony and drunkenness.
The literature course examines how Victorian novelists hinted at carnal passion without ever describing it.
Critics argued that the advertising campaign appealed to carnal appetites rather than to reason.
Their relationship began as a purely carnal attraction but slowly grew into deep love.
tc: The hermit believed that only by renouncing the ______ pleasures of the body could he achieve spiritual purity.
'Pleasures of the body', set against 'spiritual purity', points to physical desires.
se: The poem contrasts ______ love with a purer, more spiritual devotion.
physical
Both 'carnal' and 'physical' describe bodily rather than spiritual love, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: constantly finding fault or complaining about small things
x: I'm sick of my neighbour's carping comments about where I park my car.
Despite carping criticism from a few senior staff, the new system saved the company thousands.
The young scholar ignored the carping reviews and continued developing her controversial theory.
Ministers dismissed the report as the work of carping critics with no better plan of their own.
Her mother's carping remarks about her weight made every family visit an ordeal.
tc: Instead of offering helpful suggestions, the committee chair made only ______ remarks about minor flaws in the proposal.
The contrast with 'helpful suggestions' and the focus on 'minor flaws' show petty fault-finding.
se: The coach grew tired of the ______ critics who complained about every decision he made.
captious
Both 'carping' and 'captious' mean petty and fault-finding, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a sudden, violent event or disaster that causes great change or destruction

The loss of its biggest client was a cataclysm from which the small firm never recovered.
Scientists believe an asteroid impact caused the cataclysm that wiped out the dinosaurs.
The First World War was a cataclysm that redrew the map of Europe.
Her parents' sudden divorce was an emotional cataclysm that turned her teenage years upside down.
tc: Geologists say the valley was not shaped slowly over millions of years but by a single sudden ______, a massive flood that tore through the region in days.
The contrast with 'slowly over millions of years' and the 'massive flood' indicate a sudden, violent disaster.
se: The stock market crash of 1929 was an economic ______ that ruined millions of families.
catastrophe
Both 'cataclysm' and 'catastrophe' mean a sudden, devastating disaster, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

The manager issued a categorical denial that any layoffs were planned this year.
The professor was categorical: no late submissions would be accepted under any circumstances.

The contrast with 'hedging' plus 'clear' and 'never' signal an absolute, unconditional statement.

emphatic
Both 'categorical' and 'emphatic' describe a firm, unqualified statement, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a closed meeting of members of a political party or group to choose candidates or decide policy; such a group

Women in the engineering department set up a caucus to discuss pay and promotion.
The student union's left-wing caucus met privately before the vote on tuition fees.
Party members gathered for a caucus to choose their candidate for the coming election.

A closed-door meeting of party members to agree on a position defines a caucus.
se: Opposition lawmakers held a private ______ late last night to decide on their strategy.
conclave
Both 'caucus' and 'conclave' mean a private meeting of a group to make decisions, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to jump, dance or run around in an excited, playful way

'Leaping and spinning with joy' defines playful, excited movement.
se: On warm spring evenings, the lambs ______ in the meadow, leaping and chasing one another.
frolic
Both 'cavort' and 'frolic' mean to play and jump about happily, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to give up power, territory or rights, usually unwillingly

'Defeated' and 'had no choice' signal unwillingly giving up territory.
se: The ageing chairman was reluctant to ______ power to the younger board members.
relinquish
Both 'cede' and 'relinquish' mean to give up power, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to examine books, films, news or speech and remove or suppress parts considered unacceptable

Fear of embarrassment and removing scenes 'before it was broadcast' point to suppressing content.

expurgate
Both 'censor' and 'expurgate' mean to remove objectionable material from a text, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: moving or tending to move away from a centre; tending to divide or decentralise

The contrast between 'held the empire together' and 'split it' points to forces pulling away from the centre.
se: The coalition suffered from strong ______ tendencies, as each party pulled away from the centre toward its own agenda.
divergent
Both 'centrifugal' and 'divergent' describe forces moving apart from a common centre, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: the ending or stopping of something

After the cessation of their quarrel, the two old friends laughed about how silly it had all been.

The contrast with 'continuous eruptions' and 'keep rumbling' signals that the activity ended.

termination
Both 'cessation' and 'termination' mean bringing something to an end, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to publicly support, defend or fight for a cause, person or idea

'Rather than merely tolerating' and 'giving speeches in its favor' show the blank means actively support.

m: morally pure and modest in behavior; also simple and restrained in style

The architect favored a chaste design of white walls and clean lines, with no ornament at all.

Her chaste prose avoids flowery adjectives and lets the facts speak for themselves.

The contrast with 'gaudy, overdecorated' and the list of plain features show the blank means simple and restrained.
se: Their courtship was entirely ______, conducted through letters and carefully supervised visits.
pure
Both 'chaste' and 'pure' describe a courtship free of anything improper, so the meaning is the same.

m: to scold or criticize someone mildly
x: My mother used to chide me for leaving wet towels on the bed.
The manager gently chided the team for missing yet another deadline.
Reviewers chided the author for ignoring recent research that contradicted his main argument.
An editorial in the morning paper chided the city council for its slow response to the flooding.
She chided herself for snapping at her best friend over something so trivial.

The contrast with shouting and dropping the player shows the blank means a mild scolding.
se: The old teacher would ______ students who arrived late, though never harshly.
scold
Both 'chide' and 'scold' mean to tell someone off, and 'never harshly' fits both equally.

m: rude, ungracious and bad-tempered
x: It would be churlish to refuse their invitation after they had been so kind to us.
His churlish reply to a polite email from a client cost the firm an important contract.
Even critics of the study admit it would be churlish to deny its importance.
Voters were put off by the candidate's churlish refusal to congratulate his opponent.
I felt churlish for complaining about the food when my aunt had cooked all afternoon.

'Although ... courteous' sets up a contrast, and the grunting shows the blank means rude and ungracious.
se: It seemed ______ to criticize a gift that had obviously been chosen with such care.
rude
Both 'churlish' and 'rude' describe ungracious behavior toward a thoughtful giver, so the sentence means the same.

m: long and indirect; not going straight to the destination or point
x: The taxi driver took a circuitous route to avoid the traffic jam near Farmgate.
After a circuitous discussion, the meeting ended without any clear decision.
Her path to medicine was circuitous: she studied music and worked in a bank first.
Investigators traced the money through a circuitous chain of shell companies abroad.
He gave a circuitous answer rather than admitting he had forgotten our anniversary.
tc: Instead of heading straight to the station, the bus took a route so ______ that it wound through every village in the district.
'Instead of heading straight' and 'wound through every village' show the blank means roundabout.
se: The journey was long and ______, winding through narrow valleys for most of the day.
roundabout
Both 'circuitous' and 'roundabout' describe an indirect, winding journey, giving the same meaning.

m: using many words where few would do, especially to be vague or evasive
x: Skip the circumlocution and tell me plainly whether you can come to the wedding.
The memo was so full of circumlocution that nobody realized layoffs were coming.
Academic writing courses warn students against circumlocution and needless jargon.
Officials answered questions about the leak with careful circumlocution, never actually denying it.
His fondness for circumlocution made even a simple apology sound like a legal document.
tc: The spokesperson's statement was a masterpiece of ______: three long paragraphs that never directly answered the question.
The restatement 'three long paragraphs that never directly answered' defines wordy evasion.
se: Frustrated by the lawyer's endless ______, the judge told him to get to the point.
verbosity
Both 'circumlocution' and 'verbosity' mean using too many words, which is why the judge wants him to get to the point.

m: to restrict something within limits
x: Strict rules circumscribe what tenants can do with the shared garden.
Her role at the company was narrowly circumscribed: she could advise but never decide.
The scope of the study was circumscribed by a lack of funding and time.
New laws further circumscribe the power of local governments to raise taxes.
He felt his life was circumscribed by his parents' expectations about career and marriage.
tc: Far from granting the committee broad authority, the new charter seeks to ______ its powers at every turn.
'Far from granting broad authority' signals the opposite, so the blank means to limit.
se: The treaty was designed to ______ the military's ability to act without parliamentary approval.
restrict
Both 'circumscribe' and 'restrict' mean to limit the military's freedom of action.

m: to find a way around a rule, obstacle or difficulty, often cleverly
x: We circumvented the long queue by booking our tickets online the night before.
Some employees circumvent the office firewall to watch videos during lunch.
Students sometimes try to circumvent plagiarism software by rewording whole paragraphs.
The company was fined for circumventing export controls by shipping goods through a third country.
She found a way to circumvent her brother's objections by asking their father first.
tc: Rather than confronting the regulations directly, the firm hired clever lawyers to find ways to ______ them.
'Rather than confronting ... directly' points to the opposite: getting around the rules.
se: Smugglers used small fishing boats to ______ the naval blockade.
bypass
Both 'circumvent' and 'bypass' mean to get around the blockade without confronting it.

m: seemingly able to see the future or know things beyond normal perception
x: You don't need to be clairvoyant to see that this project will run over budget.
My aunt claims to have clairvoyant dreams that warn her before anything bad happens.
The analyst's almost clairvoyant forecasts made her the most respected voice at the bank.
Scientists have found no reliable evidence that anyone possesses clairvoyant powers.
He seemed almost clairvoyant, always knowing what I needed before I said a word.
c: you don't have to be clairvoyant to
tc: Her predictions about the market were so consistently accurate that her colleagues joked she must be ______.
Uncannily accurate predictions suggest someone who can see the future.
se: Without being ______, no one could have predicted the sudden collapse of the bank.
psychic
Both 'clairvoyant' and 'psychic' mean able to foresee events, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: a loud, confused noise, or a loud and persistent public demand
x: Over the clamor of the market, I could barely hear the shopkeeper quote his price.
Management finally gave in to the clamor for flexible working hours.
Growing public clamor for cleaner air pushed the government to close several old factories.
There is a clamor among students for more practical courses and fewer exams.
Amid the clamor of the family reunion, she slipped away to sit quietly with her grandfather.
tc: The ______ from the angry fans grew so loud that the stadium announcer could no longer be heard.
'Angry fans' and 'so loud' that the announcer was drowned out point to a loud outcry.
se: The decision to close the library provoked a public ______ that forced the council to reverse course.
outcry
Both 'clamor' and 'outcry' mean a loud public protest strong enough to change the decision.

m: to split or divide something sharply, especially along a natural line
x: With one swing of the axe, he cleaved the log neatly in two.
The new highway will cleave the old neighborhood in half, cutting families off from the market.
The debate over funding cleaved the department into two bitterly opposed camps.
The ship's bow cleaved the dark waves as it headed out of the harbor.
Their friendship was cleaved apart by a quarrel over money that neither could forgive.
tc: The earthquake was strong enough to ______ the hillside, leaving a deep crack running all the way down to the river.
'Leaving a deep crack' shows the hillside was split apart.
se: A single bitter issue threatened to ______ the party into rival factions.
split
Both 'cleave' and 'split' mean to divide the party into separate groups.

m: a phrase or idea used so often that it has lost its originality and force
x: 'Every cloud has a silver lining' is a cliché, but it cheered me up anyway.
Our marketing team banned clichés like 'think outside the box' from all client presentations.
Writing teachers urge students to replace clichés with fresh, precise images.
The film relies on every cliché of the genre, from the car chase to the last-minute rescue.
It may be a cliché, but she really did feel that she had found her other half.
tc: The speech was full of stale phrases, but the most tiresome ______ was the promise to 'leave no stone unturned.'
'Stale phrases' and 'tiresome' show the blank means an overused expression.
se: His essay was criticized for depending on the same tired ______ that every applicant uses.
platitude
Both 'cliché' and 'platitude' mean an overused, unoriginal remark, so the criticism is the same.

m: a small, exclusive group of people who keep others out
x: At my new school, every table in the canteen seemed to belong to a different clique.
A small clique of senior managers made all the real decisions behind closed doors.
Graduate students complained that the lab was run by a clique that ignored outsiders' ideas.
Critics accused the ruling party of being controlled by a narrow clique of wealthy families.
She drifted away from the clique she had belonged to since childhood and made new friends.
tc: The club claimed to welcome everyone, but in practice it was run by a closed ______ that rarely accepted new members.
The contrast with 'welcome everyone' and 'rarely accepted new members' point to an exclusive group.
se: Newcomers found it hard to join the ______ of artists who met at the café every Friday.
coterie
Both 'clique' and 'coterie' mean a small, exclusive group that is hard for outsiders to enter.

m: to persuade someone gently and patiently to do something
x: I finally coaxed my little brother into eating his vegetables with a promise of ice cream.
It took weeks of friendly emails to coax the supplier into lowering its prices.
Our professor has a gift for coaxing shy students to share their opinions in class.
Rescue workers spent hours coaxing the frightened dog out from under the collapsed building.
She coaxed a smile from her grandmother, who had been gloomy since the hospital visit.
tc: Rather than forcing the nervous child onto the stage, the teacher tried to ______ her with gentle encouragement.
The contrast with 'forcing' and the phrase 'gentle encouragement' show the blank means to persuade softly.
se: With patience and flattery, he managed to ______ his parents into lending him the car.
cajole
Both 'coax' and 'cajole' mean to persuade through gentle flattery, producing the same meaning.

m: a concluding section of a piece of music, a story or an event
x: The symphony ends with a quiet coda that seems to fade into silence.
As a coda to the meeting, the director thanked everyone who had worked through the weekend.
The novel's brief coda tells us what happened to each character twenty years later.
The election result was a fitting coda to a decade of rapid political change.
Their late reconciliation formed a gentle coda to a long and stormy friendship.
tc: After the final chapter, the author added a short ______ that revealed what eventually became of the family.
Something added 'after the final chapter' to round off the story is a concluding section.
se: The quiet dinner afterward served as a pleasant ______ to an exhausting day of celebrations.
epilogue
Both 'coda' and 'epilogue' mean a closing section that follows the main event.

m: to arrange rules or practices into a formal, written system
x: We finally codified our household rules about screen time and stuck them on the fridge.
The HR department plans to codify the dress code that everyone has followed informally for years.
Nineteenth-century scholars tried to codify the grammar of many spoken dialects.
Parliament voted to codify the right to protest, which had previously rested only on custom.
Over the years, our family's unspoken Eid traditions became codified into a ritual everyone expects.
tc: For centuries the rules of the game existed only as custom, until a committee decided to ______ them in a single written rulebook.
The move from 'only as custom' to 'a single written rulebook' shows the blank means to set down formally.
se: The new statute will ______ practices that courts have followed informally for decades.
formalize
Both 'codify' and 'formalize' mean to turn informal practice into official written rules.

m: the use of force or threats to make someone do something against their will
x: He insisted that he had signed the confession under coercion and wanted to withdraw it.
Employees said they had joined the union freely, without any coercion from organizers.
The course examines how coercion and persuasion differ as tools of government.
International observers reported widespread voter coercion in several rural districts.
A healthy relationship rests on trust and choice, never on coercion or guilt.
tc: The workers did not quit voluntarily; their resignations were the result of ______, with managers threatening to cut their pensions.
'Did not quit voluntarily' and 'threatening' point to force or threats.
se: The court ruled that the contract was invalid because it had been signed under ______.
duress
Both 'coercion' and 'duress' mean being forced by threats, which makes the contract invalid.

m: to think deeply and carefully about something
x: I need a day to cogitate before I decide whether to accept the job in Singapore.
The board cogitated over the merger proposal for weeks before finally voting.
Philosophers have cogitated on the nature of consciousness for thousands of years.
Researchers are still cogitating on why the drug works in mice but not in humans.
Sitting by the window during the monsoon rain, he cogitated on what his father had said.
tc: Instead of answering at once, she sat in silence for several minutes, seeming to ______ on every possible consequence.
'Instead of answering at once' and 'sat in silence' show she was thinking deeply.
se: Before making such a serious decision, he wanted time to ______ on the offer.
ruminate
Both 'cogitate' and 'ruminate' mean to think long and hard, so the sentence means the same.

m: aware of or having knowledge of something
x: Be cognizant of the time difference when you call your cousins in Toronto.
Managers must be cognizant of the stress that constant overtime places on their staff.
The researchers were cognizant of the study's limitations and said so in the final paper.
Policymakers are increasingly cognizant of the link between air pollution and childhood asthma.
She was fully cognizant of how much her parents had sacrificed for her education.
tc: Far from being oblivious to the risks, the climbers were fully ______ of the dangers awaiting them near the summit.
'Far from being oblivious' signals the opposite, so the blank means aware.
se: The new manager was ______ of the tensions within the team and handled them carefully.
aware
Both 'cognizant' and 'aware' mean knowing about the tensions, giving the same meaning.

m: to hold together firmly as a unified or logically consistent whole
x: The rice should be sticky enough to cohere when you press it into a ball.
Unless the separate departments cohere around a shared goal, the reorganization will fail.
The chapters of her thesis don't quite cohere yet; each one seems to argue something different.
For the coalition to survive, its members must cohere despite their different ideologies.
After months of tension, the family slowly began to cohere again around the new baby.
tc: The film's many subplots never ______; instead they feel like unrelated fragments stitched together.
'Unrelated fragments' is the opposite of hanging together, so the blank means form a unified whole.
se: Without strong leadership, the various rebel groups could not ______ into a single movement.
unite
Both 'cohere' and 'unite' mean to come together as one, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: logical, consistent and clearly connected, so that it is easy to understand
x: After the long flight, I was too tired to give a coherent answer to anyone.
Our team needs a coherent strategy, not a list of disconnected ideas.
A good essay presents a coherent argument in which every paragraph supports the thesis.
The government has yet to offer a coherent plan for dealing with rising food prices.
Still in shock, she could barely form a coherent sentence when the police arrived.
tc: Whereas his first draft was a jumble of unrelated notes, the final report was clear and ______.
'Whereas' contrasts with 'a jumble of unrelated notes', so the blank means logically connected.
se: The witness, though frightened, gave a clear and ______ account of what had happened.
lucid
Both 'coherent' and 'lucid' mean clear and easy to follow, so the account is described the same way.

m: secondary or additional; happening alongside the main thing, often unintentionally
x: Getting fitter was a collateral benefit of walking to work every day.
The restructuring had collateral effects on several departments that nobody had consulted.
Researchers noticed a collateral finding: the drug also seemed to improve patients' sleep.
Military planners promised to minimize collateral damage to civilian homes and hospitals.
Their divorce caused collateral hurt to friends who felt forced to take sides.
tc: The main goal of the policy was to reduce traffic, but cleaner air turned out to be a welcome ______ benefit.
The contrast with 'the main goal' shows the blank means secondary or side.
se: Higher sales were the main aim; better staff morale was one of several ______ effects of the campaign.
secondary
Both 'collateral' and 'secondary' describe side effects that were not the main aim.

m: to express sympathy or share sorrow with someone over a misfortune
x: We met for coffee to commiserate about our disastrous exam results.
Colleagues gathered around her desk to commiserate when the promotion went to someone else.
Fellow PhD students often commiserate over rejected papers and unhelpful reviewers.
After the defeat, the losing team's supporters commiserated with one another in the stands.
Our neighbors came over to commiserate when the monsoon floods ruined our ground floor.
tc: Instead of gloating over his rival's defeat, he went over to ______ with him and shake his hand.
'Instead of gloating' signals the opposite, so the blank means to offer sympathy.
se: Friends called from all over the country to ______ with her after the fire destroyed her shop.
sympathize
Both 'commiserate' and 'sympathize' mean to express sorrow for her loss.

m: roomy and comfortable; having plenty of space
x: Our new flat has a commodious kitchen with room for a dining table.
The firm moved to more commodious offices after hiring forty new engineers.
The library's commodious reading room can seat nearly three hundred students.
The new stadium is far more commodious than the old one, with seats for fifty thousand fans.
He sank gratefully into a commodious armchair after a long day.
tc: After years in a cramped studio, they were delighted by the ______ new house with its large rooms and high ceilings.
The contrast with 'cramped' and 'large rooms' show the blank means spacious.
se: The hotel suite was surprisingly ______, with enough space for the whole family.
spacious
Both 'commodious' and 'spacious' mean having plenty of room.

m: a person from the same country as someone else
x: Studying abroad, I was thrilled to meet a compatriot who also missed home-cooked hilsa.
She was the only one of her compatriots to be hired by the London office that year.
The young scientist dedicated her award to compatriots working under difficult conditions back home.
The tennis player beat her compatriot in the semifinal, guaranteeing her country a place in the final.
Far from home, he found comfort in the company of compatriots who understood his jokes.
tc: At the international conference, she was delighted to discover that the speaker beside her was her ______, born in the same country and even the same city.
'Born in the same country' defines the blank as a fellow citizen.
se: In the final round he faced his ______, so the gold medal was certain to stay in the country.
countryman
Both 'compatriot' and 'countryman' mean someone from the same country, which is why the medal stays at home.

m: involvement with others in doing something wrong or illegal
x: By staying silent about the cheating, he felt a growing sense of complicity.
Several bank employees were fired for their complicity in the fraud.
Historians still debate the complicity of ordinary citizens in the regime's crimes.
The minister denied any complicity in the leak of classified documents.
She could never forgive her sister's complicity in hiding their father's illness from her.
tc: Although he never touched the stolen money, his ______ in the scheme was clear, since he had forged the documents that made it possible.
Forging the documents shows he took part in the wrongdoing even without taking the money.
se: The inquiry found evidence of police ______ in the smuggling operation.
involvement
Both 'complicity' and 'involvement' here mean the police took part in the illegal smuggling.

m: to behave or conduct oneself in a particular way
x: Even at the noisy wedding, the children comported themselves remarkably well.
New employees are expected to comport themselves professionally when meeting clients.
Students who represent the university abroad must comport themselves with dignity.
Diplomats are trained to comport themselves calmly even during tense negotiations.
Despite her grief, she comported herself with quiet grace at her father's funeral.
tc: Although the crowd was jeering, the young speaker managed to ______ herself with calm and dignity.
'Although the crowd was jeering' contrasts with calm, so the blank means to conduct herself.
se: Guests were asked to ______ themselves quietly inside the temple.
behave
Both 'comport' and 'behave' mean to conduct oneself, so the request is the same.

m: to make a problem or difficulty worse
x: Missing the bus compounded my bad morning, and I arrived soaked and late.
The manager compounded the error by blaming the intern instead of fixing it.
Sleep deprivation can compound the stress students feel during exam season.
Heavy rain compounded the misery of families already displaced by the earthquake.
He compounded the hurt by forgetting to apologize until a week later.
tc: Rather than easing the crisis, the government's clumsy response only served to ______ it.
'Rather than easing' signals the opposite, so the blank means to make worse.
se: Ignoring the leak will only ______ the damage to the foundation.
aggravate
Both 'compound' and 'aggravate' mean to make the damage worse.

m: including all or nearly all parts or aspects; thorough
x: Before buying the used car, we got a comprehensive inspection from a trusted mechanic.
The consultants delivered a comprehensive report covering every branch of the business.
This textbook offers a comprehensive introduction to organic chemistry for first-year students.
Scientists have called for a comprehensive survey of the river's fish before the dam is built.
Her comprehensive knowledge of her friends' birthdays never ceases to amaze me.
tc: The first study looked at only a few patients, but the second was far more ______, covering thousands of cases across ten countries.
The contrast with 'only a few patients' and 'thousands of cases' show the blank means thorough and wide-ranging.
se: The museum's catalogue is remarkably ______, listing every object in its collection.
exhaustive
Both 'comprehensive' and 'exhaustive' mean covering everything, as 'every object' confirms.

m: driven by an urge that is very hard to resist or control
x: I'm a compulsive snacker, so I keep the biscuits on the highest shelf.
His compulsive checking of email made it impossible for him to focus on long tasks.
Psychologists study why some people develop compulsive habits such as constant hand-washing.
Doctors warn that compulsive gambling ruins families and often leads to crippling debt.
She was a compulsive worrier who called her children every evening to make sure they were safe.
tc: His need to check that the door was locked was so ______ that he would go back home three or four times before reaching work.
Returning home repeatedly to check shows an urge he cannot control.
se: Her ______ shopping had left her with a wardrobe full of clothes she never wore.
obsessive
Both 'compulsive' and 'obsessive' describe shopping driven by an uncontrollable urge.

m: something given up or allowed in order to settle a dispute or satisfy demands
x: As a concession to my mother, I wore a tie to the family dinner.
The union won important concessions on overtime pay after a week of talks.
In a rare concession, the author admitted that his earlier data had been flawed.
The government made no concessions to the protesters, who vowed to continue their strike.
Letting her choose the holiday destination was a small concession to keep the peace.
tc: Neither side would give an inch until the landlord finally offered one ______: he agreed to postpone the rent increase for six months.
'Neither side would give an inch' followed by the landlord agreeing to postpone shows he yielded something.
se: The government's ______ on fuel prices came only after weeks of protests.
compromise
Both 'concession' and 'compromise' mean giving ground to settle the dispute.

m: proving something beyond doubt; settling a question finally
x: The receipt was conclusive proof that I had paid the electricity bill on time.
The audit found no conclusive evidence that anyone in the finance team had acted dishonestly.
Scientists caution that the early data are promising but far from conclusive.
Election officials announced that the recount was conclusive and the result would stand.
Her letter was conclusive: she no longer wanted to be part of his life.
tc: Earlier studies had only hinted at a link, but this one was ______: it proved beyond doubt that the chemical causes the disease.
'Proved beyond doubt', contrasted with 'only hinted', defines the blank.
se: The DNA test provided ______ proof that he was the child's father.
definitive
Both 'conclusive' and 'definitive' mean the proof settles the question completely.

m: to invent a story, excuse or plan, usually a false or elaborate one
x: My son concocted an elaborate story about why his homework was missing.
Two employees concocted a scheme to claim expenses for trips they never took.
The student was expelled after it emerged that she had concocted data for her thesis.
Investigators believe the kidnapping was concocted to win public sympathy and donations.
He concocted a feeble excuse rather than admit he had forgotten her birthday.
tc: Unable to admit the truth, the boy began to ______ an elaborate tale about a stranger who had broken the window.
'Unable to admit the truth' and 'elaborate tale' show he was making up a false story.
se: The lawyer accused the witness of trying to ______ a story to protect his brother.
fabricate
Both 'concoct' and 'fabricate' mean to invent a false story.

m: agreement or harmony between people or groups
x: Our two families have lived in concord for years, sharing everything from tools to recipes.
The new manager worked hard to restore concord among the quarreling departments.
Historians describe the period as one of rare concord between the church and the state.
The treaty brought a decade of concord to the long-divided region.
After years of bickering, the sisters finally reached a kind of quiet concord.
tc: Unlike the previous decade, which was marked by constant discord, the years after the treaty were a time of remarkable ______.
'Unlike ... constant discord' points to the opposite: harmony.
se: The two villages had lived in ______ for generations until the dispute over the river.
harmony
Both 'concord' and 'harmony' mean peaceful agreement, which the dispute later broke.

m: (of a punishment) fully deserved and appropriate to the wrongdoing
x: After he scratched his brother's new bicycle, losing his own bike for a week seemed a condign punishment.
The board agreed that dismissal was a condign response to such a serious breach of trust.
Legal philosophers debate what counts as condign punishment for crimes committed by children.
Many felt the fraudster's ten-year sentence was condign, given the thousands of savers he had ruined.
She felt her loneliness was condign punishment for the way she had treated her friends.
tc: Given the scale of the fraud and the suffering it caused, the judge felt that a long prison sentence was entirely ______.
'Given the scale of the fraud' explains why the punishment is fully deserved.
se: Most readers felt that the villain's downfall at the end of the novel was ______.
deserved
Both 'condign' and 'deserved' mean the downfall matched the villain's wrongdoing.

m: a channel or means through which something, such as water, information or money, is passed
x: A plastic conduit runs along the wall to protect the electrical wiring.
Her assistant acts as a conduit for all requests to the chief executive.
Universities serve as a conduit through which new ideas reach industry.
Investigators say the charity was used as a conduit for laundering money.
For years, my aunt was the conduit through which family news reached us abroad.
tc: The ambassador was not the source of the secret offer; she merely served as the ______ through which it passed between the two governments.
'Not the source' and 'through which it passed' define a channel.
se: During the disaster, the website became the main ______ for information about missing people.
channel
Both 'conduit' and 'channel' mean the route through which information flowed.

m: a trusted person with whom one shares secrets and private matters
x: My roommate became my closest confidant during the first lonely months abroad.
As the boss's long-time confidant, he knew about the merger months before anyone else.
Letters to his confidant reveal the poet's private doubts about his own work.
Insiders say the general's closest confidant warned him about the plot days earlier.
Her grandmother was her confidant, the one person who knew about her plans to study abroad.
tc: Whenever she had a secret too heavy to keep, she turned to her oldest ______, who never repeated a word.
Someone she trusts with secrets who 'never repeated a word' is a confidant.
se: The diary reveals that the painter had only one true ______, a childhood friend with whom he shared every secret.
intimate
Both 'confidant' and 'intimate' mean a very close friend trusted with secrets.

m: to take away someone's property officially, as a penalty or by authority
x: The teacher confiscated my phone after it rang during the exam.
The company confiscates any laptop found with unauthorized software installed.
Exam invigilators at the university may confiscate notes found in a student's pocket.
Customs officers confiscated thousands of fake designer handbags at the port.
Her father confiscated her car keys after she came home three hours late.
tc: The police did not merely fine the smugglers; they also went on to ______ every boat and truck used in the operation.
Beyond a fine, taking the boats and trucks by authority means seizing them.
se: Authorities threatened to ______ the vehicles of drivers who repeatedly ignored parking rules.
impound
Both 'confiscate' and 'impound' mean to take the vehicles away officially.

m: to wrongly treat two different things as if they were the same
x: People often conflate being busy with being productive, but they are very different things.
The report conflates sales with profits, which makes the company look healthier than it is.
Students sometimes conflate correlation and causation when interpreting survey data.
Critics say the debate conflates immigration with crime, despite little evidence of a link.
She learned not to conflate his silence with a lack of affection.
tc: A careful historian will distinguish between the two revolutions rather than ______ them into a single event.
'Distinguish ... rather than' signals the opposite: merging the two into one.
se: It is a mistake to ______ wealth with happiness, since one does not guarantee the other.
confuse
Both 'conflate' and 'confuse' mean to treat wealth and happiness as the same thing.

m: behavior that follows accepted rules, standards or social norms
x: In our neighborhood every lawn is trimmed to the same height, a strange display of conformity.
The company's culture rewards conformity rather than creative risk-taking.
Psychologists have long studied conformity, showing how group pressure changes individual judgment.
All new buildings must be constructed in conformity with the earthquake safety code.
As a teenager, he rebelled against the conformity his strict parents expected of him.
tc: The school's dress code was designed to enforce ______, so students who dyed their hair or wore jewelry were sent home.
Punishing anyone who looks different shows the rule aims at uniform obedience to norms.
se: Totalitarian regimes demand strict ______ and punish anyone who questions official policy.
obedience
Both 'conformity' and 'obedience' mean following the rules without question.

m: to become thick or solid, especially as a liquid cools; also, to take definite shape
x: Leave the bacon fat in the pan and it will congeal into a white paste.
Our vague ideas for the campaign finally congealed into a clear plan during the meeting.
In the lab, we watched the protein solution congeal as it cooled.
Investigators noted that the spilled oil had congealed into thick black lumps along the beach.
The gravy congealed on my plate while I sat listening to my friend's bad news.
tc: Once the soup cooled, the fat on its surface began to ______, forming a solid white layer.
'Forming a solid white layer' as it cools shows the blank means to solidify.
se: If the sauce sits too long, it will ______ and become unpleasant to eat.
solidify
Both 'congeal' and 'solidify' mean the sauce sets into a thick, solid mass.

m: pleasant and friendly, often because of shared interests; suitable and agreeable
x: We spent a congenial evening with our new neighbors, talking about books and gardening.
She left the bank for a more congenial workplace where colleagues actually helped one another.
Many young researchers find the small college a congenial place to think and write.
The city's mild climate and low taxes make it congenial to new businesses.
He was a congenial companion on the long train journey from Dhaka to Sylhet.
tc: After years of working with hostile and unfriendly colleagues, she was relieved to find her new team so ______.
The contrast with 'hostile and unfriendly' shows the blank means pleasant and friendly.
se: The small café had an atmosphere so ______ that strangers often struck up conversations.
friendly
Both 'congenial' and 'friendly' describe a warm atmosphere that encourages conversation.

m: to bring an image or memory to mind; to produce something as if by magic
x: The smell of frying onions always conjures up memories of my mother's kitchen.
With only two days' notice, the team conjured up a presentation that impressed the client.
The word 'archive' tends to conjure up images of dusty boxes and silent reading rooms.
The advertisement conjures up an image of a carefree life that few buyers will ever enjoy.
Just hearing her voice on the phone conjured up feelings he thought he had buried.
c: conjure something out of thin air
tc: Just a few notes of the old song were enough to ______ up vivid memories of her childhood summers.
Bringing 'vivid memories' to mind from a song is what the blank describes.
se: The novelist uses only a few details to ______ the atmosphere of a busy Victorian street.
evoke
Both 'conjure' and 'evoke' mean to call up a vivid impression in the reader's mind.

m: to send or hand something over, often to an unwanted place or fate
x: I finally consigned my old textbooks to the attic, where they will probably stay forever.
The proposal was consigned to a committee that rarely reports back on anything.
Few scholars expected his theory to be consigned to obscurity so quickly.
Critics fear that the new policy will consign thousands of families to poverty.
She refused to consign her painful memories to silence and wrote a memoir instead.
tc: Most experts predict that the new technology will ______ the old typewriters to museums and storerooms.
Being replaced and sent off to 'museums and storerooms' means being relegated.
se: A single bad review can ______ a young writer's first book to obscurity.
relegate
Both 'consign' and 'relegate' mean to send the book to an unwanted fate.

m: to interpret or understand the meaning of words or actions in a particular way
x: Please don't construe my silence as agreement; I just need time to think.
Her manager construed the short email as rude, though she had only been in a hurry.
Scholars have construed the poem's final line in many different ways.
The court construed the law narrowly, ruling that it did not apply to online sales.
He construed every kind gesture from his ex-wife as an attempt at reconciliation.
tc: The ambassador's remarks were so vague that each side was able to ______ them as support for its own position.
Vague remarks allow each side to interpret them however it likes.
se: Some readers may ______ the author's irony as genuine praise.
interpret
Both 'construe' and 'interpret' mean to understand the irony in a particular way.

m: sharing a border or touching; next to each other in sequence
x: Our garden is contiguous with the park, so the children can walk straight through the gate.
The company rented two contiguous floors so that all its teams could work together.
In geography class we learned that Alaska is not part of the contiguous United States.
The fire spread quickly through contiguous blocks of wooden houses.
The brothers bought contiguous plots of land in their home village so they could live side by side.
tc: The two properties are not ______; a narrow public road runs between them.
A road running between them means the properties do not touch.
se: Officials redrew the district so that it included only ______ neighborhoods, with no gaps between them.
adjoining
Both 'contiguous' and 'adjoining' mean the neighborhoods touch each other, as 'no gaps' confirms.

m: depending on something else that may or may not happen
x: Our picnic plans are contingent on the weather, so keep an umbrella handy.
The job offer is contingent upon a satisfactory background check.
Admission to the master's program is contingent on passing the English test.
The ceasefire agreement remains contingent on both sides withdrawing their troops.
His happiness had become far too contingent on other people's approval.
tc: Funding for the second phase is not guaranteed; it is ______ on the success of the first.
'Not guaranteed' explains that the funding depends on something uncertain.
se: The sale of the house is ______ on the buyer securing a mortgage.
dependent
Both 'contingent on' and 'dependent on' mean the sale will happen only if the mortgage is approved.

m: to call people together for a meeting, or to come together formally
x: We convened in the living room to plan our grandmother's eightieth birthday party.
The manager convened an emergency meeting after the main server crashed.
The university will convene a panel of experts to review the engineering curriculum.
World leaders will convene in Geneva next month to discuss climate finance.
Every December the old school friends convene at the same restaurant to catch up.
tc: Because the crisis demanded an immediate decision, the chairman decided to ______ the board that very night rather than wait for its scheduled meeting.
An urgent need to bring the board together for a meeting points to the blank.
se: The judge will ______ a jury to hear the case next week.
assemble
Both 'convene' and 'assemble' mean to bring the jury together.

m: familiar with and knowledgeable about something
x: My grandfather is surprisingly conversant with smartphones and video calls.
Applicants for the finance role should be fully conversant with basic accounting software.
Few undergraduates are conversant with the statistical methods used in the study.
Journalists covering the trial must be conversant with complex legal terminology.
After years together, she was fully conversant with his moods and silences.
tc: Although he had never formally studied law, he was thoroughly ______ with its principles after years of working in a law firm.
Years of experience despite no formal study explain that he was well acquainted with the subject.
se: The new hire is ______ with several programming languages.
familiar
Both 'conversant with' and 'familiar with' mean having good working knowledge of the languages.

m: to communicate an idea, feeling or message; also to carry from one place to another
x: Please convey my thanks to your parents for the lovely dinner.
The chart conveys the sales trends far more clearly than a page of numbers.
A good abstract conveys the main findings of a paper in just a few sentences.
The minister's speech failed to convey any sense of urgency about the flooding.
Words could not convey how grateful she felt when her family arrived at the airport.
tc: Although the actor spoke no lines in the scene, his face managed to ______ the character's grief perfectly.
'Spoke no lines' contrasts with communicating grief through his face alone.
se: The letter was written to ______ the family's gratitude to the doctors.
express
Both 'convey' and 'express' mean to communicate the family's gratitude.

m: to tolerate, approve of, or give support to something
x: My grandmother would never countenance anyone wearing shoes inside her kitchen.
The board refused to countenance any delay in launching the new product line.
Few serious historians would countenance the idea that the pyramids were built by aliens.
The government said it would not countenance violence against peaceful protesters during the election.
She loved him dearly, but she could not countenance his constant lying to her family.
tc: The principal, a strict disciplinarian, would never ______ cheating, no matter how minor the offense seemed.
'Strict disciplinarian' and 'never... no matter how minor' show she would refuse to tolerate it.
se: The club's committee would not ______ any breach of its dress code.
tolerate
Both 'countenance' and 'tolerate' mean to accept or allow, so the committee refusing either gives the same meaning.

m: made as an exact imitation of something valuable in order to deceive
x: The shopkeeper held the note up to the light to check whether it was counterfeit.
Customs officers seized thousands of counterfeit handbags at the port last month.
Pharmacists warn that counterfeit medicines sold online can contain dangerous ingredients.
Her counterfeit smile fooled no one at the party who knew how upset she really was.
Our compliance team flagged a batch of counterfeit invoices submitted by a supplier.
tc: Although the painting looked authentic to most visitors, experts soon proved it was ______, a clever copy produced only last year.
'Although... looked authentic' and 'a clever copy' show the painting was a deceptive imitation.
se: Police arrested a gang that had been printing ______ banknotes in a basement.
fake
Both 'counterfeit' and 'fake' describe imitation money made to deceive, giving the same meaning.

m: a formal, binding agreement or solemn promise between two or more parties
x: The new homeowners were surprised to find a covenant forbidding them from painting the house purple.
Under the loan covenant, the company must keep its debt below a certain level.
In the Hebrew Bible, God makes a covenant with Noah never again to flood the earth.
Several governments have been accused of ignoring an international covenant protecting civil rights.
For them, marriage was not just a contract but a sacred covenant between two families.
tc: The two tribes sealed their peace with a solemn ______, each swearing never to raid the other's villages again.
'Sealed their peace' and 'each swearing never' describe a binding agreement.
se: The neighbors honored the ______ they had signed, which barred fences higher than six feet.
pact
Both 'covenant' and 'pact' mean a formal agreement, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: deliberately reluctant to reveal information, or pretending to be shy or modest
x: When asked about her salary, she became coy and quickly changed the subject.
The company has been coy about when its new phone will actually reach stores.
He gave her a coy smile from across the room and then looked away.
Researchers remained coy about their results until the paper was formally published.
Ministers were coy about whether fuel prices would rise again after the budget.
tc: Normally frank about his plans, the director was unusually ______ when reporters asked about his next film.
'Normally frank' contrasts with the blank, so it must mean reluctant to give details.
se: The minister was ______ about the date of the election, refusing to confirm any rumors.
evasive
Both 'coy' and 'evasive' describe someone avoiding a direct answer, as 'refusing to confirm' shows.

m: crudely insensitive and lacking refinement, tact, or intelligence
x: Joking about money at a funeral struck everyone as incredibly crass.
The manager made a crass remark about her age during the team meeting.
Critics called the advertisement a crass attempt to profit from a national tragedy.
It was a crass error to publish the results before checking the data.
His crass behavior at the wedding embarrassed his parents in front of the whole family.
tc: Unlike his tactful older brother, Rafiq was notoriously ______, often saying hurtful things without a second thought.
'Unlike his tactful older brother' signals that the blank means the opposite of tactful.
se: Many viewers found the comedian's jokes about the disaster deeply ______.
insensitive
Both 'crass' and 'insensitive' describe jokes that show no regard for people's suffering.

m: sad and disappointed, especially after a hope has been dashed
x: The children looked crestfallen when they heard the picnic was canceled because of rain.
He came out of the job interview crestfallen, convinced he had ruined his chances.
Crestfallen supporters drifted out of the stadium after their team lost in the final over.
She was crestfallen to learn that her thesis proposal had been rejected again.
The candidate gave a short, crestfallen speech after the election results were announced.
tc: Expecting a promotion, Nadia was ______ when her boss announced that the position had gone to someone else.
Her expectation of a promotion was dashed, so the blank must mean deeply disappointed.
se: The players were ______ after losing a match they had seemed certain to win.
dejected
Both 'crestfallen' and 'dejected' mean sad and disappointed after a setback.

m: to reach a final or highest point after a gradual build-up
x: Weeks of arguments between the neighbors finally culminated in a shouting match on the street.
The project will culminate in a product launch scheduled for early next year.
Her years of research culminated in a book that changed how historians view the period.
Months of protests culminated in the resignation of the transport minister.
Their long friendship culminated in marriage, which surprised nobody who knew them.
tc: The festival begins with small street performances each evening and is designed to ______ in a grand fireworks display on the final night.
The contrast between 'begins with small' and 'grand... final night' shows the event builds to a climax.
se: Years of tension between the two departments would eventually ______ in a formal complaint.
end
Both 'culminate in' and 'end in' describe the final result of years of tension.

m: increasing or growing by successive additions over time
x: The cumulative cost of all those small coffee purchases surprised me at the end of the month.
Your final grade is cumulative, so every quiz and assignment counts.
Scientists are studying the cumulative effects of air pollution on children in Dhaka.
The cumulative stress of long hours eventually forced him to take a week off work.
Over the years, the cumulative weight of small betrayals destroyed their friendship.
tc: No single dose of the drug was harmful, but the ______ effect of taking it daily for years caused serious liver damage.
The contrast between 'no single dose' and 'daily for years' points to an effect that builds up over time.
se: Doctors warned that the ______ effect of years of poor sleep could be serious.
accumulated
Both 'cumulative' and 'accumulated' describe an effect that has built up over years.

m: a bad-tempered, grumpy person, often an old one, who complains a lot
x: The old curmudgeon next door complains whenever our kids play cricket in the lane.
Despite his reputation as an office curmudgeon, he quietly helped every new intern.
The professor was a lovable curmudgeon who grumbled about everything but cared deeply about his students.
In her column, the critic plays the curmudgeon, attacking every new trend in technology.
My grandfather can be a real curmudgeon, but he softens completely around his grandchildren.
tc: Known throughout the village as the local ______, Mr. Haque grumbled at everyone and rarely smiled.
'Grumbled at everyone and rarely smiled' defines a bad-tempered person.
se: Even the building's resident ______ smiled when the children sang carols in the lobby.
grouch
Both 'curmudgeon' and 'grouch' mean a habitually grumpy person, so 'even' works the same way.

m: a person who believes that people are motivated mainly by self-interest
x: Call me a cynic, but I doubt that free gift comes without any conditions.
Office cynics predicted that the new wellness program would be dropped within a month.
Even cynics admitted that the charity's work in flood-hit villages had made a real difference.
Years of broken promises had turned her from an idealist into a cynic about politics.
Only a cynic would assume that his kindness to his mother was about the inheritance.
tc: Unlike his idealistic sister, who trusted everyone, Karim was a hardened ______ who suspected selfish motives behind every kind act.
The contrast with 'idealistic' and the phrase 'suspected selfish motives' define a cynic.
se: Only the most hardened ______ would doubt the volunteers' good intentions after the flood.
skeptic
Both 'cynic' and 'skeptic' describe someone inclined to doubt others' good motives.

m: seeming difficult to deal with in a way that discourages or intimidates
x: Cleaning the flat after the party seemed daunting, so we started with the kitchen.
Learning a new accounting system in a week is a daunting task for any team.
Applying to universities abroad can be daunting for students who have never left Bangladesh.
The government faces the daunting challenge of rebuilding thousands of homes after the cyclone.
Meeting her fiancé's large family for the first time felt more daunting than any exam.
tc: Although the 800-page novel looked ______ at first, she found it so gripping that she finished it in a week.
'Although' contrasts her first impression with how easily she finished it, so the blank means intimidating.
se: For a first-year student, the reading list for the course can seem ______.
intimidating
Both 'daunting' and 'intimidating' describe something that seems discouragingly difficult.

m: excessive indulgence in sensual pleasures such as drinking, gambling, and sex
x: The novel describes a young aristocrat who wastes his fortune on gambling and debauchery.
After a weekend of debauchery in the city, he arrived at work on Monday exhausted.
Historians have long debated whether accounts of Roman debauchery were exaggerated by later writers.
The tabloids reported a night of debauchery involving the club's star players.
She left him after years of drinking, debauchery and broken promises.
tc: Having spent his youth in drunken ______, the reformed poet later wrote hymns praising moderation and self-control.
'Reformed' and 'praising moderation' show his youth was the opposite: excessive indulgence.
se: The prince squandered his inheritance on a life of ______ in the capital.
dissipation
Both 'debauchery' and 'dissipation' mean wasteful indulgence in pleasure.

m: confident, stylish, and charming, usually describing a man
x: He looked debonair in his dark suit as he greeted guests at the door.
The film's debonair hero talks his way out of every danger with a smile.
Our new sales director is debonair and polished, and clients seem to love him.
With his silver hair and easy charm, the debonair professor was popular with students.
She fell for his debonair manner, though her friends found him a little too smooth.
tc: Far from the clumsy, shy teenager she remembered, her cousin had grown into someone ______ and self-assured, effortlessly charming every guest.
The contrast with 'clumsy, shy' and the phrase 'effortlessly charming' point to stylish confidence.
se: In old Hollywood films, the leading man was almost always ______, with perfect manners and a ready smile.
suave
Both 'debonair' and 'suave' mean smoothly charming and stylish.

m: shedding leaves every year, or falling off after a period of growth
x: Our garden has mostly deciduous trees, so autumn means hours of raking leaves.
The landscaping firm recommended deciduous trees to shade the office in summer and let light in during winter.
In biology class we learned that deciduous trees drop their leaves to conserve water in dry seasons.
Many deciduous forests in the region are being cleared for farmland and housing.
Walking through the bare deciduous woods in winter always makes her feel peaceful.
tc: Unlike evergreen pines, ______ trees such as oaks and maples lose all their leaves each autumn.
'Unlike evergreen' and 'lose all their leaves' define trees that shed leaves seasonally.
se: In autumn, the ______ trees along the river turn gold and then lose their leaves.
leaf-shedding
Both 'deciduous' and 'leaf-shedding' describe trees that lose their leaves each year.

m: worn out, weakened, or ruined because of old age or neglect
x: We rented a decrepit old house with leaking pipes and a sagging roof.
The factory still runs on decrepit machinery that breaks down almost every week.
Students complain that the university's decrepit laboratories make serious research almost impossible.
Engineers warned that the decrepit bridge could collapse during the next monsoon flood.
Her once-strong grandfather had grown frail and decrepit, and she visited him every evening.
tc: Once the grandest hotel in the city, the building is now so ______ that pieces of plaster fall from its ceilings.
'Once the grandest' contrasts with falling plaster, so the blank means worn out and falling apart.
se: Investors plan to restore the ______ mansion and turn it into a boutique hotel.
dilapidated
Both 'decrepit' and 'dilapidated' describe a building in ruinous condition that needs restoring.

m: to regard, consider, or judge something in a particular way
x: You may leave the meeting early if you deem it necessary.
Management deemed the proposal too risky and asked us to revise the budget.
The committee deemed her thesis worthy of the department's highest award.
Any building deemed unsafe after the earthquake will be closed to the public.
He did whatever his parents deemed proper, even when it made him unhappy.
tc: Although the inspectors found a few minor faults, they did not ______ the building unsafe and allowed residents to return.
'Only minor faults' and 'allowed residents to return' show they did not judge the building unsafe.
se: Teachers may ______ some essays too short to be graded.
consider
Both 'deem' and 'consider' mean to judge something to be a certain way.

m: the act of damaging someone's good reputation by making false statements about them
x: After the article appeared, the businessman sued the newspaper for defamation.
Posting false reviews about a former employer could expose you to a defamation claim.
Law students studied how courts balance free speech against protection from defamation.
Journalists warn that broad defamation laws are being used to silence critics.
She felt the rumors spread by her former friend amounted to defamation of character.
tc: Because the blogger's claims about the doctor were both false and damaging to his reputation, the court found him guilty of ______.
'False and damaging to his reputation' is the definition of defamation.
se: The actor won substantial damages for ______ after a magazine falsely accused him of fraud.
libel
Both 'defamation' and 'libel' name the offense of publishing false, damaging claims about someone.

m: to spoil the purity or sacredness of something; to make dirty or disrespect
x: Please don't defile my freshly cleaned carpet with your muddy boots.
The company was accused of defiling sacred land when it built its warehouse on an ancient burial site.
In the poem, the speaker feels that the city has defiled the innocence of his childhood.
Vandals defiled several graves in the old cemetery overnight, police said.
She felt that his lies had defiled the memory of their happiest years together.
tc: Worshippers were outraged when vandals tried to ______ the ancient temple by spraying graffiti on its altar.
Outraged worshippers and graffiti on an altar indicate violating something sacred.
se: Local people accused the tourists of trying to ______ the holy site with litter.
desecrate
Both 'defile' and 'desecrate' mean to treat a sacred place with disrespect.

m: quick, neat, and skillful in movement or in handling a situation
x: With a few deft movements, the street vendor folded the paratha and handed it to me.
Her deft handling of the angry client impressed everyone in the office.
The surgeon's deft hands repaired the damaged artery in under an hour.
The novel is admired for its deft blending of humor and tragedy.
With deft diplomacy, the mediator persuaded both sides to return to the table.
tc: Whereas the new waiter kept dropping plates, the head waiter was remarkably ______, balancing six dishes without spilling a drop.
'Whereas' contrasts him with the clumsy new waiter, and balancing six dishes shows skill.
se: The editor's ______ cuts made the long report far easier to read without losing anything important.
skillful
Both 'deft' and 'skillful' describe cuts made with neat expertise.

m: to pay all or part of the cost of something
x: We sold our old furniture to help defray the cost of moving abroad.
