The company will defray all travel expenses for staff attending the conference.
A small scholarship helped defray her tuition fees at the university in Dhaka.
The city introduced a tourist tax to defray the cost of cleaning its beaches.
His parents offered to defray the wedding expenses, which relieved the young couple enormously.
tc: To ______ the rising cost of her medical treatment, her friends organized a fundraising concert.
A fundraising concert is a way of paying for costs, so the blank means to pay.
se: The organizers asked each participant for a small fee to help ______ the cost of the venue.
cover
Both 'defray' and 'cover' mean to pay for the cost.

m: to decline or deteriorate to a worse physical, mental, or moral condition
x: What started as a friendly debate at dinner quickly degenerated into a shouting match.
Without clear leadership, the weekly meetings degenerated into long, pointless arguments.
Researchers are studying why certain nerve cells degenerate in patients with Parkinson's disease.
Peaceful protests degenerated into rioting after police fired tear gas into the crowd.
Over the years, their once-loving relationship slowly degenerated into polite indifference.
tc: The negotiations started on a hopeful note, but without trust on either side they began to ______ into bitter accusations.
'But' contrasts the hopeful start with 'bitter accusations', so the blank means to decline.
se: Unless the injury is treated soon, the joint will continue to ______ over the coming years.
deteriorate
Both 'degenerate' and 'deteriorate' mean to get progressively worse.

m: to worship someone as a god, or to admire them excessively
x: Teenagers often deify pop stars and copy everything they wear.
Some employees practically deify the company's founder, quoting his sayings in every meeting.
Ancient Egyptians deified their pharaohs, believing them to be gods on earth.
Cricket fans in Bangladesh tend to deify star players after a big win and abuse them after a loss.
She deified her late father, refusing to hear a single word of criticism about him.
tc: Rather than ______ the nation's founders as flawless heroes, the historian portrays them as ordinary people with serious faults.
'Rather than' contrasts the blank with portraying them as ordinary, so it means to treat as godlike.
se: Fans tend to ______ successful athletes, forgetting that they are ordinary human beings.
idolize
Both 'deify' and 'idolize' mean to admire someone as if they were more than human.

m: to lower someone's dignity or cause them to lose respect
x: I refuse to demean myself by begging him for a favor.
Good managers correct mistakes without demeaning the people who made them.
The study found that advertisements often demean older women by portraying them as helpless.
Critics said the new law demeans refugees by treating them as criminals.
He constantly demeaned his wife in front of guests, and she finally left him.
tc: A good teacher corrects students' errors gently, without trying to ______ them in front of their classmates.
'Gently' and 'in front of their classmates' suggest the blank means to humiliate or belittle.
se: Players were warned that any comment meant to ______ an opponent would lead to a fine.
belittle
Both 'demean' and 'belittle' mean to make someone seem less worthy of respect.

m: the death of a person, or the end or failure of something
x: The demise of our neighborhood bookshop left a gap that no café could fill.
Poor management, not competition, led to the company's sudden demise.
Scientists still debate what caused the demise of the dinosaurs about 66 million years ago.
Many commentators predicted the demise of print newspapers, yet some are still thriving.
After her husband's demise, she moved back to her family home in Sylhet.
tc: Once the most popular phone brand in the world, the company failed to adapt to touchscreens, and its ______ came within just a few years.
'Once the most popular' and 'failed to adapt' point to the company's end.
se: The rise of streaming services led to the ______ of the video rental store.
end
Both 'demise' and 'end' describe the video rental store ceasing to exist.

m: reserved, modest, and quiet in manner or appearance
x: She seemed demure at the dinner table, but she was the life of the party afterward.
The new receptionist is demure and polite, rarely speaking unless someone addresses her.
In Victorian novels, heroines are often expected to be demure and obedient.
The actress chose a demure black dress for the awards ceremony rather than anything flashy.
Behind her demure smile lay a sharp wit that her friends adored.
tc: Though she appeared ______ in class, rarely raising her hand, Tania was outspoken and fearless on the debate team.
'Though' contrasts the blank with 'outspoken and fearless', and 'rarely raising her hand' shows reserve.
se: The bride wore a ______ dress with long sleeves and a high neckline.
modest
Both 'demure' and 'modest' describe clothing that is quiet and not revealing.

m: an inhabitant of a particular place, or someone who often visits it
x: Owls and bats are among the denizens of the old barn behind our house.
Like most denizens of the corporate world, he lives by his calendar.
Marine biologists study the strange denizens of the deep ocean, many of which glow in the dark.
Denizens of Old Dhaka have watched their narrow lanes grow ever more crowded.
As a longtime denizen of the café, she knew every barista by name.
tc: The fox is perhaps the best-known ______ of these woods, though few hikers ever spot one.
A fox that lives 'of these woods' is an inhabitant, which the blank must mean.
se: As a longtime ______ of the neighborhood, she knew the history of every house on the street.
resident
Both 'denizen' and 'resident' mean someone who lives in a place.

m: to be a sign or symbol of something; to indicate or stand for
x: On this map, the red dots denote petrol stations along the highway.
In our project tracker, a green tag denotes tasks that have been completed.
In mathematics, the Greek letter pi denotes the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.
In many cultures, a white dress denotes purity, but in parts of Asia white is worn for mourning.
For her, a simple handwritten note denoted more affection than any expensive gift.
tc: In the legend at the bottom of the map, a small tent symbol is used to ______ a campsite.
A map legend explains what symbols stand for, so the blank means to indicate.
se: On the chart, an asterisk is used to ______ figures that have not yet been verified.
indicate
Both 'denote' and 'indicate' mean that the asterisk is a sign marking those figures.

m: to remove someone from a position of power, especially suddenly or by force
x: The club members voted to depose their chairman after the funds went missing.
Shareholders moved to depose the chief executive after years of falling profits.
Our history teacher explained how the army deposed the king in a bloodless coup.
The military deposed the elected president and imposed a curfew across the capital.
After the scandal, she feared her rivals would try to depose her as head of the family business.
tc: Fearing that the general was plotting to ______ him, the king had him arrested and exiled.
A king fearing a general's plot suggests the blank means to remove him from power.
se: Rebels launched an attack on the capital in an attempt to ______ the dictator.
overthrow
Both 'depose' and 'overthrow' mean to remove a ruler from power by force.

m: to make someone morally bad or corrupt
x: My grandmother was convinced that late-night television would deprave the young.
Former staff say that the pursuit of huge bonuses gradually depraved the bank's senior managers.
In the novel, wealth and power slowly deprave a once-honest young lawyer.
The censors banned the book, claiming it would deprave and corrupt its readers.
She worried that his new friends would deprave her gentle younger brother.
tc: Victorian moralists feared that cheap novels would ______ the young, leading them away from virtue toward vice.
'Leading them away from virtue toward vice' restates the meaning of the blank: to corrupt morally.
se: Censors claimed that the film would ______ young viewers and banned it outright.
corrupt
Both 'deprave' and 'corrupt' mean to make someone morally bad.

m: abandoned and left to fall into ruin through neglect
x: Kids from the neighborhood used the derelict car at the end of the street as a playground.
The company plans to turn a derelict warehouse into modern office space.
Archaeology students surveyed a derelict mill dating back to the eighteenth century.
The council has promised to clear derelict buildings that attract crime in the area.
Returning to his derelict childhood home, he felt a sharp pang of grief.
tc: The factory has stood empty and ______ for decades, its windows smashed and its roof open to the rain.
'Stood empty for decades' and the smashed windows show it is abandoned and decaying.
se: Volunteers are transforming the ______ lot behind the school into a community garden.
abandoned
Both 'derelict' and 'abandoned' describe land left unused and neglected.

m: scornful ridicule or mockery
x: His suggestion that we walk home in the rain was met with derision from his friends.
The new logo drew widespread derision from employees, who called it childish.
Galileo's theories were once treated with derision by many scholars of his day.
The minister's claim that crime had fallen was greeted with derision by opposition leaders.
She could not bear the derision in his voice whenever he spoke about her dreams.
tc: Far from earning respect, the singer's off-key performance was greeted with ______, as the audience jeered and laughed.
'Far from earning respect' and 'jeered and laughed' show the blank means mockery.
se: His plan to sell ice to people in the Arctic was met with ______ by the investors.
ridicule
Both 'derision' and 'ridicule' mean mocking laughter at something thought foolish.

m: to catch sight of or detect something that is distant or hard to see
x: Standing on the balcony, I could just descry the lights of the airport in the distance.
Analysts struggled to descry any clear pattern in the market's wild swings.
The astronomer was the first to descry a faint comet near the horizon.
Through the fog, the sailors finally descried the outline of the harbor.
She thought she could descry a hint of sadness behind his cheerful words.
tc: Though the fog was thick, the lookout managed to ______ the faint outline of a ship on the horizon.
'Though the fog was thick' and 'faint outline' show the blank means to catch sight of something hard to see.
se: From the hilltop, hikers could just ______ the village far below.
discern
Both 'descry' and 'discern' mean to make out something distant with difficulty.

m: to damage or treat a sacred place or thing with violent disrespect
x: Visitors were warned not to desecrate the shrine by entering with their shoes on.
The developer was fined for desecrating an old graveyard while clearing land for a shopping mall.
The professor explained how invading armies often desecrated temples to humiliate conquered peoples.
Police are searching for vandals who desecrated a mosque with graffiti last night.
To him, selling his grandfather's medals felt like desecrating the old man's memory.
tc: To the villagers, building a parking lot over the ancient burial ground would ______ a place they regarded as holy.
'A place they regarded as holy' signals that the blank means to violate something sacred.
se: Vandals broke into the church and tried to ______ the altar.
defile
Both 'desecrate' and 'defile' mean to treat a sacred object with disrespect.

m: to steal valuable things from a place, or strip it of its value or beauty
x: Thieves despoiled the abandoned house of everything valuable, even the copper pipes.
Critics accuse the mining company of despoiling the hills and leaving nothing behind.
Historians record how invading soldiers despoiled the city's libraries and palaces.
Activists say illegal logging has despoiled vast areas of forest in the region.
He felt that the divorce lawyers had despoiled him of both his savings and his pride.
tc: After the army captured the town, soldiers moved from house to house to ______ it of anything valuable, leaving the residents with nothing.
Taking 'anything valuable' and 'leaving the residents with nothing' define plundering.
se: Invaders came to ______ the temples, carrying off gold and jewels.
plunder
Both 'despoil' and 'plunder' mean to rob a place of its valuables by force.

m: using dishonest or underhanded tricks to get what one wants
x: My little brother came up with a devious plan to get out of washing the dishes.
She used devious methods to get her colleague's project canceled.
In the study, children as young as four used devious strategies to win the game.
Investigators uncovered a devious scheme to divert relief funds into private accounts.
He was charming on the surface, but his ex-wife knew how devious he could be.
tc: Unlike his honest, straightforward partner, Tareq was ______, always looking for sneaky ways to gain an advantage.
'Unlike his honest, straightforward partner' and 'sneaky ways' show the blank means dishonest.
se: The con artist used ______ tricks to persuade elderly people to hand over their savings.
cunning
Both 'devious' and 'cunning' describe clever, dishonest tricks used to deceive.

m: showing skill and quickness, especially in using the hands
x: My grandmother's dexterous fingers could thread a needle in seconds, even in dim light.
The new assembly robots are more dexterous than older machines and can handle fragile parts.
In the lab, students need dexterous hands to handle tiny glass pipettes.
A dexterous negotiator, the diplomat secured a ceasefire within days of arriving.
He was a dexterous dancer, guiding his partner smoothly across the crowded floor.
tc: Watchmakers must be extremely ______, since even a slight slip of the hand can ruin a delicate mechanism.
'A slight slip of the hand can ruin' shows the job requires great skill with the hands.
se: Years of practice made the pianist's fingers remarkably ______.
nimble
Both 'dexterous' and 'nimble' describe fingers that move quickly and skillfully.

m: a short statement expressing a general truth or principle, or a formal pronouncement
x: My father followed the dictum that you should never borrow money from friends.
Our manager lives by the dictum that no meeting should last longer than half an hour.
Students of design learn the famous dictum that form follows function.
Economists have long questioned the old dictum that a rising tide lifts all boats.
She remembered her mother's dictum: never go to bed angry with someone you love.
tc: The coach repeated his favorite ______ to every new player: practice does not make perfect; perfect practice makes perfect.
The colon introduces a short guiding saying, which is what the blank must mean.
se: Many writers follow the ______ that less is more.
maxim
Both 'dictum' and 'maxim' mean a short saying that states a guiding principle.

m: to become or make wider, larger, or more open
x: Your pupils dilate when you walk from bright sunlight into a dark room.
The eye doctor put drops in my eyes to dilate the pupils before the examination.
Some medicines dilate blood vessels, so pilots must check with doctors before taking them.
In physics class we learned that metals dilate slightly when heated.
Her eyes dilated with fear as the stranger stepped closer.
tc: While cold causes blood vessels to narrow, heat causes them to ______, which is why your face turns red in a hot room.
'While' contrasts the blank with 'narrow', so it must mean widen.
se: In dim light, the pupils begin to ______ so that more light can enter the eye.
widen
Both 'dilate' and 'widen' mean the pupils open further to let in more light.

m: to deny responsibility for, knowledge of, or connection with something
x: The restaurant disclaims any responsibility for coats left in the cloakroom.
The manager quickly disclaimed any knowledge of the missing files.
The author disclaims any intention of offending readers in her preface.
The militant group disclaimed responsibility for the attack, blaming a rival faction.
He disclaimed any interest in her, but his friends could see he was clearly smitten.
tc: Rather than admit his role in the scandal, the senator chose to ______ any knowledge of the bribes.
'Rather than admit' signals the blank means the opposite: to deny.
se: The company was quick to ______ responsibility for the faulty product, blaming its supplier.
deny
Both 'disclaim' and 'deny' mean to refuse to accept responsibility.

m: to unsettle someone and disturb their composure or confidence
x: The silence on the other end of the phone began to disconcert me.
Some interviewers deliberately ask odd questions simply to disconcert nervous candidates.
The examiner's constant frowning disconcerted the nervous student during her viva.
The sudden fall in share prices disconcerted investors across Asia.
His habit of staring without blinking disconcerted her on their first date.
tc: The bowler hoped his fierce stare would ______ the batsman, but the young player remained perfectly calm.
'But... remained perfectly calm' contrasts with the blank, so it means to unsettle.
se: Nothing seemed to ______ the experienced pilot, even when the engine failed.
rattle
Both 'disconcert' and 'rattle' mean to make someone lose their composure.

m: to show disapproval of something in order to discourage it
x: My parents discountenanced any talk of politics at the dinner table.
The firm's leadership has always discountenanced office romances, though it has never formally banned them.
The university discountenances the use of mobile phones during lectures.
The government officially discountenanced the protest, warning citizens not to attend.
Her family discountenanced the marriage, but she went ahead with it anyway.
tc: Although it does not ban the practice outright, the medical board continues to ______ doctors accepting gifts from drug companies.
'Although it does not ban the practice outright' shows the board disapproves without forbidding.
se: The headmaster has always tried to ______ bullying of any kind.
discourage
Both 'discountenance' and 'discourage' mean to show disapproval so that something happens less.

m: serious spoken or written communication or debate about a subject
x: Mealtimes in our house were full of lively discourse about books and films.
Our team values respectful discourse, even when we strongly disagree.
Her dissertation examines the discourse surrounding climate change in national newspapers.
Many people worry that social media has coarsened political discourse.
Their long discourses about life and love, often lasting until dawn, sealed their friendship.
tc: Instead of the thoughtful ______ the organizers had hoped for, the debate quickly descended into personal insults.
'Instead of' contrasts the blank with insults, so it means reasoned discussion.
se: Shouting and name-calling have replaced reasoned ______ in many parliaments.
debate
Both 'discourse' and 'debate' mean serious exchange of views, which shouting has replaced.

m: individually separate and distinct from other parts
x: I divided my weekend chores into discrete tasks so they felt less overwhelming.
The project is broken into discrete phases, each with its own budget and deadline.
In statistics, discrete data can only take certain values, such as whole numbers.
Researchers identified three discrete groups of voters with very different priorities.
Over time she learned to treat work and family as discrete parts of her life.
tc: Rather than one continuous process, learning a language involves several ______ stages, each with its own challenges.
'Rather than one continuous process' signals the blank means separate.
se: The course is divided into four ______ modules that can be taken in any order.
separate
Both 'discrete' and 'separate' describe modules that stand apart from one another.

m: wandering from one subject to another without a clear focus; rambling
x: My uncle's discursive stories about his youth could last an entire afternoon.
The report was so discursive that the board asked for a one-page summary.
The professor's discursive lectures wandered from economics to poetry and back again.
Critics described the minister's speech as long, discursive and short on concrete policies.
Her letters were warm and discursive, full of gossip, recipes and memories.
tc: The editor asked the writer to cut the ______ passages, which wandered away from the main argument for pages at a time.
'Wandered away from the main argument' defines writing that digresses.
se: His ______ speech touched on a dozen topics but never reached a clear conclusion.
rambling
Both 'discursive' and 'rambling' describe a speech that drifts between topics without focus.

m: angry, dissatisfied, and resentful about how one has been treated
x: Passengers grew disgruntled as their flight was delayed for the third time.
A disgruntled employee leaked the confidential memo to the press.
Disgruntled students complained that the exam covered material never taught in class.
Farmers, disgruntled by the low price of rice, blocked the highway in protest.
He grew increasingly disgruntled with his marriage but never spoke about it.
tc: Promised a pay rise that never came, the factory workers grew increasingly ______ and finally went on strike.
A broken promise leading to a strike shows the blank means resentful and dissatisfied.
se: The airline offered free meals to ______ passengers stranded by the storm.
dissatisfied
Both 'disgruntled' and 'dissatisfied' describe unhappy passengers the airline wants to placate.

m: untidy and messy in appearance, especially hair or clothes
x: After the long bus ride, I arrived at my cousin's wedding hot and disheveled.
He walked into the meeting late, his hair disheveled and his tie hanging loose.
The disheveled professor looked as though he had slept in his office, which he probably had.
Rescue workers found the disheveled survivors huddled together beneath a collapsed roof.
She laughed when she saw his disheveled appearance after a night of looking after the baby.
tc: Normally neat and well-groomed, the lawyer appeared in court looking ______, with a wrinkled shirt and uncombed hair.
'Normally neat' contrasts with the blank, and 'wrinkled shirt and uncombed hair' describe untidiness.
se: She caught sight of her ______ reflection and quickly combed her hair.
unkempt
Both 'disheveled' and 'unkempt' describe a messy, uncombed appearance.

m: a great difference, especially an unfair one, between two or more things
x: There's a huge disparity between what the advertisement promised and what we actually received.
The audit revealed a disparity in pay between male and female staff doing the same work.
Researchers documented a wide disparity in literacy rates between urban and rural districts.
Rising income disparity has become a central issue in this year's election.
Despite the disparity in their ages, the two became close friends.
tc: Although the two schools receive the same funding, there is a striking ______ in their students' exam results.
'Although... the same funding' sets up a contrast, so the blank means a big difference.
se: The report highlights the ______ between rich and poor neighborhoods in access to clean water.
gap
Both 'disparity' and 'gap' mean an unequal difference between the two groups.

m: to enjoy oneself in a lively, carefree way; to frolic
x: On Friday afternoons, children disport themselves in the shallow pond behind the village school.
Freed from their desks, the staff disported themselves at the company picnic with games and music.
In the poem, nymphs and shepherds disport themselves beside a sparkling stream.
Tourists disported themselves on the beach while the locals went quietly about their work.
The young couple disported themselves on holiday as if they had no cares in the world.
tc: After weeks of exams, the students were finally free to ______ themselves on the beach, swimming and playing football until sunset.
'Finally free' after exams and 'swimming and playing football' show carefree enjoyment.
se: Dolphins were seen to ______ in the waves just off the shore.
frolic
Both 'disport' and 'frolic' mean to play about happily and energetically.

m: a person who openly opposes an official policy, especially of an authoritarian state
x: Her grandfather was a dissident who spent years in prison for criticizing the regime.
Within the company, a few dissidents openly opposed the merger at the annual meeting.
The historian's new book traces the lives of Soviet dissidents who wrote in secret.
Several prominent dissidents were arrested hours before the planned demonstration.
At the book club, Ahmed was the lone dissident who thought the bestseller was dull.
tc: Hasan became the regime's most outspoken ______, openly criticizing its abuses while other party members praised it.
'Openly criticizing its abuses' while others praised the regime defines someone who opposes official policy.
se: The government arrested the best-known ______ in the country just before the election.
dissenter
Both 'dissident' and 'dissenter' mean someone who openly opposes the authorities.

m: to extract the most important ideas or essence from something larger
x: Can you distill your complaint into one sentence so I know what to fix?
Our consultant managed to distill two hundred pages of data into five clear recommendations.
A good abstract distills the main findings of a research paper into a single paragraph.
The report distills decades of climate research into a few urgent warnings for governments.
Her letter distilled years of love and regret into a few simple lines.
tc: The best speechwriters can ______ a complicated policy into one memorable phrase that voters will repeat.
Turning 'a complicated policy into one memorable phrase' means extracting its essence.
se: Her task was to ______ a long technical report into a brief summary for the board.
condense
Both 'distill' and 'condense' mean to reduce something long to its essential points.

m: so deeply upset and worried that one cannot think or behave calmly
x: She was distraught when she realized she had left her passport in the taxi on the way to the airport.
A distraught client called the office three times before lunch, demanding to know why the shipment was late.
Distraught over failing his final exam, Rafi locked himself in his room and refused to speak to anyone.
Rescue workers tried to comfort distraught families waiting for news after the ferry capsized in the river.
He looked so distraught after the breakup that his friends took turns staying with him that week.
tc: Far from being calm when the hospital called, she was utterly ______ and could barely hold the phone.
'Far from being calm' and 'could barely hold the phone' signal that the blank means extremely upset.
se: The ______ mother searched the crowded market for hours after losing sight of her young son.
frantic
Both 'distraught' and 'frantic' describe someone wild with worry, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: active or occurring during the daytime rather than at night; also, happening every day
x: Unlike their nocturnal cousins, most squirrels are diurnal and spend the daylight hours searching for food.
Our office cat seems to have no diurnal rhythm at all; she sleeps whenever and wherever she likes.
The biology lecture compared diurnal and nocturnal animals and explained how their eyes have adapted differently.
Scientists recorded the diurnal temperature swing in the desert, which can exceed thirty degrees between noon and midnight.
As a diurnal creature by nature, I find working night shifts at the hospital exhausting and lonely.
tc: Owls hunt at night, but hawks are ______ birds that do most of their hunting while the sun is up.
The contrast with 'at night' and the phrase 'while the sun is up' show the blank means active by day.
se: Most songbirds are ______ species, feeding during the day and roosting quietly after dark.
daytime
Both 'diurnal' and 'daytime' describe creatures active during daylight, giving the same meaning.

m: showing a great deal of variety; made up of very different kinds of people or things
x: The market near our house sells a diverse range of fruit, from local mangoes to imported kiwis.
Our team is wonderfully diverse, with engineers from six countries and backgrounds in everything from physics to music.
The seminar attracted students with diverse interests, which made the discussions lively and unpredictable.
Coral reefs are among the most diverse ecosystems on Earth, supporting thousands of species in a small area.
Although my friends have diverse personalities, they all share a willingness to listen without judging.
tc: Far from being uniform, the city's population is remarkably ______, with dozens of languages spoken in a single neighborhood.
'Far from being uniform' and 'dozens of languages' indicate the blank means highly varied.
se: The museum's collection is extremely ______, including ancient pottery, modern sculpture and medieval manuscripts.
varied
Both 'diverse' and 'varied' describe a collection of many different kinds of objects.

m: comic or badly written verse, usually with a clumsy, irregular rhythm
x: My uncle writes birthday cards full of cheerful doggerel that rhymes 'cake' with 'make no mistake.'
For the office farewell party, Nadia composed a bit of doggerel about the boss's love of spreadsheets.
The professor dismissed the student's poem as mere doggerel, pointing out its forced rhymes and clumsy meter.
Advertising jingles are often little more than doggerel, yet they stick in the public's mind for decades.
He was embarrassed when his girlfriend read aloud the doggerel he had written for her as a teenager.
tc: Critics hoped for serious poetry from the young author, but his new collection proved to be little more than clumsy ______.
The contrast with 'serious poetry' and the word 'clumsy' point to badly written verse.
se: He recited a few lines of comic ______ at the wedding, and the guests laughed at its clumsy rhythm.
rhyme
Both 'doggerel' and 'rhyme' here mean light, unpolished verse, so the meaning stays the same.

m: expressing sorrow; mournful and gloomy
x: The puppy gave me such a doleful look that I shared my sandwich with him.
Everyone in the meeting room fell silent as the manager delivered the doleful news about layoffs.
The historian read a doleful letter written by a soldier to his mother just days before the battle.
A doleful tune drifted from the radio as the city mourned the victims of the earthquake.
She sat by the window in a doleful mood, waiting for a call that never came.
tc: Instead of the cheerful song we expected at the festival, the band played a slow, ______ ballad that left many listeners in tears.
'Instead of the cheerful song' and 'left many listeners in tears' show the blank means sorrowful.
se: The ______ expression on his face told us the interview had not gone well.
mournful
Both 'doleful' and 'mournful' describe a sad, gloomy expression.

m: to show excessive, often uncritical love or fondness for someone (usually 'dote on')
x: My grandmother dotes on her youngest grandson and slips him sweets whenever his parents aren't looking.
The new manager dotes on the interns, praising even their smallest contributions in every team meeting.
Some students complain that the professor dotes on his favorites and ignores the rest of the class.
Fans dote on the young cricket captain, crowding the airport whenever the team returns from a tour.
He doted on his wife throughout their marriage, bringing her tea in bed every morning for forty years.
tc: Though she had been strict with her own children, she began to ______ on her grandchildren, indulging their every whim.
The contrast with 'strict' and the phrase 'indulging their every whim' show the blank means to lavish excessive affection.
se: Aunts and uncles often ______ on the youngest child in the family, praising everything she does.
fawn
Both 'dote on' and 'fawn on' mean to show exaggerated affection, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: amusing in a dry, odd or quietly whimsical way
x: Our tour guide had a droll way of describing the city's potholes as 'traditional water features.'
His droll remarks during the budget meeting kept everyone awake through two hours of dull figures.
The lecturer's droll asides about famous mathematicians made the dense material surprisingly easy to follow.
Critics praised the novel's droll portrait of small-town politics, calling it gently satirical rather than cruel.
She loved him for his droll sense of humor, which could make even a flat tire seem funny.
tc: Although he delivered his lines with a perfectly straight face, his ______ commentary had the audience quietly chuckling all evening.
A straight face combined with an audience chuckling signals dry, understated humor.
se: Her ______ observations about office life made the newsletter the most popular email of the week.
witty
Both 'droll' and 'witty' describe cleverly amusing remarks, giving the same meaning.

m: easily drawn out or shaped without breaking; also, easily led or influenced
x: Copper is ductile enough to be drawn into the thin wires that carry electricity through our homes.
The engineers chose a more ductile alloy so the beams would bend rather than snap during an earthquake.
In the materials lab, we compared how ductile and brittle metals behave when stretched to the breaking point.
Gold is so ductile that a single gram can be stretched into a wire more than two kilometers long.
Young recruits are often ductile, adopting the habits and opinions of whoever trains them first.
tc: Cast iron is brittle and cracks under stress, whereas steel is far more ______ and can be bent without breaking.
'Whereas' contrasts the blank with 'brittle', and 'can be bent without breaking' defines it.
se: Because the alloy is ______, the frame bends under heavy loads instead of shattering.
pliable
Both 'ductile' and 'pliable' describe a material that can bend or deform without breaking.

m: sweet and soothing to hear (often used humorously or ironically)
x: I woke to the dulcet tones of my neighbor's rooster, which crows at four every morning.
The receptionist's dulcet voice made even the news of a two-hour wait sound almost pleasant.
During the music lecture, we listened to the dulcet strains of a flute sonata from the eighteenth century.
Listeners called the radio station to praise the new host's dulcet voice and calm, unhurried delivery.
Lying on the bed, she drifted off to the dulcet sound of monsoon rain on the tin roofs nearby.
tc: Unlike the harsh, grating voice of the previous announcer, the new presenter's ______ tones soothed the audience.
'Unlike the harsh, grating voice' and 'soothed' show the blank means sweet and pleasant to hear.
se: The singer's ______ voice filled the small hall and calmed the restless children.
melodious
Both 'dulcet' and 'melodious' describe a voice that is sweet and pleasing to hear.

m: to become gradually smaller or fewer
x: Our savings dwindled quickly after we moved to the city and started paying rent.
Enthusiasm for the project dwindled once the team realized the deadline had been moved up a month.
Attendance at the evening lectures dwindled as the exams approached and students stayed home to revise.
Fish stocks in the bay have dwindled sharply over the past decade because of overfishing and pollution.
Their friendship slowly dwindled after she moved abroad, until they exchanged only birthday messages.
tc: As the drought continued month after month, the village's water supply began to ______ until only a few muddy pools remained.
The continuing drought and 'only a few muddy pools remained' show the supply was steadily shrinking.
se: Without fresh funding, the charity's reserves will ______ over the next year.
diminish
Both 'dwindle' and 'diminish' mean to become gradually smaller.

m: to overshadow or surpass someone or something, making them seem less important
x: My little sister's cooking has completely eclipsed mine, so the family now asks her to make dinner.
The new product's success eclipsed everything else the company launched that year.
Her later research eclipsed her early work, which is now rarely cited by other scholars.
The scandal threatened to eclipse the government's achievements in health and education.
He felt eclipsed by his brilliant older brother and spent years trying to step out of his shadow.
tc: The young pianist's dazzling performance seemed to ______ the efforts of every other competitor, who appeared ordinary by comparison.
'Appeared ordinary by comparison' shows the blank means to outshine or overshadow.
se: The film's stunning visual effects tend to ______ its rather weak plot.
overshadow
Both 'eclipse' and 'overshadow' mean to draw attention away by being more impressive.

m: feeling or showing overwhelming happiness or joyful excitement
x: We were ecstatic when the plumber finally fixed the leak that had kept us awake for weeks.
The team was ecstatic to hear that the client had signed the contract without any changes.
Rina was ecstatic when she received an admission letter from her first-choice university in Canada.
Ecstatic crowds poured into the streets to celebrate after the national team won the championship.
He gave her an ecstatic hug at the airport after six long months apart.
tc: Far from being disappointed by the result, the young candidate was ______, hugging everyone in sight.
'Far from being disappointed' and 'hugging everyone in sight' show the blank means overjoyed.
se: Fans were ______ when the band announced a reunion tour after ten years apart.
thrilled
Both 'ecstatic' and 'thrilled' express great excitement and joy.

m: a large, imposing building; also, a complex system of beliefs or ideas
x: The old courthouse is a grand stone edifice with columns that dominate the town square.
Our company headquarters is a glass edifice that turns into a greenhouse every afternoon.
In her thesis, she argued that the whole theoretical edifice rested on one untested assumption.
Investigators found that the bank's financial edifice was built on fraud and fake accounts.
One lie can bring down the whole edifice of trust that a couple has built over the years.
tc: The tiny wooden chapel that once stood here has been replaced by a cathedral, a massive stone ______ that towers over the city.
'Massive stone' and 'towers over the city' restate that the blank is a large, imposing building.
se: The university's main library is an imposing ______ of red brick and marble.
building
Both 'edifice' and 'building' refer to the library as a large constructed structure.

m: successful in producing the desired result; effective
x: My grandmother swears that ginger tea is the most efficacious cure for a sore throat.
Short daily stand-up meetings proved more efficacious than long weekly reviews for keeping our project on schedule.
The study tested whether spaced repetition is more efficacious than cramming for long-term vocabulary retention.
Health officials say the new malaria vaccine is highly efficacious in young children.
Talking openly with each other turned out to be more efficacious than any couples therapy they had tried.
tc: After several drugs had failed to help, doctors finally found a treatment that was ______, and the patient recovered within weeks.
The contrast with drugs that 'failed' and the recovery that followed show the blank means effective.
se: The trial showed that the new drug is highly ______ in reducing blood pressure.
effective
Both 'efficacious' and 'effective' mean producing the intended result.

m: an unpleasant or harmful smell or discharge, such as foul vapor or waste
x: The effluvium from the overflowing drain made us hold our breath every time we walked past.
Office workers complained about the effluvium drifting in from the fish market across the street.
The chemistry lab was evacuated after a strange effluvium began seeping from a broken flask.
Residents near the tannery have protested for years about the toxic effluvium released into the river.
He tried to hide the effluvium of stale cigarettes with cologne, but his girlfriend noticed immediately.
tc: Instead of the fresh sea breeze they had expected, the tourists were greeted by the foul ______ of rotting seaweed.
The contrast with 'fresh sea breeze' and the word 'foul' show the blank is an unpleasant smell.
se: A nauseating ______ rose from the garbage dump on hot afternoons.
stench
Both 'effluvium' and 'stench' mean a foul, unpleasant smell.

m: an excessive sense of self-importance, often shown by talking constantly about oneself
x: His egotism is exhausting; every conversation somehow ends up being about his car or his salary.
The manager's egotism prevented him from admitting that the intern's plan was better than his own.
Some biographers attribute the scientist's quarrels with colleagues to sheer egotism rather than principle.
Voters grew tired of the candidate's egotism after he spent most of the debate praising himself.
She finally ended the relationship, unable to bear his egotism and constant need for admiration.
tc: Although she was famous for her modesty, her brother was notorious for his ______, constantly bragging about his achievements.
The contrast with 'modesty' and the phrase 'constantly bragging' show the blank means excessive self-importance.
se: The actor's ______ alienated his co-stars, who were tired of hearing him praise himself.
conceit
Both 'egotism' and 'conceit' mean an inflated opinion of oneself.

m: the act of going out, or a way out; an exit
x: Please don't park in front of the gate, because it blocks the egress for everyone in the building.
Fire inspectors fined the factory because its only means of egress was locked during working hours.
The architecture students had to design a stadium that allowed rapid egress for fifty thousand spectators.
After the crash, the jammed doors blocked the passengers' egress from the train carriage.
Feeling trapped at the awkward dinner party, he looked around for a polite means of egress.
tc: The building has only one entrance, but in an emergency, occupants can use three separate points of ______ to leave quickly.
The contrast with 'entrance' and the phrase 'to leave quickly' show the blank means a way out.
se: Firefighters cleared the stairway to provide a safe ______ for the trapped residents.
exit
Both 'egress' and 'exit' mean a way out of a place.

m: to make someone extremely happy and excited
x: Nothing elates my son more than a surprise trip to the ice-cream shop on a hot afternoon.
The unexpected bonus elated the whole department, and someone ordered pizza for everyone.
The results of the experiment elated the research team, who had waited three years for a breakthrough.
News of the peace agreement elated citizens who had lived through decades of conflict.
Her letter, full of warm words and good news, elated him for days afterward.
tc: Whereas the rejection letter had depressed her, the job offer that arrived a week later seemed to ______ her beyond words.
'Whereas' sets up a contrast with 'depressed', so the blank means to make very happy.
se: A win in the final would ______ the whole country after years of disappointing results.
thrill
Both 'elate' and 'thrill' mean to fill with great joy and excitement.

m: a feeling of great happiness and excitement
x: I felt a rush of elation when I finally found my lost keys under the sofa cushion.
There was elation in the office when we heard that the merger had been approved.
Her elation at passing the final exam quickly gave way to anxiety about job hunting.
Scenes of elation followed the announcement that the missing miners had been found alive.
Their elation at the birth of their first child was mixed with nervousness about the future.
tc: The players' initial ______ after scoring the winning goal turned to dismay when the referee disallowed it.
'Turned to dismay' signals a contrast, so the blank must mean great joy.
se: She could not hide her ______ when she learned that her novel would be published.
joy
Both 'elation' and 'joy' mean intense happiness at good news.

m: to escape or avoid, especially cleverly; also, to fail to be grasped or achieved by someone
x: The name of that actor eludes me, though I can picture his face perfectly.
Despite years of effort, a promotion continued to elude him while younger colleagues moved ahead.
The solution to the equation eluded the class until the teacher suggested a simple substitution.
The suspect managed to elude the police for three weeks by hiding in a friend's village home.
Happiness seemed to elude her, no matter how many goals she achieved.
tc: For decades, the cause of the disease managed to ______ researchers, who kept running into dead ends.
'Kept running into dead ends' shows the cause escaped the researchers' understanding.
se: The thief managed to ______ the guards by slipping out through a service door.
evade
Both 'elude' and 'evade' mean to escape cleverly from someone.

m: abnormally thin and weak, usually from illness or lack of food
x: We found an emaciated kitten under the stairs and nursed it back to health with milk and patience.
After months of skipped meals and late nights at the office, he looked pale and emaciated.
The medical students studied photographs of emaciated patients to learn the signs of severe malnutrition.
Aid workers described emaciated children arriving at the camps after weeks of walking without food.
She barely recognized her emaciated father when she visited him in the hospital after his long illness.
tc: Once a robust and muscular athlete, he had become so ______ during his illness that his clothes hung loosely on his frame.
The contrast with 'robust and muscular' and loosely hanging clothes show the blank means extremely thin.
se: The rescued horses were ______, their ribs clearly visible beneath their dull coats.
gaunt
Both 'emaciated' and 'gaunt' describe bodies made thin and bony by hunger.

m: to involve someone deeply in a conflict or difficult situation
x: I try not to embroil myself in my neighbors' arguments about parking spaces.
The accounting error embroiled our department in a month-long internal investigation.
The professor became embroiled in a bitter dispute with a former student over credit for the research.
The country was soon embroiled in a civil war that lasted nearly a decade.
He didn't want to embroil his family in his legal troubles, so he kept the lawsuit secret.
tc: Hoping to stay neutral, the small nation refused to let its larger neighbors ______ it in their territorial conflict.
'Hoping to stay neutral' shows the nation wanted to avoid being drawn into the conflict.
se: The minister feared the leaked emails would ______ him in a corruption scandal.
entangle
Both 'embroil' and 'entangle' mean to draw someone into a troublesome situation.

m: to correct and improve a text by removing errors
x: Before sending the wedding invitations, my mother asked me to emend the spelling of several guests' names.
The editor emended the report carefully, correcting figures without changing the author's conclusions.
Scholars have emended the ancient manuscript in several places where scribes clearly copied words incorrectly.
The newspaper later emended the online article, correcting the misquoted statistics and adding a clarification.
Before posting his apology to his girlfriend, he asked his sister to emend the clumsiest sentences.
tc: Instead of rewriting the entire essay, the tutor asked her to ______ only the sentences that contained grammatical errors.
'Only the sentences that contained grammatical errors' shows the blank means to correct a text.
se: Before publication, the editor will ______ the manuscript to remove any factual mistakes.
correct
Both 'emend' and 'correct' mean to fix errors in a text.

m: the ability to understand and share another person's feelings
x: A good doctor shows empathy, not just expertise, when explaining a frightening diagnosis to a patient.
Our team leader's empathy makes it easy to admit mistakes without fearing punishment.
Researchers found that reading literary fiction may increase empathy by helping readers imagine other lives.
Social workers need deep empathy for families struggling with poverty, addiction or illness.
What she valued most in her husband was his empathy; he always knew when she needed quiet.
tc: Unlike his cold and indifferent predecessor, the new principal displayed genuine ______ for students facing hardship at home.
The contrast with 'cold and indifferent' shows the blank means understanding others' feelings.
se: Nurses who show ______ toward patients often help them recover with less anxiety.
compassion
Both 'empathy' and 'compassion' describe caring understanding of another's feelings.

m: to declare public approval or support of someone or something
x: My dentist strongly endorses this toothpaste, so I decided to give it a try.
The board endorsed the proposal to let employees work from home two days a week.
The department endorsed her research proposal and agreed to fund the first year of fieldwork.
Several major newspapers have endorsed the reform plan, calling it overdue and sensible.
Her parents eventually endorsed her decision to study abroad, though they worried about the distance.
tc: Although the committee had initially opposed the plan, it voted unanimously to ______ it after the revisions were made.
'Although ... initially opposed' signals a reversal, so the blank means to approve or support.
se: The medical association refused to ______ the diet, saying there was no evidence it worked.
approve
Both 'endorse' and 'approve' mean to give official backing.

m: to give someone a right, especially the right to vote; also, to free from slavery
x: Lowering the voting age would enfranchise millions of teenagers who already work and pay taxes.
The company's new share scheme aims to enfranchise employees by giving them a vote on major decisions.
Our history seminar examined how the reforms of 1918 enfranchised many women for the first time.
Activists are campaigning to enfranchise citizens living abroad, who currently cannot vote in national elections.
She felt truly enfranchised when she cast her first ballot, proud to have a say in her country's future.
tc: Whereas earlier laws had excluded them from elections entirely, the new constitution sought to ______ all adult citizens, regardless of property or gender.
The contrast with 'excluded them from elections' shows the blank means to grant the right to vote.
se: The reform was designed to ______ workers who had long been denied a voice in politics.
empower
Both 'enfranchise' and 'empower' here mean to give people a political voice they previously lacked.

m: to absorb all of someone's attention or interest
x: The puzzle engrossed my nephew so completely that he forgot to eat his lunch.
The quarterly report seemed to engross my boss, who didn't look up when I entered.
Her research on ancient trade routes engrossed her for years, leaving little time for anything else.
The trial engrossed the nation, with millions following every twist on television.
They were so engrossed in conversation that they missed their stop on the train.
tc: The novel was so gripping that it managed to ______ even my restless younger brother, who usually cannot sit still for ten minutes.
'So gripping' and the contrast with a restless reader show the blank means to absorb completely.
se: A good documentary can ______ viewers who have no prior interest in the subject.
captivate
Both 'engross' and 'captivate' mean to hold someone's full attention.

m: to instruct or urge someone firmly to do something; in law, to forbid by court order
x: My mother enjoined us to be home before dark whenever we went out to play cricket.
The memo enjoined all staff to change their passwords before the end of the week.
The supervisor enjoined the students to cite every source, warning that plagiarism would not be tolerated.
The court enjoined the company from dumping waste into the river until the case was decided.
Before he left, his grandfather enjoined him to look after his younger sisters.
tc: The new safety rules will not merely suggest that workers wear helmets; they will ______ every worker to wear one at all times on site.
The contrast with 'not merely suggest' shows the blank means to order firmly.
se: The coach told his assistant to ______ the players to stay off social media before the final.
instruct
Both 'enjoin' and 'instruct' mean to direct someone firmly to do something.

m: the great wickedness or seriousness of a wrong act; also, enormous scale
x: Only years later did he understand the enormity of the lie he had told his parents.
The staff were shocked by the enormity of the manager's betrayal when the embezzlement came to light.
Historians continue to study the enormity of the crimes committed during the war.
The enormity of the massacre horrified the world and led to calls for an international tribunal.
She could not forgive the enormity of his cruelty toward the people who loved him most.
tc: The jury was horrified by the sheer ______ of the crime, which involved deliberately poisoning dozens of innocent people.
'Horrified' and 'deliberately poisoning dozens of innocent people' point to monstrous wickedness.
se: Few people at the time grasped the ______ of the regime's crimes against its own citizens.
wickedness
Both 'enormity' and 'wickedness' convey the extreme evil of the crimes.

m: to settle someone or oneself firmly in a safe, comfortable or secret place
x: On rainy afternoons I like to ensconce myself in the armchair with a cup of tea and a novel.
Within a week of joining, the new director had ensconced herself in the corner office with the best view.
By exam week, she was ensconced in the library from opening time until the guards turned off the lights.
The deposed leader is reportedly ensconced in a heavily guarded villa abroad.
Once the children were ensconced in bed, the couple finally had an hour to talk.
tc: Tired of the noisy party, she decided to ______ herself in a quiet corner of the garden, where no one could find her.
'A quiet corner ... where no one could find her' shows the blank means to settle snugly and securely.
se: After a long day, he likes to ______ himself on the sofa with a bowl of popcorn.
settle
Both 'ensconce' and 'settle' mean to make oneself comfortable in a place.

m: to involve something as a necessary part or consequence
x: Owning a dog entails early morning walks, regardless of the weather.
The new role entails frequent travel to client sites in Chittagong and Sylhet.
A PhD entails years of independent research, often with very little guidance.
Critics warned that the policy would entail higher taxes for middle-income families.
Marriage entails compromise, as both of them discovered during their first year together.
tc: Before accepting the job, ask exactly what the role will ______, because some positions require far more hours than advertised.
The restatement 'require far more hours' shows the blank means to involve as a necessary part.
se: Expanding the factory would ______ hiring at least two hundred new workers.
require
Both 'entail' and 'require' mean to make something necessary.

m: to capture someone's fascinated attention; to charm completely
x: The street magician enthralled a crowd of children outside the shopping mall.
Her presentation enthralled the clients, who asked for a contract before she had finished.
The visiting astronomer enthralled the first-year students with stories about black holes.
The live broadcast of the moon landing enthralled audiences around the world.
He was enthralled by her laughter from the moment they met at a friend's wedding.
tc: Although the audience expected a dull lecture, the speaker's vivid stories managed to ______ them for two full hours.
The contrast with 'a dull lecture' shows the blank means to fascinate.
se: Her storytelling could ______ even the most restless children in the class.
mesmerize
Both 'enthrall' and 'mesmerize' mean to hold someone spellbound.

m: to attract or tempt someone by offering pleasure or advantage
x: The smell of fresh bread enticed us into the little bakery on the corner.
The company tried to entice experienced engineers with higher salaries and flexible hours.
Universities offer scholarships to entice talented students away from rival institutions.
Supermarkets often entice shoppers with discounts on essentials placed near the entrance.
He tried to entice her back with flowers and promises, but she had already moved on.
tc: To ______ reluctant customers back into its stores, the struggling chain offered steep discounts and free delivery.
Offering discounts to 'reluctant customers' shows the blank means to tempt or attract.
se: The resort uses free breakfasts to ______ tourists during the off-season.
lure
Both 'entice' and 'lure' mean to attract someone with an incentive.

m: to pronounce words clearly; also, to state an idea clearly and precisely
x: Please enunciate when you leave voice messages; I can never understand your phone number.
The CEO enunciated the company's new strategy in a short, clear speech.
Our pronunciation teacher made us enunciate every syllable of 'particularly' until we got it right.
The new minister enunciated three principles that would guide her foreign policy.
She enunciated each word slowly so her elderly grandfather could follow the conversation.
tc: Instead of mumbling as he usually did, the student made a real effort to ______ every word during his presentation.
The contrast with 'mumbling' shows the blank means to pronounce clearly.
se: Actors are trained to ______ clearly so that people in the back row can hear every line.
articulate
Both 'enunciate' and 'articulate' mean to pronounce words distinctly.

m: to put poison into something; to fill with bitterness or hatred
x: One careless comment at dinner was enough to envenom the whole family gathering.
Office gossip can envenom relationships between colleagues who once worked well together.
The historian argued that propaganda envenomed public opinion against the minority for decades.
Some hunters once envenomed their arrow tips with toxins taken from frogs and plants.
Years of jealousy had slowly envenomed her feelings toward her sister.
tc: Instead of calming the dispute, his bitter remarks only served to ______ the already hostile relationship between the two families.
'Instead of calming' and 'bitter remarks' show the blank means to fill with bitterness.
se: Endless online insults can ______ public debate until compromise becomes impossible.
poison
Both 'envenom' and 'poison' mean to fill something with hostility and bitterness.

m: a short, witty saying or poem that expresses an idea cleverly
x: My father has an epigram for every occasion, and he quotes them at breakfast whether we want to hear them or not.
The speaker ended her presentation with a sharp epigram that the whole office quoted for weeks.
In our literature class, we studied how Oscar Wilde packed entire philosophies into a single epigram.
The columnist is known for epigrams that sum up complicated political debates in a single line.
He wrote her a witty epigram on a napkin, and she still keeps it in her purse.
tc: Rather than giving a long speech, the comedian summed up his view of marriage in one brief, clever ______ that drew huge laughs.
The contrast with 'a long speech' and 'brief, clever' point to a short witty saying.
se: The essay opens with a memorable ______ about the folly of trying to please everyone.
witticism
Both 'epigram' and 'witticism' mean a short, clever remark.

m: occurring at irregular intervals; also, made up of loosely connected separate parts
x: The internet in our building is episodic at best, working for an hour and then vanishing again.
Progress on the project has been episodic, with bursts of activity followed by weeks of silence.
Critics described the novel as episodic, a series of loosely linked adventures rather than one continuous plot.
Doctors say the patient's symptoms are episodic, flaring up for a few days and then disappearing for months.
Their friendship was episodic, renewed every few years when they happened to live in the same city.
tc: The violence in the region is not constant but ______, erupting suddenly every few months and then subsiding.
'Not constant but' and 'every few months' show the blank means occurring at irregular intervals.
se: His attacks of back pain are ______, occurring a few times a year without warning.
intermittent
Both 'episodic' and 'intermittent' describe something that comes and goes irregularly.

m: calm and even-tempered; (of climate) moderate and free from extremes
x: Our neighbor has such an equable temperament that even my noisy drum practice doesn't bother her.
An equable manager is a blessing during a crisis, when everyone else is panicking.
Geography students learned why coastal regions tend to have more equable climates than inland areas.
The island's equable weather attracts retirees who want to escape harsh winters and scorching summers.
Her equable nature balanced his quick temper, and their friends said they made a perfect pair.
tc: Unlike his volatile brother, who exploded at the smallest provocation, Karim was famously ______ and rarely raised his voice.
The contrast with 'volatile' and 'rarely raised his voice' show the blank means even-tempered.
se: The teacher's ______ temperament helped calm the nervous students before the exam.
calm
Both 'equable' and 'calm' describe a steady, untroubled temperament.

m: straying from the proper course or standards; behaving wrongly
x: I spent twenty minutes searching for an errant sock that had somehow ended up in the kitchen.
HR met privately with the errant employee who had been leaking confidential reports to competitors.
The physicist traced the errant results to a faulty sensor rather than any flaw in the theory.
An errant missile struck a residential area, killing several civilians and prompting an official apology.
Her errant husband finally came home at dawn, full of excuses about where he had been.
tc: Most of the students followed the rules carefully, but a few ______ pupils kept sneaking out of class to visit the canteen.
The contrast with students who 'followed the rules' shows the blank means misbehaving.
se: The coach benched his ______ striker after he skipped training for the third time.
wayward
Both 'errant' and 'wayward' describe someone who strays from proper behavior.

m: wrong; incorrect
x: My map app gave erroneous directions and sent us down a road that ended at a river.
An erroneous invoice was sent to our biggest client, charging them ten times the agreed price.
The paper was retracted after reviewers discovered that its conclusions rested on erroneous data.
The newspaper apologized for publishing an erroneous report that the bridge was unsafe.
She had the erroneous impression that he disliked her, when in fact he was simply shy.
tc: The audit revealed that the figures in last year's report were ______, so the company had to correct its earnings statement.
'Had to correct its earnings statement' shows the figures were wrong.
se: The theory was based on the ______ assumption that all markets behave rationally.
mistaken
Both 'erroneous' and 'mistaken' mean incorrect.

m: former; having been something in the past
x: My erstwhile roommate now lives in Toronto, and we chat online every few weeks.
She was surprised to find her erstwhile rival sitting across the table at the job interview.
The professor's erstwhile students organized a conference in his honor when he retired.
The two countries, erstwhile enemies, have signed a trade agreement that would have seemed impossible decades ago.
He bumped into his erstwhile girlfriend at a café and was surprised by how little he felt.
tc: The two politicians, once close allies, are now bitter enemies; the ______ friends no longer even greet each other in parliament.
'Once close allies' and 'now bitter enemies' show the blank means former.
se: His ______ business partner is now his most aggressive competitor.
former
Both 'erstwhile' and 'former' mean having been something in the past.

m: a feeling of intense happiness and excitement
x: After the long run, I felt a strange euphoria that lasted the rest of the afternoon.
The euphoria of landing the contract faded once we saw how much work it involved.
Psychologists study why winning the lottery produces euphoria that rarely lasts more than a few months.
Euphoria swept through the capital when the national team won its first World Cup match.
In the euphoria of their engagement, they hardly noticed how expensive the wedding would be.
tc: The investors' ______ after the stock's spectacular rise soon gave way to panic when prices collapsed.
'Gave way to panic' signals a contrast, so the blank means intense happiness.
se: A wave of ______ spread through the crowd as the final whistle blew.
elation
Both 'euphoria' and 'elation' mean a surge of intense joy.

m: to reveal or show clearly a feeling, quality or attitude
x: My niece evinced no interest in the expensive toy and played with the box instead.
The candidate evinced a deep knowledge of the industry during her interview.
His thesis evinces a careful reading of the primary sources and a talent for argument.
The minister's speech evinced little sympathy for the families affected by the floods.
Although she evinced no emotion at the funeral, she wept for hours once she was alone.
tc: Despite his attempts to appear calm, his trembling hands seemed to ______ the anxiety he was trying so hard to hide.
The contrast with 'trying so hard to hide' shows the blank means to reveal clearly.
se: The children's drawings ______ a surprising sense of color and composition.
display
Both 'evince' and 'display' mean to show a quality clearly.

m: to praise highly; to raise in rank, power or character
x: My grandmother exalts her late husband as the kindest man who ever lived.
The company newsletter tends to exalt senior managers while ignoring the people who actually do the work.
Romantic poets exalted nature as a source of moral and spiritual truth.
The regime's propaganda exalted the leader as a hero who could do no wrong.
Love can exalt even ordinary moments, turning a cup of tea together into something special.
tc: Rather than criticizing the volunteers' work, the mayor chose to ______ their efforts in a speech that hailed them as heroes.
The contrast with 'criticizing' and 'hailed them as heroes' show the blank means to praise highly.
se: Many cultures ______ motherhood as the noblest of human callings.
glorify
Both 'exalt' and 'glorify' mean to praise something as supremely worthy.

m: open to objection; likely to cause offense or disapproval
x: My neighbor finds almost everything I do exceptionable, from my music to the color of my curtains.
HR asked him to remove several exceptionable jokes from his presentation before the conference.
The journal's reviewers found nothing exceptionable in the methodology and recommended the paper for publication.
Many parents considered the film's violent scenes exceptionable for a family audience.
His exceptionable behavior at the wedding embarrassed his wife and offended her relatives.
tc: The censor removed only the scenes he judged ______, leaving everything inoffensive in the film untouched.
The contrast with 'everything inoffensive' shows the blank means objectionable.
se: The committee found nothing ______ in her proposal and approved it without debate.
objectionable
Both 'exceptionable' and 'objectionable' mean open to objection.

m: to cut out or remove something completely
x: I excised all the sugary snacks from my kitchen cupboard after the doctor's warning.
The lawyer advised us to excise the controversial clause from the contract before signing.
My supervisor told me to excise two chapters from my thesis to meet the word limit.
Surgeons excised the tumor completely, and the patient is expected to make a full recovery.
After the breakup, she excised him from her life, deleting every photo and message.
tc: To make the film suitable for younger audiences, the studio decided to ______ several violent scenes entirely rather than merely shorten them.
'Entirely rather than merely shorten them' shows the blank means to cut out completely.
se: The editor asked the author to ______ the paragraphs that repeated earlier arguments.
remove
Both 'excise' and 'remove' mean to take out the unwanted paragraphs.

m: to make someone feel very happy, lively and excited
x: Driving along the coast with the windows down never fails to exhilarate me.
Closing the biggest deal of the year exhilarated the whole sales team.
Solving a difficult proof can exhilarate a mathematician in a way few other experiences can.
The first images from the space telescope exhilarated scientists and the public alike.
Their first dance together exhilarated her more than she had ever expected.
tc: Though he had expected the roller coaster to terrify him, the ride actually seemed to ______ him, and he queued up again immediately.
The contrast with 'terrify' and queuing again immediately show the blank means to thrill.
se: A brisk walk in the cold morning air can ______ even the sleepiest commuter.
invigorate
Both 'exhilarate' and 'invigorate' mean to make someone feel lively and energized.

m: to drive out an evil spirit; to get rid of something troubling, such as a memory or fear
x: I finally exorcised my fear of dogs by volunteering at an animal shelter.
The new CEO vowed to exorcise the culture of blame that had poisoned the company.
Writing her dissertation helped her exorcise years of doubt about her academic abilities.
The country is still trying to exorcise the ghosts of its violent past.
He traveled alone for a month, hoping to exorcise the memory of his failed marriage.
tc: The priest was called to the old house to ______ the spirit that, according to local legend, haunted its halls.
A priest dealing with a haunting spirit signals the blank means to drive out an evil presence.
se: Therapy helped him ______ the painful memories that had haunted him since childhood.
banish
Both 'exorcise' and 'banish' mean to get rid of something troubling.

m: a person who lives outside their native country
x: The café near our apartment is popular with expatriates who miss proper European bread.
Our firm hires many expatriates, so meetings often switch between three or four languages.
The sociologist interviewed Bangladeshi expatriates in the Gulf about how they send money home.
Expatriates living in the city were advised to register with their embassies after the protests began.
As an expatriate in London, she felt homesick every winter holiday when her family gathered without her.
tc: Having left his homeland at twenty and never returned, he spent his whole adult life as the kind of ______ who feels at home everywhere and nowhere.
'Left his homeland ... and never returned' defines someone living outside their native country.
se: She joined a club for every ______ living in the city who wanted to practice the local language.
expat
Both 'expatriate' and 'expat' mean a person living abroad.

m: to make amends or atone for guilt or wrongdoing
x: He tried to expiate his forgetfulness by cooking his wife an elaborate anniversary dinner.
The company sought to expiate its environmental damage by funding a large river cleanup program.
Medieval Christians often went on long pilgrimages to expiate their sins.
The former official has spent years doing charity work, hoping to expiate the corruption of his past.
No apology could expiate the hurt she felt when she discovered his betrayal.
tc: Haunted by the wrong he had done, the old man devoted his fortune to charity in an effort to ______ his guilt.
'Haunted by the wrong he had done' and giving to charity show the blank means to atone.
se: He confessed everything to the priest, hoping to ______ his guilt before he died.
purge
Both 'expiate' and 'purge' here mean to cleanse oneself of guilt through atonement.

m: to argue earnestly with someone in order to protest against or dissuade them from an action
x: When the waiter tried to charge us for bread we hadn't ordered, my father expostulated with him for several minutes.
Several staff members expostulated with the manager about the new weekend shifts, but she refused to change the schedule.
The professor expostulated with the committee, insisting that cutting the library budget would hurt every department.
Residents expostulated loudly at the town meeting when officials announced that the park would become a car park.
She expostulated with her brother for hours, trying to persuade him not to quit his job so suddenly.
tc: Rather than quietly accepting the unfair decision, Rahim went straight to the principal's office to ______ with him.
'Rather than quietly accepting' signals that he protested earnestly, which is what expostulate means.
se: Several passengers began to ______ with the airline staff when the flight was cancelled without explanation.
remonstrate
Both 'expostulate with' and 'remonstrate with' mean to protest earnestly to someone, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: to remove material considered offensive or unsuitable from a book, film, or other text
x: The publisher expurgated the novel for schools, cutting every scene its editors considered too violent or explicit.
Before the report went to the board, someone had expurgated all references to the failed product launch.
Students were surprised to learn that the version of the play they had studied was heavily expurgated.
Government censors expurgated the documentary, removing interviews that criticised the ruling party's handling of the floods.
My grandmother told us an expurgated version of her youth, leaving out the parts she thought would shock us.
tc: Worried that parents would complain, the editor decided to ______ the anthology, removing every poem that contained crude language.
'removing every poem that contained crude language' defines the blank as cutting out offensive material.
se: The studio agreed to ______ the film for television, removing several violent scenes before broadcast.
censor
Both 'expurgate' and 'censor' mean to remove unsuitable content, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: to make an offence or fault seem less serious by offering partial excuses
x: The judge accepted that extenuating circumstances, including the defendant's serious illness, justified a lighter sentence.
Nothing can extenuate his decision to read his colleague's private emails without permission.
In her essay, the historian argued that poverty and famine partly extenuated the rebels' violent acts.
My boss said that even Dhaka traffic could not extenuate missing an important client meeting twice in one week.
She tried to extenuate her rudeness at dinner by explaining that she had just received bad news.
tc: Although his lawyer pointed to his difficult childhood, the jury felt that nothing could ______ the cruelty of the crime.
'Although' and 'nothing could' show the defence tried, and failed, to make the crime seem less serious, which is what extenuate means.
se: Her lawyer argued that her long history of abuse should ______ her guilt in the eyes of the court.
mitigate
Both 'extenuate' and 'mitigate' mean to make guilt seem less serious, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to destroy or root out something completely
x: The new government vowed to extirpate corruption from every level of the civil service.
Farmers spent years trying to extirpate the invasive weed, which kept returning after every rainy season.
The disease was finally extirpated from the region after a decade-long vaccination campaign.
Some scholars argue that colonial schools tried to extirpate local languages rather than teach alongside them.
Therapy helped him extirpate the deep sense of guilt he had carried since childhood.
tc: The campaign was not meant merely to reduce the pest population but to ______ it entirely from the island.
'not merely to reduce ... but ... entirely' signals total destruction, the meaning of extirpate.
se: Health officials believe they can ______ polio from the country within the next five years.
eradicate
Both 'extirpate' and 'eradicate' mean to wipe out completely, so the sentence means the same.

m: to obtain money or something else from someone by force, threats, or blackmail
x: The gang extorted money from small shopkeepers, threatening to wreck their stalls if they refused to pay.
Police arrested a hacker who tried to extort the company by threatening to leak its customer data.
In the novel, a corrupt landlord extorts rent from tenants who can barely afford to feed their families.
Journalists revealed that local officials had been extorting bribes from truck drivers at checkpoints.
He felt his sister was extorting favours from him by threatening to tell their parents his secret.
tc: Rather than asking politely, the officials used threats of arrest to ______ payments from the street vendors.
'used threats of arrest' shows the money was obtained by force, which is what extort means.
se: The kidnappers hoped to ______ a huge ransom from the businessman's family.
extract
Both 'extort' and 'extract' mean to obtain something by pressure or force, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to estimate or conclude something unknown by extending known facts or trends
x: Based on last year's sales figures, the team extrapolated that demand would double within two years.
You can't extrapolate from one bad experience that all online shopping is unreliable.
Scientists extrapolated future sea levels from a century of tidal measurements along the coast.
In her thesis, she extrapolated broader conclusions about urban migration from interviews with garment workers in Dhaka.
He tends to extrapolate wildly, assuming that one argument means his marriage is falling apart.
tc: Since no one had measured the glacier in recent years, researchers had to ______ its current size from older surveys.
'no one had measured' and 'from older surveys' show they estimated by extending past data, which is extrapolate.
se: It is risky to ______ national voting patterns from the results of a single small town.
infer
Both 'extrapolate' and 'infer' mean to draw a conclusion about the unknown from limited data, so the sentence means the same.

m: to show or feel great joy, especially after a success or victory
x: The whole neighbourhood exulted when Bangladesh beat a much stronger team in the final over.
She exulted in her new freedom after finally moving into a flat of her own.
After months of failed experiments, the researchers exulted when the vaccine finally showed promising results.
Employees exulted at the news that the company had secured its biggest contract ever.
Instead of exulting over his rival's defeat, he quietly walked over and offered to shake her hand.
tc: Far from feeling sorry for his defeated opponent, the champion seemed to ______ in her humiliation.
'Far from feeling sorry' signals the opposite of sympathy, so the blank must mean rejoice triumphantly.
se: Fans poured into the streets to ______ after their team won the championship for the first time in decades.
celebrate
Both 'exult' and 'celebrate' express great joy at a victory here, so the sentence means the same.

m: inclined to form quarrelling groups or to cause dissension within a group
x: The party's factious members spent more time attacking each other than opposing the government.
