A factious board made it almost impossible for the new chief executive to get any decision approved.
Historians describe it as a factious era, when rival families competed bitterly for control of the court.
Our student union became so factious that two separate groups claimed to be the legitimate leadership.
Family gatherings have been factious ever since the argument over my grandfather's property.
tc: Instead of uniting behind the new leader, the ______ committee split into three rival camps within a month.
'Instead of uniting' and 'split into three rival camps' show the committee was prone to dissension.
se: The coalition collapsed because of ______ disputes among its smaller parties.
divisive
Both 'factious' and 'divisive' describe disputes that split a group, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: capable of making mistakes or being wrong
x: Even the best doctors are fallible, so it's wise to get a second opinion before major surgery.
Our manager reminded us that the software is fallible and that every figure should be checked by hand.
Psychologists have shown that human memory is fallible and easily shaped by later experiences.
Eyewitness testimony is far more fallible than most juries assume, according to several recent studies.
Growing up, I realised that my parents were fallible people, not the perfect heroes I once imagined.
tc: Because every human judge is ______, the legal system allows appeals to correct mistakes.
'allows appeals to correct mistakes' implies judges can be wrong, which is what fallible means.
se: The study shows that even experts are ______ when they estimate risks without reliable data.
error-prone
Both 'fallible' and 'error-prone' mean liable to make mistakes, so the sentence means the same.

m: (of land) left unplanted to restore its fertility; by extension, inactive or unproductive
x: The farmer leaves one field fallow each year so that the soil can recover its nutrients.
After the factory closed, the land lay fallow for over a decade before developers bought it.
Many writers go through fallow periods when ideas simply refuse to come, however hard they try.
The research programme has been fallow since its funding was cut three years ago.
Sales had a fallow quarter, but the team expects business to pick up after the holidays.
tc: Instead of planting wheat every season, the farmers let the field lie ______ for a year so the soil could rest.
'Instead of planting' and 'so the soil could rest' indicate land left unplanted, which is fallow.
se: The composer's talent remained ______ for nearly a decade before he wrote his greatest symphony.
dormant
Both 'fallow' and 'dormant' describe a period of inactivity, so the sentence means the same.

m: a deceptive movement or action meant to distract an opponent from one's real intention
x: The boxer threw a feint with his left hand, then landed a powerful punch with his right.
The attack on the northern border turned out to be a feint to draw troops away from the capital.
Her offer to resign was only a feint; she wanted the board to beg her to stay.
At chess club, our coach taught us to recognise a feint before reacting to an obvious threat.
With a clever feint, the striker sent the goalkeeper diving the wrong way.
tc: The general's dramatic advance on the river was merely the ______; his real attack came from the hills.
'merely' and 'his real attack came from the hills' show the advance was a deceptive move.
se: The company's announcement of a price cut was simply a clever ______ to distract rivals from its new product.
ruse
Both 'feint' and 'ruse' mean a deceptive move meant to mislead, so the sentence means the same.

m: to cut down a tree, or to knock or strike someone down
x: Workers felled dozens of old trees to widen the road, angering residents who had enjoyed their shade.
The forestry department plans to fell only diseased trees, leaving the healthy ones standing.
A single punch felled the champion in the opening seconds of the fight.
Researchers are studying how quickly forests recover after loggers fell the largest and oldest trees.
Weeks of overwork finally felled him, and he spent ten days in bed with a high fever.
tc: The builders were told to ______ the ancient oak, but they redesigned the house so the tree could keep standing.
The contrast with 'so the tree could keep standing' shows the order was to cut the tree down.
se: The storm was strong enough to ______ dozens of trees along the river.
topple
Both 'fell' and 'topple' mean to bring something down, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: a state of agitation, excitement, or unrest, especially in society
x: The country was in political ferment after the disputed election results were announced.
The 1960s were a period of intellectual ferment, when students questioned almost every tradition.
News of the merger caused a ferment in the office, with rumours of layoffs spreading by lunchtime.
Her mind was in a ferment the night before her university admission interview.
There is a creative ferment in the city's music scene, with new bands forming every month.
tc: Far from being calm, the capital was in ______ as protesters filled the streets night after night.
'Far from being calm' and protesters filling the streets point to a state of unrest.
se: The sudden resignation of the vice-chancellor threw the university into ______ for weeks.
turmoil
Both 'ferment' and 'turmoil' mean a state of agitation and confusion, so the sentence means the same.

m: (of a problem or bad feeling) to grow worse over time because it is ignored
x: If you don't talk about your anger, it will only fester and come out later in uglier ways.
Complaints about unpaid overtime were allowed to fester until half the team resigned.
The wound festered because he refused to see a doctor for nearly a week.
Sociologists warn that resentment festers in neighbourhoods where young people see no future for themselves.
The rivalry between the two departments has festered for years, mostly over who controls the shared laboratory.
tc: Instead of addressing the dispute openly, the managers let it ______ until it poisoned the entire department.
'Instead of addressing' and 'until it poisoned' show the problem was ignored and grew worse.
se: Unless the government acts quickly, public anger over rising prices will continue to ______.
smoulder
Both 'fester' and 'smoulder' describe anger that persists and grows beneath the surface, so the meaning is the same.

m: using words in a non-literal, metaphorical way to create a vivid effect
x: When my mother said the house was a zoo, she meant it in a figurative sense.
Our literature teacher asked us to underline every figurative expression in the poem.
Lawyers avoid figurative language in contracts, because every phrase may later be read literally.
The minister's promise to 'build a bridge' with the opposition was figurative, though some reporters took it literally.
Telling someone they have a heart of gold is a figurative compliment, not a medical observation.
tc: When he said he was drowning in work, he was being ______, not describing an actual accident at sea.
'not describing an actual accident' shows the statement was non-literal, which is figurative.
se: The word 'storm' is used in a ______ sense in the headline, referring to public outrage rather than weather.
metaphorical
Both 'figurative' and 'metaphorical' mean non-literal, so the sentence means the same.

m: to steal something small or of little value, usually in a sneaky way
x: My little brother used to filch biscuits from the kitchen tin when he thought nobody was watching.
Someone keeps filching pens from my desk, so I've started hiding them in a drawer.
The student was accused of filching ideas from an online essay without acknowledging the source.
Police say pickpockets filched dozens of phones during the crowded festival on Saturday.
She admitted she had filched a few photographs from her ex-boyfriend's album before returning it.
tc: The boy never robbed the shop outright; he would just ______ a chocolate bar now and then when the owner looked away.
The contrast with robbing 'outright' and the small item show the word means to steal something minor sneakily.
se: The waiter was fired after a camera caught him trying to ______ coins from the tip jar.
pilfer
Both 'filch' and 'pilfer' mean to steal small amounts secretly, so the sentence means the same.

m: active or occurring in irregular bursts; not steady or continuous
x: After drinking coffee late at night, I fell into a fitful sleep and woke up every hour.
Progress on the project has been fitful, with long delays followed by sudden bursts of work.
The economy made a fitful recovery, growing one quarter and shrinking the next.
Her attention in the lecture was fitful, drifting between the slides and her phone.
A fitful breeze did little to cool the passengers waiting at the crowded bus stop.
tc: Rather than a steady night's rest, she managed only ______ sleep, waking at every sound from the street.
'Rather than a steady night's rest' and 'waking at every sound' signal sleep that was broken and irregular.
se: Peace talks have made ______ progress, stalling for months and then suddenly moving forward.
intermittent
Both 'fitful' and 'intermittent' describe progress that starts and stops, so the sentence means the same.

m: recklessly bold in a way that ignores obvious danger
x: It was foolhardy to drive through the flooded street when the water was already above the tyres.
Investing your entire savings in one untested startup would be foolhardy, no matter how good the pitch sounds.
The professor warned that it would be foolhardy to submit a thesis without checking it for plagiarism.
Critics called the government's plan to cut flood defences foolhardy, given the forecasts for heavy rain.
My friends thought it foolhardy of me to propose after three months, but we've been happily married for ten years.
tc: Brave but ______, the young climber ignored every storm warning and set off for the summit alone.
'Brave but' and ignoring every warning show boldness that has become reckless.
se: Experts said it would be ______ to cut the health budget in the middle of an epidemic.
reckless
Both 'foolhardy' and 'reckless' mean dangerously careless of consequences, so the sentence means the same.

m: relating to the scientific investigation of crimes, or to courts of law and formal argument
x: Forensic experts found traces of the suspect's DNA on the broken window.
The auditors carried out a forensic examination of the company's accounts after millions went missing.
She is studying forensic science and hopes to work in a police laboratory after graduating.
The debate coach praised his forensic skills, saying he could dismantle any argument in minutes.
My uncle reads the newspaper with forensic attention, hunting for mistakes in the cricket scores.
tc: The case was solved not by a confession but by ______ evidence, including fingerprints and blood samples from the scene.
'fingerprints and blood samples' describe scientific evidence used to investigate crimes, which is forensic.
se: She specialises in ______ medicine, applying medical knowledge to questions raised in courts of law.
legal
'Forensic medicine' and 'legal medicine' are names for the same field, so the sentence means the same.

m: to give up or do without something desirable
x: I decided to forgo dessert tonight because I'm trying to cut down on sugar.
Several directors agreed to forgo their bonuses so that junior staff could keep their jobs.
Many students forgo sleep before exams, even though research shows it hurts their memory.
The government cannot afford to forgo the tax revenue that the new tariff would bring in.
She chose to forgo a scholarship abroad so that she could stay home and care for her sick mother.
tc: To save money for his sister's wedding, he was willing to ______ the new phone he had wanted for months.
'To save money' shows he would give up something he wanted, which is what forgo means.
se: The defendant chose to ______ his right to a jury trial.
waive
Both 'forgo' and 'waive' mean to give up a right voluntarily, so the sentence means the same.

m: to encourage or promote the growth or development of something
x: Good teachers foster curiosity by encouraging students to ask questions rather than memorise answers.
Our team leader tries to foster a culture where people feel safe admitting their mistakes.
Shared festivals can foster a sense of unity among neighbours from very different backgrounds.
The new policy aims to foster innovation by giving small firms easier access to loans.
Reading together every night helped foster a close bond between the father and his daughter.
tc: Rather than stifling dissent, the new director hoped to ______ open debate among the staff.
'Rather than stifling' signals the opposite, so the blank means to encourage.
se: The scholarship programme was designed to ______ talent among students from poor rural families.
nurture
Both 'foster' and 'nurture' mean to help something grow and develop, so the sentence means the same.

m: a noisy, disorderly fight or quarrel
x: A fracas broke out at the wedding when two uncles started arguing over the seating plan.
Security guards had to break up a fracas in the office car park on Friday evening.
Three fans were arrested after a fracas outside the stadium following the match.
The seminar ended in a fracas when two professors began shouting about each other's research.
I was embarrassed to get caught up in a fracas over a parking space at the supermarket.
tc: What began as a polite disagreement over the bill soon turned into a noisy ______, with chairs knocked over and the police called.
'noisy', 'chairs knocked over' and 'police called' describe a rowdy fight, which is a fracas.
se: The ______ outside the nightclub left two men with minor injuries.
brawl
Both 'fracas' and 'brawl' mean a noisy, rough fight, so the sentence means the same.

m: filled with something undesirable, such as danger or difficulty; also, causing anxiety
x: Crossing the border at night was fraught with danger, but the family had no other choice.
Negotiations with the union have been fraught with tension since the pay cuts were announced.
The history of the region is fraught with disputes over land and water.
Relations between the two neighbours became fraught after a quarrel over a fallen tree.
Planning a group holiday with ten friends turned out to be a fraught experience.
tc: Far from being simple, the move to a new country was ______ with paperwork, delays, and unexpected costs.
'Far from being simple' signals a situation full of difficulties, which is fraught.
se: The early days of the expedition were ______ with danger, as storms and disease threatened the crew.
rife
Both 'fraught with' and 'rife with' mean full of something bad, so the sentence means the same.

m: wildly excited, uncontrolled, or frantic
x: Shoppers made a frenzied rush for the doors as soon as the sale began.
The last week before the deadline was frenzied, with everyone in the office working until midnight.
Investors engaged in frenzied buying after rumours of a takeover spread through the market.
She made a frenzied search of her bag before realising the passport was in her pocket.
Students spent the night before the exam in frenzied revision, highlighting almost every line of the textbook.
tc: In contrast to his usual calm manner, the coach paced the sidelines in ______ agitation during the penalty shootout.
'In contrast to his usual calm manner' signals the opposite of calm, so the blank means wildly excited.
se: Reporters crowded around the minister in ______ pursuit of a comment.
frantic
Both 'frenzied' and 'frantic' mean wildly hurried and excited, so the sentence means the same.

m: to waste time, money, or energy on trivial things, little by little (often 'fritter away')
x: I frittered away the whole Saturday scrolling through videos instead of finishing my assignment.
The company frittered its profits on lavish parties instead of investing in new equipment.
Critics say the government has frittered away foreign aid on projects that were never completed.

He regrets frittering away his twenties in a relationship that made neither of them happy.
tc: Instead of saving his bonus as he had promised, he managed to ______ it away on clothes and expensive meals within a week.
'Instead of saving' signals the opposite: wasting money bit by bit on trivial things.
se: Many people ______ their savings on lottery tickets every month.
squander
Both 'fritter' and 'squander' mean to waste money foolishly, so the sentence means the same.

m: a person who persistently annoys or criticises others in order to provoke them into action
x: Socrates called himself a gadfly, stinging the people of Athens into examining their beliefs.
The retired journalist has become a local gadfly, attending every council meeting to question the budget.
At work she was known as a gadfly who challenged every decision the management made.

Online gadflies keep pressing the company to disclose how it handles customer data.
tc: Unpopular but valuable, the senator acted as the ______ of the chamber, constantly needling colleagues to keep their promises.
'constantly needling colleagues' describes someone who provokes others through persistent criticism.
se: Every organisation needs at least one ______ who keeps asking awkward questions about how things are done.
critic
Both 'gadfly' and 'critic' here mean a person who keeps challenging how things are done, so the sentence means the same.

m: to gather or collect something, especially information, support, or praise
x: Her first novel garnered glowing reviews from critics across the country.
The proposal garnered enough support among the staff to be presented to the board.
Researchers garnered data from more than two thousand households for the survey.

Through years of quiet kindness, my grandmother garnered the respect of everyone in the village.
tc: Despite a tiny campaign budget, the young candidate managed to ______ enough votes to win the seat.
'Despite a tiny ... budget' and 'enough votes to win' show she gathered support, which is garner.
se: The documentary is expected to ______ several awards at this year's festival.
collect
Both 'garner' and 'collect' mean to gather or win, so the sentence means the same.

m: polite, refined, and respectable, often in an affected or old-fashioned way
x: They live in a genteel neighbourhood of quiet streets, old trees, and well-kept gardens.
My aunt's genteel manners hide a surprisingly sharp sense of humour.
The novel satirises the genteel society of the period, where appearances mattered more than honesty.

The seaside town has a faded, genteel charm that attracts retired couples looking for a quiet life.
tc: Though the family had lost most of its money, they kept up their ______ lifestyle, serving tea in fine china and speaking in carefully polished tones.
Tea in fine china and 'carefully polished tones' point to refined, respectable manners kept up despite lost wealth.
se: The old hotel retains its ______ air, with string music in the lobby and staff in formal uniforms.
refined
Both 'genteel' and 'refined' describe an elegant, polished atmosphere, so the sentence means the same.

m: (of a seed) to begin to grow; (of an idea) to start to develop
x: These seeds will germinate within a week if you keep the soil warm and moist.

Their friendship slowly germinated over shared lunches during their first year at the company.

'took years' and 'eventually grew into' show the idea began to develop slowly, the meaning of germinate.
se: In this warm, damp soil, the seeds should begin to ______ within a few days.
sprout
Both 'germinate' and 'sprout' mean a seed begins to grow, so the sentence means the same.

Protesters gesticulated at the police line, shouting slogans and waving their placards.

'Unable to speak' and 'point' show she communicated with hand movements, which is gesticulate.

gesture
Both 'gesticulate' and 'gesture' mean to move the hands and arms to communicate, so the sentence means the same.

m: an insulting or mocking remark

barb
Both 'gibe' and 'barb' mean a mocking, cutting remark, so the sentence means the same.

m: in a careful or cautious manner, so as to avoid harm or noise

cautiously
Both 'gingerly' and 'cautiously' mean in a careful way to avoid harm, so the sentence means the same.

'piece by piece' signals gathering information gradually, which is glean.

gather
Both 'glean' and 'gather' mean to pick up information, so the sentence means the same.

m: to stare angrily or sullenly at someone

The student glowered silently as the teacher read out his low exam score to the class.

glare
Both 'glower' and 'glare' mean to stare angrily, so the sentence means the same.

m: an excessive supply of something, more than is needed or wanted

surplus
Both 'glut' and 'surplus' mean more supply than is needed, so the sentence means the same.

'Unlike the soothing tones' signals the opposite, a harsh and irritating sound.

jarring
Both 'grating' and 'jarring' describe an unpleasant, harsh sound, so the sentence means the same.

m: a real or imagined wrong that gives cause for complaint or resentment

'even more reason to complain' shows the blank is a cause for complaint, which is a grievance.
se: Staff members should raise any ______ about pay with the committee.
complaint
Both 'grievance' and 'complaint' mean a matter someone is unhappy about, so the sentence means the same.

m: strangely distorted or ugly in a way that is shocking, absurd, or repulsive

In that rubber mask, he looked so grotesque that my little niece burst into tears.

The distorted features described, a 'huge swollen nose' and 'tiny eyes', signal something bizarrely ugly.
se: The horror film features ______ creatures with twisted limbs and gaping mouths.
hideous
Both 'grotesque' and 'hideous' describe something shockingly ugly, so the sentence means the same.

m: to act in an excessively humble or obedient way to win someone's favour or forgiveness

The minister grovelled before the press, apologising repeatedly for his misleading statement.
Some students grovel to professors for extra marks, but most lecturers find it irritating.
The dog grovelled at my feet after chewing up my new shoes.

'Proud to the end' contrasts with behaving in a humiliatingly humble way, which is grovel.
se: Many junior employees felt they had to ______ to the director to keep their jobs.
kowtow
Both 'grovel to' and 'kowtow to' mean to behave with excessive humility toward someone, so the sentence means the same.

m: given, granted, or allowed reluctantly or resentfully

The opposition gave grudging support to the bill, while warning that it did not go far enough.
The researchers earned grudging respect from sceptics after their results were replicated twice.
tc: Although he had opposed the plan from the start, he eventually gave it his ______ consent.
'Although he had opposed the plan' shows his consent was given reluctantly.
se: The coach gave ______ praise to the referee, admitting that the decision was probably correct.
reluctant
Both 'grudging' and 'reluctant' mean given unwillingly, so the sentence means the same.

m: an outward appearance or form that often hides the true nature of something

Under the guise of a team-building exercise, the company was really assessing whom to promote.
In her essay, the student examined how ancient myths return in new guises in modern films.
Critics argue that the law restricts free speech under the guise of protecting public order.
He visited every evening in the guise of a helpful neighbour, though he really wanted to see my sister.

'hiding his true purpose' shows the blank refers to a false outward appearance.

pretence
Both 'under the guise of' and 'under the pretence of' mean while falsely appearing to do something, so the sentence means the same.

m: lacking any obvious plan, order, or direction; random

Their friendship developed in a haphazard fashion, through chance meetings at the same tea stall.

'Unlike ... methodical' and 'without any order' signal a random, unplanned approach.
se: Inspectors criticised the ______ way in which the hospital stored its medicines.
disorganised
Both 'haphazard' and 'disorganised' mean lacking order or method, so the sentence means the same.

m: to pay careful attention to advice or a warning and act on it
x: I should have heeded my mother's advice to carry an umbrella; the rain soaked me on the way home.

Residents who heeded the evacuation order were safe when the cyclone struck the coast.
She finally heeded her friends' warnings and ended the relationship before it got worse.
tc: Had the captain chosen to ______ the storm warnings instead of ignoring them, the ship would never have sunk.
'instead of ignoring them' signals the opposite, paying attention to the warnings.
se: Drivers who fail to ______ the speed limits in school zones face heavy fines.
obey
Both 'heed' and 'obey' mean to follow a rule or warning, so the sentence means the same.

m: to signal or announce the approach of something

The new contract heralds a period of growth for our small design firm.
Scientists hailed the discovery as heralding a new era in cancer treatment.
The election of a new president heralded sweeping changes in the country's foreign policy.
For my grandmother, the smell of freshly made pitha always heralded the start of winter.
tc: The appearance of the first swallows seemed to ______ the end of the long, cold winter.
The swallows are a sign of what is coming, so the blank means to signal the approach of something.
se: Economists believe the falling interest rates will ______ a recovery in the housing market.
signal
Both 'herald' and 'signal' mean to indicate that something is coming, so the sentence means the same.

m: completely airtight; also, sealed off or isolated from outside influence

Critics say the finance ministry operates in a hermetic bubble, cut off from ordinary people's concerns.
Some academic disciplines have become so hermetic that outsiders cannot understand their journals.
tc: Because even a little air would spoil the samples, the laboratory stored them in ______ jars.
'even a little air would spoil' means the jars must be completely airtight.
se: Medicines must be packed in ______ containers so that humidity cannot reach them.
airtight
Both 'hermetic' and 'airtight' mean sealed so nothing can get in, so the sentence means the same.

m: unwilling to accept new ideas because of rigid devotion to tradition or convention

Younger staff are frustrated by the hidebound management, which rejects every new software proposal.
The university's hidebound curriculum has barely changed since the 1980s.
Reformers accuse the hidebound civil service of blocking even modest changes to outdated rules.
She left her hidebound village to study in the city, where she felt free to think for herself.
tc: Far from being open to innovation, the ______ committee rejected every proposal that departed from long-established practice.
'Far from being open to innovation' signals rigid devotion to tradition.
se: The new director promised to modernise the ______ institution and welcome fresh ideas.
conservative
Both 'hidebound' and 'conservative' describe resistance to change, so the sentence means the same.

m: very old and overused or trite; also, grey or white with age

My manager trotted out the hoary cliché that there is no 'I' in team.
Psychologists have long challenged the hoary myth that geniuses work best in isolation.
Politicians keep reviving the hoary argument that tax cuts will pay for themselves.
With his hoary beard and gentle eyes, her grandfather looked like a figure from an old painting.
tc: Instead of offering a fresh insight, the critic fell back on the same ______ phrases reviewers have been using for a century.
'Instead of offering a fresh insight' and 'using for a century' signal something old and overused.
se: The novel relies on the ______ plot of a poor boy who becomes rich through hard work.
hackneyed
Both 'hoary' and 'hackneyed' mean old and overused, so the sentence means the same.

m: strongly urging or encouraging someone to take a particular course of action
x: The principal's hortatory speech urged every student to read for at least an hour a day.
Our chief executive's emails have a hortatory tone, always urging us to work harder and dream bigger.

My father's letters were mostly hortatory, full of reminders to study hard and pray regularly.
tc: Rather than simply describing the problem, the report is openly ______, repeatedly urging readers to change their habits.
'repeatedly urging readers' defines the blank as encouraging action, which is hortatory.
se: The coach's ______ address before the final inspired the players to give everything they had.
exhortative
Both 'hortatory' and 'exhortative' describe a speech that strongly urges action, so the sentence means the same.

m: unfriendly or aggressive feeling or behaviour; open opposition
x: The new neighbours were puzzled by the hostility they met from the family next door.
There was open hostility between the sales and finance teams after the budget was cut.
The proposal to raise tuition fees met with widespread hostility from students.
Researchers found that online anonymity can increase hostility in comment sections.
She could sense his hostility the moment she walked into the room, though he said nothing.
tc: Instead of the warm welcome they had expected, the visitors were greeted with suspicion and open ______.
'Instead of the warm welcome' signals the opposite, unfriendly feeling.
se: Years of border disputes had left deep ______ between the two nations.
animosity
Both 'hostility' and 'animosity' mean strong unfriendly feeling, so the sentence means the same.

m: extremely happy, peaceful, and picturesque, like an ideal scene
x: We spent an idyllic weekend in a cottage by the lake, with no phones and no traffic.

The brochure described an idyllic campus, but students complained about crowded dormitories and slow internet.
Few office jobs are as idyllic as they look in recruitment videos.
The island's idyllic beaches hide serious problems with plastic pollution, according to a new report.
tc: From a distance the farm looked ______, but up close the fields were flooded and the barn was falling apart.
'but up close' contrasts the grim reality with a perfectly peaceful, picturesque appearance.
se: She often remembers her ______ childhood on the coast, spent swimming and reading under the trees.
blissful
Both 'idyllic' and 'blissful' describe a perfectly happy time, so the sentence means the same.
